A new site design and wordmark for Hyperallergic’s next era.

From the start in 2009, Hyperallergic has been kicking at the doors of the art world status quo, challenging assumptions about what is worthy of investigation and investment, and the supposed neutrality of those decisions. Today, 17 years later, we are no longer a young upstart blogazine but a daily source of trusted news, reviews, and opinions for millions in the art community.

We’ve transformed our strategy for sustainable revenue and evolved our editorial approach several times over the years to meet the unique challenges of each internet era. While so many of our peers have disappeared, we’ve survived as an independent media company throughout it all. It’s never been easy, but it’s always been worth it.

As we enter yet another new era, with social media becoming ever more toxic and AI seemingly overtaking every aspect of our lives, we want to refocus ourselves on being the best place for our community to gather. For all of us to learn, to grow, to laugh, and to feel connected to each other.
Today, we are excited to introduce the next transformation of this site, with a whole new look, a dynamic homepage, and the third version of our wordmark.

It’s clear that the insistent and demanding bright cyan of the site is no longer needed, and it is time for Hyperallergic to look more like the authoritative publication it has now become. (And for those who always loved the blue, you’ll see it re-emerge in spots over time.)

The Brooklyn-based design cooperative, Partner & Partners , has created a warm and inviting new look and organizational framework that fits our evolving output and will help us expand into the future.

Our new wordmark is drawn from Hyperallergic TwoOneFive, a new custom typeface made for us by Commercial Type . It is a grotesque that harkens back to the days of the Bauhaus and is full of unique quirks that push it into the future. Letting go of the uppercase blue condensed wordmark, the new logotype leans towards classic while remaining full of energy. The high bar of the capital H leads us into the lowercase title; this itself is a marker that we no longer need the screech of all caps.

Hyperallergic is by and for art-focused readers and writers, so the site has to encourage both. Spectator, a new serif typeface also from Commercial Type, brings a richness and warmth to the screen. Compared with more traditional typefaces, Spectator is clean with soft corners and is bolder all around, encouraging the eye to move from line to line.
We’re foregrounding our authors' names to highlight our team and many guest contributors, and the effort and care that goes into all the work you see on the site.

With a vast archive of tens of thousands of posts from thousands of writers and spanning nearly two decades, we’ve built a whole new search experience and a reorganized tagging system to allow readers to discover connections between writers, themes, and subjects that might otherwise get lost.
This new site design allows for more diversity in article layouts and lets us give prominence on our homepage to stories we think deserve more of your attention.

But ultimately, one of the design’s strongest elements is its ability to get out of the way. While vastly improving the user experience, it rarely draws attention to itself, instead allowing the focus to be on the content of the site, rather than the frame.

This redesign is just one part of a bigger shift. You may have noticed we now ask you to sign in to a free account to read most articles. That’s because we want to build a closer relationship with our readers and a more sustainable platform to publish the news, reviews, and commentary that keep you engaged, informed, inspired, and entertained. All while speaking truth and challenging the status quo in the art world.

Open-source tools like Ghost allow us to remain insulated from the whims of platforms funded by venture capital, with sky-high investments and unrealistic valuations that inevitably force them to pivot or shut down. Tools like these have allowed us to keep publishing without fear for the past 17 years and invest in what matters most: connecting our writers to our readers.
When a Ceramics Studio Becomes a Stage
In Matthew Lutz-Kinoy’s "The Mud Room," the gallery acts as a site of production.

At the center of Matthew Lutz-Kinoy’s The Mud Room, a raised platform containing a large kiln, two ceramicists’ alcoves, and buckets of clay acts as a stage. The first play explored the intersections of farming, the kiln, and the emergence of the artspeak-adjacent locavore chef.

While Amant’s on-site restaurant served its own fare of purple radicchio and Block Island anchovies to the audience, seated in a perimeter around the action, the protagonist, Marin — a failed curator turned restaurateur in rural France — droned on about her hopes for a publisher to appreciate her culinary foray as a radical “linguistic concept” and “rhizomatic” project.

Meanwhile, four paintings surrounding the stage ridicule the posturing of the art-world types in the first performance. Directly opposite the entrance, monstrous figures swallow one another’s entrails and phallic appendages while exchanging the fruits of their labor: ceramics. To the right, Lutz-Kinoy’s “The Rose Garden” (2026) combines an homage to Keith Haring’s “Crack Is Wack” (1986) with silhouettes reminiscent of Aaron Douglas’s New Deal-era public commissions. Opposite it, another painting pays tribute to Douglas, as well as to Philip Guston and Reuben Kadish’s restored “The Struggle Against War and Fascism” (1934–35).

Visionary curator and mixed-media artist Tamlin Blake was found murdered in her Riebeek West home in South Africa on Sunday, November 22, at age 51.

As the chief curator at Spier Arts Trust, a Cape Town-based nonprofit dedicated to connecting South African artists with larger audiences and collectors, Blake conceived programs to help artists advance their careers. How Alison Luchs, the “Museum Rizzler,” Became Gen Z’s Goated Art Historian
The National Gallery of Art's 78-year-old Early European sculpture curator and designated baddie gives us the deets on how she became a social media superstar overnight.

Lock in, chat, because we're about to drop some major lore on a new internet personality who puts every influencer to shame. During a recent kiki with Hyperallergic , designated baddie Alison Luchs, a curator of Early European sculpture and Deputy Head of Sculpture and Decorative Arts at the National Gallery of Art (NGA) in Washington, DC, gave us the deets on how she became a social media superstar overnight by using Gen Z lingo in an educational video series about collection objects.

This has been a goated year for Luchs, who has worked with the NGA for over four decades. Now known as the “Museum Rizzler,” the 78-year-old curator has garnered millions of views on her videos translating art and anthropological history into accessible stories for younger generations. Connecting centuries-old artifacts and mythologies to contemporary pop culture with terms like “chopped,” “sigma,” “aura points,” “gagged,” “popping off,” “chud,” and so on, Luchs has drawn a reverent audience that gassed her up so much she was honored with two Webby Awards .

Luchs and NGA's head of marketing and communications, Sydni Myers, broke down the making of the Museum Rizzler, the virtual and in-person impacts of the series' instant virality, and the behind-the-scenes process that goes into each video. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

What’s the Right Way to Honor Ana Mendieta?
Should a planned MoMA survey of the artist discuss her gruesome death, or should it privilege her art?

I hate the rain, but I recognize the poetic justice of a tarnished colonial commemoration through Thursday’s forecasted washout. In the era of fast fashion, data centers, and big agriculture, the world’s most precious resource will (hopefully) nourish the land while disturbing those who exploit it. It’s hard to be mad at that, even if the sensation of wet socks squelching in soaked shoes makes me want to jump out of my own skin and start orbiting earth.

The Museum of Modern Art’s experimental arm, MoMA PS1, just announced that it’s hosting a group exhibition on Latin American art and fashion next spring. Malvestir will broach a variety of topics, including reclaiming Indigenous cosmologies and craftsmanship from the commoditized grip of Western appropriation, apparel’s role in counterculture and empowering the marginalized, and the creative, function-forward reuse of the incalculable textile waste that the United States unceremoniously dumps onto Central and South America.

Also on the topic of land and its resources, MoMA announced its forthcoming Ana Mendieta retrospective opening in late 2027, which will focus on the late artist’s material expansion, cross-cultural infusions, and boundary-shattering interdisciplinary process in chronological fashion. Like the major exhibition that’s still on at the Tate Modern, MoMA’s retrospective also veers away from discussing Mendieta’s untimely death and the speculation surrounding it. It’s an ongoing dilemma — allowing Mendieta’s work to be displayed and contextualized outside of the implications of her tragically punctuated life is interpreted by some as prioritizing the artist’s agency and impact and message, while others regard it as a deliberate erasure of part of her story, considering the subject matter she tackled.
I don’t know what the right call is.

The retrospective will also unpack Mendieta’s provocative early performance art, including the confrontational interventions she staged as a reaction to the rape and murder of a fellow University of Iowa student, Sarah Ann Ottens, in 1973. The world has changed beyond recognition in the last 50 years, but the needle has merely twitched in regard to addressing and remedying misogyny and violence against women in contemporary society, as the last few months (if not the decade) would indicate. At the International Center of Photography, Spanish artist Laia Abril combs through the historic, systemic, and interpersonal bolsters of rape culture. Abril’s Black-and-white photos document the clothes worn by survivors of all ages at the time of their assault, the material culture codifying assault and kidnapping as colonial and war-related “conquests,” and other astonishingly overt examples of subjugation and dehumanization as they simultaneously evolve in contemporaneity while channeling centuries of mistreatment.

This is some heavy stuff to ruminate on, but the much-needed dead air between marquee auctions and Miami Art Week offers some breathing room away from the market frivolity obscuring the true power of art. I hope the rain and the long weekend will give me a nice blank slate to meditate on.
Have a safe and healthy holiday season, everyone. Travel safely, and take care.

After shuttering in 2007 to undergo a €6.2 million ($6.8 million) renovation, the Old Acropolis Museum reopened yesterday, November 23, in Athens, Greece.

Built in 1874 as Greece's first purpose-built museum, the refurbished institution is outfitted with digital displays and live conservation areas open to public view, according to the Associated Press .

The stone-clad museum is situated southeast of the Parthenon, offering an unrivaled view of the preeminent monument. When the museum closed in 2007, it was converted into an administrative building, while its previous holdings were moved to the New Acropolis Museum , which had been established over a century after its older counterpart.
Performance Artists Who Put Their Bodies on the Line
With its emphasis on embodied experience, performance provides a necessary counteraction to cheap political theater and the dissociation and isolation of our fractured, digitized society.

Why do a performance art festival tied to national political issues foregrounded in the midterm election? In a moment when cultural and political institutions are retreating from provocative stances into solipsism and leisure, and government funding for the arts is but one of the many areas being slashed by right-wing political operatives, it might seem like the opposite of common sense to be opening a museum dedicated to presenting and preserving the least marketable and most controversial aspect of contemporary art: performance.

Instead, the opening of the Performance Art Museum in Los Angeles, the first US museum dedicated to this ephemeral medium, has been met with tremendous support. This is because performance, with its emphasis on embodied experience, altered psychological states, challenging social dynamics, and the absurd, provides a necessary counteraction to the dissociation and isolation of our fractured and digitized society.

Since the early 20th century, artists have deployed performance as a medium for political commentary. Dada artists in Zurich and Berlin played with the emptiness of political speech in war-torn Europe while Mavo artists in Meiji Japan used cross-dressing and shock value to mock the nation’s entanglement in colonial wars in China and Russia. With the midterm elections unfolding against a backdrop of unrelenting genocide, the embodied stakes of performance serve to sharpen its critique. The influencer news cycle has shortened our attention spans from 24 hours, already a significant shift manifested via CNN and Headline News during the Gulf War and honed during 9/11, to a far shorter, dopamine-fueled spike of rage-and-crash out that can be repeated multiple times in a single day. The war on Gaza has both numbed us to atrocities in our feed, and disconnected us from our own bodies and communities as we quietly absorb the unspoken impacts of the violence that we outsource.

In the 1960s and 1970s, this absorbed violence erupted in the work of the Actionist artists including Hermann Nitsch , Rudolf Schwarzkogler, Valie Export , and Gina Pane. High Performance magazine was the first outlet to cover these artists in the United States and an emerging generation of artists informed by them, including Chris Burden and Kim Jones, who took significant physical risks in performances that openly critiqued the prolonged war in Vietnam. At the same time, the sexual revolution was underway and artists including Barbara T. Smith, Suzanne Lacy, and Johanna Went put their bodies on the line accordingly, looking at the pleasures and the risks of erotic life from feminist perspectives. Artist and poet Sue Dakin, the publisher of High Performance , ran a campaign for president as an independent candidate in 1984.

These histories inform the two-year Performance Art Museum initiative, High Performance: A 2 Year Conference for which my colleague Leon J. Hilton and I organized Public Spirits: A Performance Art Festival on October 23, 2026.

Emerging out of these practices and the magazine’s coverage of them, the 1980 Public Spirit festival, organized by the Highland Art Agents (including Paul McCarthy, Barbara T. Smith, Chip Chapman, John Duncan, and High Performance editor Linda Frye Burnham) through LACE, LA’s longest-running experimental art space, featured 60 artists and over 100 performances over two weeks in May and four weeks in October. Many of the works were staged in rooms at the American Hotel and were intimate in scale. Some, like the Feminist Art Workers’ Bill of Rights advocating for the ill-fated Equal Rights Amendment or The Waitresses’ Coffee Cauldron honoring women in service work, were explicitly political in nature. Many followed participant Allan Kaprow’s model for Happenings, being unscripted actions that turned absurd, comedic, or disturbing. Some involved singing, dancing, or traditional theatrical presentations — including a musical by Carole Caroompas about unreliable exes, a dance number by Nancy Buchanan about covert US intervention in Central America, and a play by Alexis Smith and Heidi Hardin titled “Stardust” that featured an unknown Whoopi Goldberg. The photographer never asked to be born into her parents’ successful art and social lives. Her observations about the latter taint the former, and the result is a pervasively superficial…

The central, perplexing conundrum of the “nepo baby” arguably is this: Does the nepo baby possess talent, and is that talent to any degree independent of the considerable social and financial benefits bestowed upon said nepo baby from birth?

In I Regret I Am Able To Attend: A Life Among Artists (2026), photographer Jessica Craig-Martin, daughter of Irish painter Michael Craig-Martin and Jan Hashey (sometime artist but more successful real estate broker), chooses to quote Paul Auster, a giant of 20th-century American literature, in the introduction to her memoir: “Stories only happen to those who tell them.” The quote is meant to underline her insistence that this book is not a memoir, nor a narrative, only a collection of tales, thereby excusing any requirement for fact-checking or referencing, despite it very clearly being an exhaustive narrative of her life and that of her parents. The choice of quote also underlines the book’s tone: These stories are remarkable because of who they happened to, regardless of whether they are actually interesting or not. And that is how celebrity — the condition of being famous simply for being famous — works.

Craig-Martin weaves her parents’ experiences into her own, with several chapters throughout returning entirely to their lives as side quests, detailing which houses they bought and how they were decorated and who their friends were and how much money they earned, variously bouncing between London and New York and dragging the author between them. Where there is an excess of material and social detail, however — the name-dropping comes in lists — there is a mystifying sense of disengagement or interest in her parents’ own artistic enterprises. We are told what Michael did and what accolades he received but nothing substantial about Craig-Martin’s emotional or intellectual connection to his work. Her tonal detachment at attending, say, the first-ever performance of Gilbert George’s “ The Singing Sculpture ” (1969) cleaves a divide between her, dragged to the debut as par for the course of a daughter of a well-connected artist, and us, mortals who would have killed to witness this legendary moment in art history. What is present from the start is a keen eye for fashion, even if it is delivered via observations about how her mother was painfully more chic than the other parents picking their kids up from school.

Visa has a new look by Base Design. So what’s actually changed?
The payment giant has had its first significant refresh since 2021, yet its famous wordmark hasn’t changed. So what’s new? And how far can a studio nudge a legendary brand that billions of…

The payment giant has had its first significant refresh since 2021, yet its famous wordmark hasn’t changed. So what’s new? And how far can a studio nudge a legendary brand that billions of people already know by heart? We find out.

It’s one of those logos you see pretty much every day but don’t think much about. Perhaps it’s because it means we’re about to spend some hard-earned cash. Or maybe we just don’t care. But you’ll know the Visa logo when it’s mentioned. It’ll flash up in your head as familiar as the faces of the people you love. So when you look at Base Design’s new identity for the brand, can you spot the difference?

That’s what I find most fascinating about a job like this. When a logo is so famous and features on a zillion cards and on shop doors all over the world, how much room does a design studio really have to play with? You certainly can’t rip it up and you can barely touch it. Yet Visa wanted to feel fresh for a new generation of spenders, so something had to give.

“When you’re working with a brand as iconic as Visa, the challenge isn’t recognition. It’s relevance,” says Min Lew, managing partner and executive creative director at Base Design. “Our ambition was to build on Visa’s extraordinary equity while giving it a renewed sense of energy and expression, one that feels as relevant to the net generation as it does to the generations who have grown up with it.”

So what has changed? Three things, apparently. Base worked on the overhaul with Visa’s in-house studio to create a new symbol, a graphic device and a typeface. What’s interesting is that every one of them is borrowed from something Visa already owned.

The symbol, for example, is a ‘V’ lifted straight from the wordmark and it still has the little wingtip on its corner. This will begin to appear on some cards and across Visa’s digital assets, where four letters can prove to be a squeeze. Base stresses that it doesn’t replace the wordmark we all know and always appears alongside it. What it has ditched is the blue, white and yellow flag symbol that was introduced in 2021.

The typeface, Visa Sans, was created by Displaay Type Foundry and takes inspiration from the wordmark, too. It’s geometric for consistency at every scale, and its rounded forms hope to warm things up.

Then there’s the “hero graphic device”, a phrase coined by Base. It’s a bar, derived from the bands of the original Visa logo. Which sets us up nicely for a history lesson: when Bank of America launched BankAmericard in 1958, the name sat between a blue band and a gold one, and those bands stayed put when the card became Visa in 1976. They disappeared in the mid-2000s, leaving the wordmark to breathe on its own. Now those bands are back, sort of, as a single bar that can hold the wordmark, ‘V’ symbol or a message.

It’s only a tiny change but graphic designers will see it as the boldest. The wordmark can now be cropped at the bar’s right-hand edge, so ‘Visa’ runs off the side as if it’s pulling everything forward. It’s what Kellogg’s has done for ages, showing just a hint of the full wordmark and yet we all know exactly what it is.

“The most powerful identities are built on simple ideas with extraordinary depth,” adds Lew. “More than a framing device, the hero graphic device brings movement, direction, and possibility to the identity. This simple gesture becomes the foundation for a visual language that can be energetic at a global sporting event, confident and bold in a B2B environment, or vibrant and elevated for affluent audiences. Each expression is distinct, yet unmistakably Visa.”
How far is far enough, though?

It’s worth taking notes from Visa’s last brand refresh. In 2021, Mucho redrew the wordmark, brightened the blue and then split the tricolour symbol off as an asset in its own right. Five years on and that symbol is being retired, yes, but Mucho’s wordmark has become the source material for everything else.
On asked how far it could go, Base seems to have said, backwards. It’s dipped into the archive and found something meaningful in the four letters themselves.

Booms & Shakes: who’s moved where in November, from Neville Brody to Uber’s creative leader
Neville Brody has a new job. So does Uber’s creative leader who’s joined a legal AI firm, of all places. And the independents are having a field day. Here’s what’s been happening this month…

Neville Brody has a new job. So does Uber’s creative leader who’s joined a legal AI firm, of all places. And the independents are having a field day. Here’s what’s been happening this month across the creative industry.
It’s not every day that one of the most influential graphic designers of the last five decades changes jobs, but Neville Brody has done just that, making November quite the surprise.

Reading through everything else this month, it’s clear design is playing a much bigger role across the board. Apple’s agency, TBWA\Media Arts Lab, has never had a global chief design officer before, and now it does. Brody says he’s moved to Toaster so that brand thinking is right there from the beginning, not some kind of afterthought. Then there’s Legora, a legal AI firm that poached someone from Uber. Landor and Design Bridge have also been busy, changing their leadership within a month of each other. And gosh, TBWA\Media Arts Lab kept popping up again and again – it’s clearly a place where the best people are trained.

Another thing that stood out was AI, which gets a mention in almost every press release we read. Mostly it’s about why human judgment matters more than ever. Meanwhile, the wins belong to the independents this month. We’ve got news of an agency less than a year old now leading creative for Hargreaves Lansdown and a whole load of news from the smaller studios, too. November, you’ve been brilliant. Here’s why.
Neville Brody takes the creative chair at Toaster

The man behind The Face has left Brody Associates to become creative chair at Toaster , the creative product marketing agency founded in 2010 by former Google creatives. It formalises a long relationship, as he was already on the board as an adviser. In his new role, he’ll work across clients and set up a lab exploring where creative meets tech, with Toaster Labs launching on his arrival. He isn’t starry-eyed about AI. It can speed up complex, repetitive work, he says, but “it also risks creating a spiral of homogenisation”.
TBWA\Media Arts Lab names its first global chief design officer

James Taylor has been promoted from global head of design at Apple’s dedicated agency , off the back of the Cannes Lions Grand Prix-winning Apple TV rebrand and the new Apple Music identity (which we wrote about recently, and which involved using sound to move liquid ). Taylor, a former creative director at Jones Knowles Ritchie, joined in 2021 and has since put designers alongside writers and art directors because “design is a way of finding the idea as much as expressing it,” he says.
Landor takes from Interbrand and JKR to boost its leadership team

There are three senior arrivals and one new role at Landor this month. Oliver Maltby joins from Interbrand New York as global executive creative director, with LEGO, the Sydney Opera House and Ford Racing all in his portfolio. Andrew Miller, formerly chief growth officer at Interbrand, joins from BeenThereDoneThat as global executive strategy director. Carolyn Griffin joins from JKR as executive strategy director, bringing healthcare expertise.
Meanwhile, Marc Lamothe relocates from Hong Kong to take a newly created role leading applied AI and brand intelligence. “The most valuable brands are unmistakable,” Maltby says.
Astronaut Monastery takes one back from Landor

Jordan Taylor, a former creative director at Landor, has moved to independent creative studio Astronaut Monastery as head of design. The studio, founded by Cody Min, works with clients across venture, consumer goods, fashion, art and technology.
Design Bridge and Partners appoints Ann Higgins as global president

Ann Higgins adds the role to her existing job as chief client officer for WPP Brand & Design, which she joined earlier this year from Ogilvy Consulting, where she was EMEA CEO. She’ll work with global and regional leadership to champion the agency’s creative culture and strengthen client relationships. It lands in the agency’s 40th year, and amid a wider reshaping of WPP’s brand and design businesses under global CEO Jane Geraghty.

The Florida studio has created a full brand universe for Vollie, a new haircare company on a mission to “Bottle the salon”.

Salon-quality haircare at home sounds fantastic, doesn’t it? For precisely this reason, though, the number of competitors in this space is enormous. So if you’re launching a new brand, how do you convince people you’re worth investing in? That was the challenge facing Yungbld , an independent, female-owned branding and design studio based in Florida, when its founder was building a haircare startup called Vollie.
Yungbld set out to strike a perfect balance between premium and approachable. No mean feat, and they didn’t stop at a logo and a label.

“The founder came to us with an idea to ‘bottle the salon’ and a formula,” explains Laura Miller, founder and creative chief at Yungblud. “And we built the brand into a full visual universe spanning strategy, identity, packaging, product design, CGI and animation, launch imagery, and an immersive digital experience at vollieverse.com.”

The new brand evolved from a clever tagline: ‘Handle With Haircare’. It’s a neat play on the warning you’d typically see on fragile parcels, and beautifully sets up the tension the brand is built on. Namely, that haircare products are meant to be gentle by design, but powerful in performance.

“We developed the entire experience around the idea ‘Handle With Haircare’, using sleek forms, dreamy textures, soft shadows and a restrained palette to create something that feels both premium and emotionally warm,” says Laura.
That restraint shows most clearly in the colour system. Yungbld has limited the palette to three pastels—candy pink, lilac, and pale periwinkle—anchored by black and a cool grey.
In one of the launch images, the studio depicts this literally as a Pantone swatch strip held over a model’s face, listing 230 C, 2635 C, 2120 C, Black 7 C and Cool Gray 2 C.

To balance all that softness, the typography is based around heavy, chunky, all-caps sans-serif. Black and bold, it’s the perfect choice for the wordmark, a series of one-word campaign posters (Oiled, Glossed, Brushed, Stacked) and crossheads on the website.
On launch, Vollie’s range features three products: Super Soft, a softening and strengthening hair mask; Dream Defender, a prepare-and-protect hair oil; and So Glazed, a resurfacing gloss.
Each gets its own pastel. All three share a cylindrical bottle with a ribbed cap and a pointed nozzle. The wordmark is moulded into the bottle in relief rather than printed.
Yungbld also designed products beyond the bottles, including a wide-tooth comb with the wordmark running down its spine and clear tinted zip pouches that show the bottles inside.

The CGI work leans into that idea of ‘dreamy textures’, with generous use of pastel soft gradients. The live-action imagery, though, takes a different route: warm, grainy and purposely lo-fi; again, achieving a lovely visual balance.
Overall, this brand launch impressed me by its heady combination of confidence and scale.

It would have been tempting to launch Vollie with a brief Instagram teaser, and a nice bottle and not much else. Instead, Yungbld has come out guns blazing, crafting a full brand world where packaging, product, motion, photography, and web all benefit from a shared language.
It’s soft where it needs to be and bold where it counts… just like the haircare products themselves.
Atmospheric computer game invites you to unwind in the world of Brutalist architecture
Tiny Brutalism is a novel mismatch of city-building computer games and imposing, concrete structures. Unless you’ve been living under a rock, you can’t have missed that this week has been a…
Tiny Brutalism is a novel mismatch of city-building computer games and imposing, concrete structures.

Unless you’ve been living under a rock, you can’t have missed that this week has been a big one for computer games. But while most people are having fun unblocking their crazy ex’s sink in Grand Theft Auto 6, Tiny Brutalism invites you to unwind in the world of imposing architecture that emerged in the United Kingdom in the post-war years.

Due to be released on Steam soon, Tiny Brutalism is the creation of Mati Ernst from Jimjum Studios. Teased in a tweet that has since gone viral , Mati explains that he took the cosy, cottagecore aesthetics of the 2024 city-building game Tiny Glade and reimagined them with a Brutalist twist. Hence the name.

Playing with Brutalism may sound like a peculiar way to unwind, but upon watching the video, its appeal is obvious. Unlike the barrage of lights and sounds some games rely on, Tiny Brutalism pares things back with black-and-white graphics, atmospheric rain sounds, and a tranquil soundtrack.

“Tiny Brutalism is a relaxing diorama building game based on brutalist architecture,” the game’s Steam page explains. “Create strange monuments, impossible structures, concrete towers, or just a really big wall. Then explore inside them in first person. There’s no goal and no right way to build. Make whatever you feel like making.”

So far, the game is still in the demo phase. However, it’s packed with features that show plenty of promise. These include relaxing diorama building, where players can construct Brutalist architecture at their own pace, with no deadline pressure.

As if that wasn’t enough, you can also explore your creations in first-person. But perhaps the most appealing aspect of the game is its complete sense of creative freedom. There’s no overarching goal to Tiny Brutalism, except to help you feel at ease, so you don’t have to worry about stressful resource management.

Tiny Brutalism builds on Jimjum’s impressive reputation as an award-winning studio that makes games all about kindness and co-operation. Its previous release, Community: Build Together, facilitated over one million acts of kindness, and it hopes that Tiny Brutalism will bring people together in a similar way with its bleak but strangely playful world.

Luckily, it seems to have appealed to audiences. In response to Mati’s viral tweet, social media users have praised the dark atmosphere, moody lighting, and complexity of building options. “Tiny Glade with Brutalist proportions is such a good mismatch,” said one user. “The hard edges make the builder feel like a tiny architectural toy.” Meanwhile, another added: “Making a good-looking brutalist anything is very hard, but as an appreciator of brutalist, I love it.”
At time of writing, there’s no official release date for the completed game, but if the video has whetted your appetite, then the demo is available to play on Steam now .

Amsterdam agency Verve finds a refreshingly different way to brand Helsinki startup Zero.
Here’s a riddle for you. When is a flight delay actually a good thing?
When it gives you a bizarre but brilliant slice of inspiration for an identity project, of course.

This is exactly what went down when Amsterdam creative agency Verve flew to Helsinki to throw around some ideas with the founders of AI startup Zero. Stuck in the city with time to kill, the Verve team wandered into a small museum, the Amos Rex , which is known for its subterranean galleries topped by undulating, dome-like skylights. As part of its Generation 2026 exhibition, there was a piece by ceramic artist [Johan Urrutia], depicting a typewriter that had turned to stone.
“Extinct office technology: that was the story,” says creative director Walewijn den Boer. And this simple idea became the key to the visual identity they created for Zero.
“The old tools are turning to stone, and Zero is bringing the new ones,” says Walewijn. “The more you live an assignment, the richer your associations get, and the more personal the work becomes.”

The new identity dramatises this notion by treating Zero’s arrival as an extinction event. Legacy CRM is presented as a Stone Age world of cracked earth and fossilised tools. Zero is something so advanced it barely reads as technology at all. And the line “Make CRM history” ties everything together.
CRM, which stands for Customer Relationship Management, is one of the oldest categories in business software and has long been dominated by two huge companies: Salesforce and HubSpot.

“What I love about Zero is that it’s a story of evolution,” says strategy director Eveline Koppejan. “Salesforce and HubSpot were once the challengers kicking against what came before and now, decades later, they’re the incumbents, and a new generation is ready to kick back. The brand gives Zero the conviction to say that out loud.”

Zero isn’t only up against the big names, though. A wave of AI-native rivals is springing up, and most share the same dark-mode, crypto-adjacent startup look. To separate Zero, Verve offered founders several different visual territories, from an anti-brand rebellion to a safer lifestyle-tech route, but the extinction event won out.

“Compared with the other AI-native players, the product gap is slim, because everybody copies each other’s features and that’s easy to do now,” says Walewijn. “When the product becomes a chat interface, there’s no feature or screenshot left to hide behind. Brand is what differentiates.”

Visually, they’ve really taken the idea and run with it. A hand-illustrated Neolithic landscape by Verve illustrator Kevin Lebon is full of cracked earth, drifting monoliths and fossilised tools. Cave drawings show the age-old frustrations of selling with legacy CRM.

References range from the dawn-of-man opening of the movie 2001: A Space Odyssey (1969) to the ship hovering over the desert in Arrival (2016). Zero’s brand identity sits over the top, sleek and precise, showing how each of those problems gets solved.

Verve also created a brand character called Zorb: a gleaming, all-knowing space object with a small dot-matrix face it uses to emote. It makes its moods known through force fields made from hand-drawn cave inscriptions.

Previously, Zero was known for its signature yellow, which came about after the founders originally came up with the startup’s name in a restaurant with yellow tables. Nobody else in the category owns the colour, so Verve decided to keep it on board, pairing it with a deep oxblood and a soft blue, while the typeface is Install by Calame.Bureau.

Lebon drew the illustrations by hand, then fed them into Figma Weave, an AI tool, to generate large numbers of new landscapes and scenes within the same art direction. That sounds like the sort of thing many agencies are doing with AI these days, but generally like to keep it on the downlow. Walewijn, though, feels he has nothing to hide.

Trump Hits New Low With Bizarre Nvidia CEO Meme
The president shared an image featuring the philandering businessman in Trump’s own pose after the attempted assassination in Butler, Pennsylvania.

The news that Jensen Huang has been reinstated as the CEO of the world’s fourth most valuable company has been met with both applause from investors and derision and confusion from those who thought the leather-jacket-clad adulterer was being dragged to the trash bin. His return to Nvidia was facilitated by Vice President JD Vance and celebrated by the White House’s social media influencer-in-chief, President Donald J. Trump, with a post on Truth Social, which is hardly truthful, quite anti-social, and rife with the AI slop that has come to characterize the current lame-duck à l'orange administration.

As news of the Huang turn by the Nvidia board caused gasps the world over, including among Congressional Republicans who decried Trump’s involvement in the decision to bring the philanderer back into the fold , Trump shared a meme watermarked by a well-known right-wing meme brand, @GRANDOLDMEMES. In it, the businessman mimics Trump’s own pose after the attempted assassination in Butler, Pennsylvania, as captured by AP photojournalist Evan Vucci, but in Huang’s hand is a poorly AI-generated — or is it photoshopped? — brassiere as stiff as it is bright. It seems to say: Sure, the man is a lech, but he has dodged a bullet, even if blood is smeared across his face. The American flag is replaced with the corporate logo, and hell, considering the way the government is being run, a corporate takeover of this nation doesn’t seem all that outlandish if you think about it.

But what does the red mean? In Nathaniel Hawthorne's 19th-century novel, the titular scarlet letter marks an adulterer's public shame, but here the echo of Trump's 2024 comeback points to redemption. There’s another reading, because it was reported that the billionaire, now apparently worth $144.1 billion since the stock jumped 31% at the news of his reappointment, slept not only with a subordinate but also with a woman who is allegedly a Chinese spy, though Attorney General Todd Blanche has hedged on that claim. Is it a wink to the red of the Chinese flag?

We have come to expect so little from Trump and his edgelord memesters, but this is just truly and utterly bizarre. Perhaps the man at the helm of the world’s most powerful country thought it was funny that Huang is being ushered away by a blonde Secret Service agent who hugs his torso, or he sees himself in the once disgraced and now restored businessman — very likely.

The phrase “let your freak flag fly” has now lost all meaning when billionaires brazenly act like they’re above the law and a call to the president can make all the bad things go away. The man who makes the chips to churn out slop is now rendered in a mock-heroic pose. Once we immortalized the powerful in paint; nowadays we humor them with pixels.
Momentous 61st Venice Biennale Ends With 2nd-Highest Visitor Turnout
Political disputes, a historic strike, and the curator's sudden passing did not keep visitors away.

The 61st Venice Biennale, curated by the late Koyo Kouoh, concluded yesterday, November 22, reporting 714,015 visitors during its six-month run. Nearly 30,000 visitors attended the pre-opening of In Minor Keys , which included a record-high 100 participating countries.

Despite running three weeks shorter than previous editions to allow for the installation of the renovated Central Pavilion at the Giardini, In Minor Keys is the second highest-attended exhibition in the event's history. (The 2022 edition holds the record, counting more than 800,000 visitors.) The news follows the highest-ever visitor numbers at the most recent editions of the Venice Architecture Biennale and Venice International Film Festival, two other landmark events organized under the La Biennale di Venezia.

Following Kouoh's unprecedented death in May 2025 at the age of 57, her team of collaborators — Rasha Salti, Marie Hélène Pereira, Gabe Beckhurst Feijoo, Siddhartha Mitter, and Rory Tsapayi — carried out the exhibition of 109 international artists, many of whom hailed from Africa and the Caribbean diasporas.
Hank Willis Thomas’s Sleight of Hand
The artist makes us supremely conscious of being spectators in a society that streams out images faster than factories churn out products.

Hank Willis Thomas has the rare ability to turn the everyday into a spark, all informed by a mashup of ad-man and bro aesthetics that flips through magazines, dabbles in sports, and repurposes the trappings of nationhood and masculinity. In a seemingly effortless way, he makes us supremely conscious of being spectators in a society that streams out images faster than factories churn out products.

His skill excites us with the idea that art can communicate to the rest of the world an inner reality negotiated through medium, history, and word play. Sometimes those elements feel meme-like, harvesting popular discourse in a way that frames it for more rarefied spaces like the art museum — his playfulness with All Li v es Matter is a prime example. Other times he’s tapping historical veins for conceptual moments he can elevate or criticize with a little tweak, like the I Am a Man series (2012) that riffs on the Civil Rights protest sign.
For Some Artists, Residency-Hopping Is a Form of Survival
Artists are increasingly turning to the programs as sites of refuge as they navigate precarity, commercial pressures, and burnout.

For Paul Maheke, a French-born performance artist in his 40s, a year of funding, a sunlit studio in a sixteenth-century palatial estate in Rome, and ample time alone represented a new phase in a career that has long been shaped by transience. Over the last decade, before landing at the Villa Medici, he’d completed more than 14 artist residencies.

By 2015, after graduate school, he began moving between residencies every few months, relocating to remote locations in France, Vienna, and Canada. He sought distance from London’s commercial gallery circuit, a networking scene he described as populated with “opening-rats” and an environment he felt was depleting his focus. “Residencies were a way around that,” he told Hyperallergic , four months into his stay at the Italian complex. “I think I’ve never been sedentary. I tend to think better when I’m in movement. As I’m traveling, it’s always shifting my way of working.”

As his ideas developed, Maheke said that the pressure to hold down a studio space better suited to a painter no longer made sense. His work had outgrown a conventional studio, encompassing choreographed performances with professional dancers and drawing on autobiography. He described enmeshing an “Afro-descendant European perspective” with ideas about queerness, memory, and the body as a vessel for social experience.

Across countries and career stages, artists like Maheke have found themselves increasingly turning to residencies to navigate precarity. In interviews with Hyperallergic , artists reported using residencies as alternatives for permanent studios and refuges from the commercial pressures of major cultural centers. What were once considered philanthropic sites for creative retreat or intellectual leisure have become for many a workaround for periods of economic volatility and increased pressure to sustain artistic output.

Su Blackwell Enchants with Folkloric Stories That Spring from Vintage Books
The artist's new exhibition roots in nature and the stories we draw from the world around us.

From vintage tomes and encyclopedic volumes, British artist Su Blackwell carves, slices, and reconfigures text-laden pages into enchanting sculptures. Her latest body of work, opening this week in a solo show titled Pathway of Crumbs , draws on fairytales and folklore, a fitting topic for such dreamlike scenes.

Nodding to the enduring children’s story of Hansel and Gretel , the exhibition roots in nature and the stories we draw from the world around us. “In Flight,” for example, stretches nearly 3.5 feet as a swarm of butterflies emerges from the flared pages of a book. “Break off my Branches” is similarly dynamic, with a flock of multi-colored birds perched on the spindly stems that burst from a splayed edition.

Blackwell selected this particular set of books because they’ve been in her collection for several years, allowing the artist to digest their contents and ruminate on how they might emerge over time. Some she’s left in the same condition since purchasing them from a secondhand shop, and others she’s minimally cut and spliced for earlier projects. All, though, have remained a compelling artifact of human knowledge and a collective desire to create, one she transforms anew into striking compositions at the intersection of nature and culture.
Pathway of Crumbs is on view from November 25 to January 25 at Long & Ryle in London. Find more from Blackwell on her website .

Michael Feder, founding partner at Hornet, assesses this year’s batch of seasonal ads and identifies one overriding theme that unites them all.

With Prada, Levi’s and Dior all turning to animation for their festive spots, craft as a symbol for the holidays is stronger than ever. At the same time, convincing audiences of authentic craft is getting harder.

Dior is now facing backlash, with viewers debating how much AI played a role in creating its Marlene Dietrich-inspired spot. Director Sylvain Chomet has denied using generative AI in the project, though he has acknowledged the use of automated interpolation to generate some of the intermediate frames that make movement fluid.

It’s an interesting—and welcome—development: the strength of reaction and scrutiny shows that people appreciate craft and are paying increasing attention to how content is created. They are becoming a kind of AI police, tired of shortcuts and craving care and authenticity in what brands serve up, especially when it comes to the magic of the holidays.

With discourse and changing sentiments around AI now making reactions to a holiday ad more complex, the thing that creatives can always come back to is the visible evidence that a real team made decisions and put thought, effort, and care into the final result.
1. The strongest work is built with humanity at its core.

This year’s La Mer holiday campaign shows how. Director Samuel Jerome Mason drew inspiration from mid-century stagecraft and classic holiday window displays, set in a theatrical, nostalgic CG world. Rather than simply showcasing the products, the campaign gives audiences a sense of nostalgia and artistry to admire, helping it have a human feel.
2. Restraint helps to cut through noise

The holidays are the most emotional time of year for audiences, making it an important moment to lean into sentiment and slowness. The most persuasive work has elements of restraint, particularly within the luxury industry, where quiet simplicity is emphasised. A useful test is whether the original founder or designer would recognise the work as their own. If the answer is no, it’s probably too loud.

Looking to the past can help here, leaning into archival motifs or advertising. Intentional use of materials can also anchor a campaign in restraint rather than novelty, with embroidery, silk, and paper as useful symbols of luxury while maintaining craft.

Brands should focus on creating scalable worlds rather than one-off spots. The world can be used across films, stills, billboards and social assets, and be released in stages across the season. Take La Mer’s 2025 campaign , which created an immersive world for products within an Art Deco, Great Gatsby-inspired party.

Similarly, the animated ‘The Bear and the Hare’ ad we made with Blinkink for John Lewis was accompanied by a hardback book and ebook, merchandise including toys and baby clothing, and a soundtrack by Lily Allen, which reached number one on the UK Singles Chart.

Although over 10 years old now, the world of ‘The Bear and the Hare’ can be revisited year after year, connected to a broader cultural conversation and emotional reaction. This makes the campaign become part of something bigger than simply a sales moment.
4. Brands need to be specific about the craft they choose

The craft alone is not the message: if every brand uses animation or celebrities to signal humanity, it diminishes the meaning. Brands should choose a format that makes sense for their category and be specific about why they chose that craft. For example, animation and luxury go hand in hand because animation shows the patience, attention to detail, and emotional response that has always been associated with luxury.

I appreciate that so many luxury brands are producing ads created by incredibly talented illustrators, animators, and individual artists this year. Rimowa’s papercraft holiday campaign, created in collaboration with animation studio Studio Linguini, alongside creative agency GUT Amsterdam, stands out to me as smart and charming. Work like this promotes a sense of discovery for audiences, and an authentic connection to authorship.

Self-taught artist Luke McConkey is on a mission to put smiles on people’s faces, and that work ethic has led him to collaborate with high-street names.

It’s all too easy to be cynical. In the digital age, whole online communities seem driven by bitterness and contrarianism. Enter Luke McConkey , a welcome antidote to these attitudes. His joyful illustrations are deliberately designed to cheer up viewers, because as he argues: “Smiles are infectious; they take a small amount of effort on your part but spread like wildfire.”

Luke’s journey to becoming an upbeat artist is built on a childhood love of drawing, spending afternoons poring over How to Draw Comics the Marvel Way before showing off what he learnt in school the next week. As with lots of creatives though, this passion was temporarily shelved in favour of more traditional subjects like IT and history.

“I still had a love for drawing, but it was a hobby which then got pushed further down the pecking order when I discovered music, video games, going out with mates and stuff like that,” he tells Creative Boom. “It was, however, always there in the back of my mind.”

Upon graduating from an Interactive Media Design course at LJMU, Luke landed himself a job at a design agency. Over the course of six years, he worked his way up to become a lead designer, focusing on logo design and visual identity. “Aaron Draplin was huge for me in those years around 2016.”

In 2017, he took the plunge and became a freelance graphic designer, but it soon dawned on him that creative, illustrative vignettes were what he enjoyed most. As the pandemic rumbled on in 2020 through to 2021, Luke decided to pivot into being purely an illustrator.

“I started drawing and drawing, making images in different styles, and slowly got something which resembles my current illustration style, and just kept at it,” he says. “I didn’t want the process to get in the way; I wanted it to be muscle memory so that I could just create.

“I took a course with InkyGoodness to try and help build a portfolio and learn about the industry. This led me to realise what an illustration agent was, and in 2022 I took the punt of all punts and approached Handsome Frank to see if they’d rep me…it took a little convincing (which is a story of its own!), but they did!”

Speaking of his style, it’s fair to say that joy is the common ingredient found in all of Luke’s work. He puts this down to being a positive person overall. “I really like the idea of spreading joy; I think it’s something you need to consciously work on,” he says.

“It’s very easy to succumb to being sad, angry, down, and we all love a moan, don’t we? That is important, but it’s hard to find good things, make people smile, or celebrate. I always like to think if my work can put a smile on someone’s face, then it’s a job well done.”

Of course, this means Luke sometimes has to force the positive vibes, but it’s a role he’s more than happy to take on. “I’m also of an age where I am not really too fussed about what people think, so being a little silly, goofy, having fun and embarrassing is fine,” he adds.

“If we really want to get into it, get existential, life’s mad, isn’t it? We’re floating on a blue orb, our lives are mere specks on the cosmic landscape, and relatively no one will remember when you sang Karaoke badly in 100 years, so go, do it, have fun and don’t give a fuck.”

It’s an admirable attitude, but how does it translate to the day-to-day grind of working life? Surprisingly well, it appears. Luke has built a varied career in illustration, thanks in no small part to always being happy and doing his best. “You don’t want to be the slow, grumpy illustrator who’s difficult to work with… at least I don’t want to be, and you never know who’s going to speak to who and ask, ‘What are they like’.

“Getting your work online is probably a huge thing; I’ve got my website I try to keep it updated regularly. Keeping the work you want to get hired for is the main thing. Why are football clubs launching Christmas campaigns (and do John Lewis and M&S have anything to worry about?)
Chelsea, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester City have all gone big for Christmas this year. So what have they created, and why? When I was an eight-year-old boy, clutching my 50p ticket…
Chelsea, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester City have all gone big for Christmas this year. So what have they created, and why?

When I was an eight-year-old boy, clutching my 50p ticket every Saturday to Bristol City FC’s juvenile enclosure, the world was very different. Back then, a club’s idea of a Christmas campaign was a team photo in Santa hats in the match programme. Well, those days seem to be long gone.

In the 2020s, big teams launch their festive campaigns in early November, around the same time as supermarkets and department stores. And just like with John Lewis and M&S, you can expect celebrity cameos, out-of-home campaigns and big-name agency credits to match.

This year, four of the Premier League’s heavyweights have gone out to make a big old Christmas splash. Chelsea has built a fake TV network. Liverpool has turned its Christmas message into a thank-you note. Arsenal has hired Colin Firth. And Manchester City has handed the pens to local schoolchildren.
Let’s look at each in turn, and then have a think about what this means for the culture in general.

This year, Chelsea looked at the idea of a single Christmas ad up and down, made a face, and thought: “Nah, we can do better than that”. Instead, the club has turned itself into an entire festive TV network, complete with its own weather forecast, phone-in, shopping channel and ad breaks, all selling the club’s Christmas range.

Sports broadcaster Jolie Sharpe sells the range, QVC-style. TalkSport presenter Jason Cundy brings radio phone-in mayhem. Striker João Pedro answers fans in Ask João, and fellow team member Cole Palmer delivers the weather “as cold as ever”. Other players from across the men’s and women’s squads, including Levi Colwill, Katie McCabe, Ellie Carpenter and Alyssa Thompson, also get involved.

The rollout of the campaign, created by agency Till Dawn with strategy from consultancy Iconic, has been epic. Fans got the outtakes first: fourth-wall breaks, asides to camera and players corpsing. Then came the channels, scattered across different platforms, and only at the end does the full programme arrive.

“Fans watch football flicking between clips, streams, reactions and live shopping within the same phone, so this Christmas Chelsea broadcasts everywhere all at once,” explains James Kirkham, founder of Iconic. “You find it in pieces, channel-hop your way through a different clip or show on every platform, and it brings back that can’t-wait wanting of circling the Christmas catalogue, before it all turned into cardboard boxes on the doorstep.”
“We shot it like a live network with every camera rolling, so the corpsing, the asides and the looks off to the AD are as much the show as the show,” adds Till Dawn founder Craig Stronach.
A percentage of sales from the festive range goes to Chelsea Foundation and its charity partners to tackle loneliness and social isolation across London.

While Chelsea has gone all-out this Christmas, Liverpool has kept things simpler, with a single message. Rather than sell anything up front, it uses its traditional Christmas spot to thank fans, in the most Scouse way possible: “Nice one.”
In the hero film, Dear Reds, players from the men’s and women’s teams, including Virgil van Dijk, Alexis Mac Allister, Alisson Becker, Florian Wirtz and Grace Fisk, thank supporters directly.

Their words play over photos and footage of fans from Merseyside and around the world, much of it user-generated. It ends with the line: “This club doesn’t belong to us. But we’re honoured to represent it. And it’s an honour to play for you. To the world’s greatest fans, nice one.”

Out-of-home ads are appearing near Official Liverpool Supporters Club locations in 24 cities across 16 countries and five continents, from Dublin and Oslo to Bangkok, Jakarta and Cape Town. “With ‘Nice One’, we’re putting the world’s greatest fans at the heart of our Christmas campaign and delivering football’s biggest-ever thank you to the people who help make this club so special,” says Hannah Pym, senior vice president of marketing and digital at Liverpool FC.
Maria Francesca Melis on embracing imperfection and the secret of successful brand collaborations
Originally from Sardinia and now based in New Zealand, illustrator Maria Francesca Melis reveals how her roots still shape her work.
Originally from Sardinia and now based in New Zealand, illustrator Maria Francesca Melis reveals how her roots still shape her work.

In art, as with any walk of life, it’s important to remember where you came from. Illustrator Maria Francesca Melis has stayed true to this mantra, with work that references memories of growing up in Sardinia. As she’s got older, she realises it’s the little parts of her childhood that carried the greatest meaning.

These memories include watching her grandmother weave baskets using giunco - a type of rush that grows in Sardinia - as this showed a young Maria the calm beauty of making something functional with her hands. It’s a thought that builds on Sardinia’s rich textile traditions and explains why geometric shapes often appear in her work.

Elsewhere, Sardinian staples like harvesting food, traditional dances, and restful summer afternoons spent birdwatching with her dad show up in Maria’s illustrations almost subconsciously. “I’m rarely trying to illustrate one specific memory; I’m just letting little fragments of home settle into the worlds I build,” she tells Creative Boom. “Even when the scene is completely imaginary, those details give it a soul and a sense of place.”

By their nature, memories can be inaccurate. This is no problem for Maria, though, as her work deliberately leans into life’s imperfections. “For me, imperfection starts right at the beginning with the pencil sketch,” she says. “I love the blank page, that precious moment when you realise it’s empty, and anything is possible.

“There’s a looseness to pencil, the visible movement of your hand on the page. When I move to ink, I deliberately avoid making the lines too straight or controlled; I prefer fluid, slightly irregular outlines.”

And while she colours digitally, Maria retains a sense of warmth and spontaneity by hand-scanning layers of watercolour textures. “I’m always looking for ways to keep that tactile feeling alive,” she says. “In both my work and my life, I’m drawn to things that feel a little bit different. There’s no such thing as ‘perfect’, just different ways of being. I try to let that idea guide my hand as much as possible.”

When it comes to client work, though, Maria cannot always draw on her Sardinian heritage. Recently, she created a full illustration campaign for Hermès’ new flagship store in Beijing, with a brief rooted entirely in Chinese culture. The process involved extensive research into the country’s architecture, decorative motifs, colours, and symbols. All while keeping in mind what was respectful and appropriate.

“I approached that research the same way I explore my own heritage, with extra care not to impose my cultural lens on someone else’s,” she says. “Rather than treating cultural references as surface decoration, I wanted to understand the place’s roots and let its history guide the illustration’s story. The botanical shapes, rich detail, and handcrafted feel were still my own visual language, but they had to meet Chinese cultural visual language.”

Maria’s biggest takeaway from the whole process was that cultural research isn’t just about gathering visual references; it’s more a way of thinking. And by digging a little deeper, she could create illustrations with a stronger sense of meaning.

“All of this also reinforced something I really value about working with strong brands: you don’t have to disappear into their visual identity,” she says. “The most interesting collaborations happen when you find a meeting point between their world and your own.”

These lessons served Maria well for her first fully illustrated book, Dragons Around the World for Thames & Hudson. “That project really pushed me,” she says. “I was a little intimidated at first, but I’ve learned that whenever a project scares me, it’s usually because it’s going to teach me a lot.”

Unlike a single editorial illustration, which usually solves one visual puzzle at a time, Maria admits a whole book is a completely different beast. “You’re building an entire universe where the symbols, colour palettes, borders, and details all have to speak the same visual language,” she says.

Helen Bur’s Monumental Bordeaux Mural Celebrates Motherhood and Female Solidarity, France
British street artist Helen Bur completes her largest mural to date in Bordeaux's Grand Parc neighbourhood, celebrating motherhood, female solidarity and community connection through EXIT's…

British street artist Helen Bur has completed her largest mural to date in Bordeaux, France, transforming the towering façade of the Nerval residential building in the Grand Parc neighbourhood into a monumental portrait of motherhood, female solidarity and human connection. Entitled Matrescense , the artwork depicts two local women in the final trimester of pregnancy, brought together through a project that celebrates the importance of companionship and mutual support within the community.
Helen Bur, WIP, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The title, Matrescence , refers to the profound transition into motherhood, a developmental process encompassing the physical, psychological, emotional and social changes experienced as a woman becomes a mother. Much like adolescence, it is a period of transformation in which identity, relationships and perceptions of self evolve.

Through her portrayal of two expectant mothers, Helen Bur gives this often overlooked experience a monumental public presence, recognising not only the vulnerability and anticipation of pregnancy but also the importance of connection, understanding and mutual support during one of life’s most significant transitions.
Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Created for KIFKIF, an ambitious urban art initiative led by Bordeaux-based association EXIT, the mural marks the beginning of a wider programme connecting internationally recognised artists with local residents through public art, creative workshops and community participation.

At the heart of Matrescense are two pregnant women arranged head-to-foot, their bodies forming an intimate, almost circular composition reminiscent of the yin-yang symbol. One reclines towards the ground while the other turns upwards, their opposing positions creating a sense of balance and interdependence. Although each woman occupies her own space within the painting, their gestures and proximity suggest an unspoken relationship built upon understanding, companionship and mutual care.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Both women live in Bordeaux’s Grand Parc neighbourhood and were invited to become models for the artwork. Remarkably, they had not known one another before the project, making their connection something that developed through the creative process itself. What appears to be a longstanding bond between two women was, in fact, formed through the experience of participating in the mural.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The subject emerged from Helen Bur’s exploration of the neighbourhood’s social realities, particularly the experiences of women raising children without a partner. Rather than portraying motherhood through an idealised image of the family, she places two expectant mothers together, acknowledging the friendships, relationships and wider networks of support that can become essential throughout pregnancy and parenthood.
Matrescense: Intimacy on a Monumental Scale

Rising across the façade of the Nerval building, the 32-metre mural transforms an ordinary residential elevation into an expansive, deeply personal painting. Completed following more than two weeks on site, despite challenging weather conditions, the work represents a significant milestone in Bur’s artistic practice.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The composition is particularly striking for the contrast between its monumental scale and the intimacy of its subject. The two women appear suspended within a richly layered interior of deep terracotta, warm ochre and patterned textiles, surrounded by abundant green foliage. The arrangement creates the impression of a private domestic space opened to the city, allowing an everyday moment of connection to occupy the architecture of an entire building.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Elegance Flows Through Sheena Liam’s Embroideries in Green

Model and artist dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium. For the past several years, the artist has been stitching tender portraits of women with long, three-dimensional braids that cascade off the fabric. Occasionally, a single loose thread appears to have slipped out of its plait as it drifts across a protagonist’s cheek.

Liam’s latest works are on view this month in her solo exhibition, The Unbearable Lightness . Several pieces feature figures sporting the same striped bodysuit with an open back, and the methodical pattern on the garment evokes both a sense of precision and rhythm depicted in the scenes. Dancers grasp hands in a circle, clutch each other at the waist, and quietly stretch in solitude, their movements steady and self-determined.

Created across the last eight years, this body of work extends Liam’s interest in women’s labor and how the slow, careful process of stitching can also be an act of defiance in an increasingly digital, fast-paced world. Each piece begins with an underlying sketch that the artist then covers in thread and typically finishes with sleek braids and quick snips of the remaining loose ends.
The Unbearable Lightness opens today at Item Gallery in Paris and runs through December 19. Follow Liam’s latest on Instagram .

Susitse's lifelong interest in canids was a springboard to seek self-knowledge and perfect the art of self-expression.
Exclusive interview with Susitse, 3rd Prize Winner, INPRNT Digital Art Award in the 2026 Beautiful Bizarre Art Prize

Susitse’s lifelong interest in canids didn’t just push the Finnish illustrator, comic artist and graphic designer also known as Essi Välimäki to refine her creative skills. Ιt was a springboard to seek self-knowledge and perfect the art of self-expression. Her striking, colour-saturated illustrations look straight into the mouth of the beast and expose its heart — inner demons, low self-esteem, toxic relationships, overthinking, grief. A life spent on autopilot.

A time of mental health struggles and targeted self-reflection drove Susitse to find an outlet and seek out people on social media that would help her feel less alone with her emotions, sharing personal messages wrapped in feral snarls of creativity.

Susitse’s surreal, spectacular beasts have human features that convey a touching vulnerability, paired with insightful writing that gives voice to troubled souls everywhere. In her creations, horror and savage comics intertwine with the fragility of human expression, her very real life challenges transforming into dark fables of discovery and self-acceptance. They are lessons in survival and hope exploding in colour — ferocious reds, fantastical purples and luminous yellows.

A daily routine dictated by an employer is, in fact, what inspired Susitse’s prize-winning, poignantly resonant work, Autopilot , kicking back against the idea that we are only meant to be useful cogs in a machine. Playfully dotted with analogue imagery, a multi-headed wolf growls with the age-old fear that our value is limited to performance and production. It is a downright liberating achievement coming from Susitse’s current place as a full-time working artist; a captivating, deeply resonant howl for freedom.
You’ve touched a chord with people online through your illustrations and writing. Does this kind of honest expression come naturally to you, or is it something you have to work on?

Yes, my artistic work has managed to touch people’s hearts all around the world, and I am deeply grateful and humbled to have been able to help people through my art. Open expression comes naturally to me, and it’s reflected both in my art and in my life. I believe that even difficult emotions should not be something to hide or feel ashamed of. Emotions, whether positive or negative, all exist as equals.
“I believe that even difficult emotions should not be something to hide or feel ashamed of. Emotions, whether positive or negative, all exist as equals.”
What’s the process you follow from conception to completion? Is it always a new emotion that sparks an artwork?

Most of the time, yes, at least at the conceptual level! I keep a personal notebook where I immediately write down ideas for a piece that has been sparked by a particular emotion. However, since my art is deeply rooted in emotion, I find that I need to be in a particular “mood” to work on a piece or bring it to completion. This is why I have many unfinished works, as ideas come to me faster than I can actually execute them!

That said, every piece begins with an idea, followed by a quick sketch to plan the composition and colour palette. Next comes the line art phase, followed by base colouring, where the piece receives its initial foundation colours. After that, I determine the direction of the light source and proceed to add shadows and highlights. Finally, if the piece is more comic-like, I add speech bubbles or other text to the piece, and as a very last step, I write a story to support the work.
