Yoshitomo Nara’s Beloved Wide-Eyed Figures Return to New York
A blockbuster solo show in New York has people lining up down the street.

The first time I encountered Yoshitomo Nara ’s work was when I opened the mailbox as an angsty teenager. A friend a few years older had recently visited the Walker Art Center , where she bought a postcard printed with two of the artist’s portraits and scribbled a note to her friend (me) still stuck in their tiny Wisconsin hometown. As is wont to happen to teenagers on the cusp of adulthood, I took that postcard as a sort of guiding light—a reminder that the world was bigger than the tractors and small-town gossip I was surrounded by—and promptly cut and taped the works to fit within my clear phone case. I carried this pair of strange characters everywhere I went for years after.

Nara also was born and raised in a rural region, albeit on the other side of the globe. The artist has described his childhood in Aomori on the northern tip of Japan’s main island as solitary and removed from the culture of the cities, instead flanked by the endless expanse of the Pacific Ocean and the snowy ridges of the Hakkōda Mountains. These early years indelibly informed his sensibility, and even in his most emotionally charged works, there’s a deep sense of calm that comes from immersion in nature.

In his first solo presentation in New York in almost a decade, Nara takes over two of David Zwirner ’s galleries. The self-titled exhibition includes nearly 100 works from the last several decades, spanning paintings, drawings, and monumental bronze sculptures. Central are the artist’s signature childlike figures with large heads and eyes and an underlying sense of innocence, their skeptical, bored, and even rebellious expressions providing a necessary counterbalance—one that also spoke to my teenage sensitivities.

Profoundly enigmatic, Nara’s works are also instantly recognizable, relatable, and broadly appealing. According to the gallery , 4,000 visitors lined up to see the exhibition on opening night, with 26,000 attending in the first week alone.

Ranging in scale from intimate miniatures to larger-than-life, Nara’s two-dimensional portraits emerge from soft, pastel-hued palettes. Several also often contain pithy phrases that hearken to our collective challenges. Both “world peace” and “tomorrow’s far away” drip with longing and speak to the artist’s broader concern for the contentious state of human relations.

Introducing clay into his practice also emerged from unease and grief, when Nara picked up the earthen material after the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake . The disastrous event killed nearly 20,000 people and injured and displaced many more around the artist’s hometown. In the moment, the tactile medium offered a reprieve the canvas couldn’t.

In the exhibition, Nara’s monochromatic bronzes, coated in white urethane paint, capture these forays into three-dimensions and evoke the icy, snow-blanketed landscapes of his youth. Based on smaller ceramic prototypes, the sculptures bear the traces of the handmade, as if he had sculpted each head with an enormous thumb.

As an exhibition statement says, Nara’s overarching impulse is simple: he “creates art in order to express and communicate what he feels unable to convey in words, and his distinctive body of work has evolved through his ongoing search to identify what is uniquely his: his upbringing in rural northern Japan at a particular moment in time and, above all, his profound concern for humanity, including those outside mainstream society.”

The artist recently wrapped up a large-scale project at the Hirshorn Sculpture Garden, and next fall, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art will host a major retrospective of his work. Until then, see Yoshitomo Nara through December 12 in New York.
‘We’re Still Here’ Celebrates Remarkable Quilts by 15 Contemporary Black Artists
"Black history is American history," says curator, historian, and quilter Carolyn Mazloomi.

In the wee hours of a busy Saturday morning, on June 28, 1969, police raided The Stonewall Inn in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village, a renowned hangout for the LGBTQ+ community. During the 1950s and 1960s, few businesses openly welcomed gay people, and the legal system was against them—even two consenting adults in the privacy of their own home could face years in prison or a psychiatric institution if convicted of the crime of sodomy. Bar raids were common, but this one was particularly fraught due to the volume of people, and police quickly lost control. A riot erupted, which sparked even further protests over the coming weeks in what became known as the Stonewall uprising .

Among those on the front lines, from the raid onward, was Marsha P. Johnson —the “P” stands for Pay It No Mind—a Black transgender woman who advocated throughout the 1960s and 1970s for gay and transgender rights, LGBTQ+ youth, and those affected by HIV and AIDS. Known fondly as The Saint of Christopher Street, nodding to the well-known and welcoming area for the gay community (and home of The Stonewall Inn), she was widely known for her effervescent smile, creative clothing, and the flowers she would often wear in her hair.
For quilter Rosy Petri , Johnson proved a beautiful and vibrant personality for a large-scale textile work in We’re Still Here: Quilted Works Curated by Carolyn Mazloomi at Claire Oliver Gallery .

The works of 15 contemporary quilt artists take center stage in the expansive group exhibition. The show emphasizes work created by members of the Women of Color Quilters Network ( WCQN ), which historian, curator, and quilter Carolyn Mazloomi founded in 1985. Boldly pictorial and incorporating a wide range of materials, the pieces in We’re Still Here transcend the definition of quilts as stitched bed coverings; the compositions are rooted in the timeless craft of piecing and sewing, yet their portraits, stories, and collages surge into the realm of art.

L’Merchie Frazier ’s “Climate Change in my Head: Afro Future Still Here,” for example, adopts a watercolor-like appearance with layers of nylon. Like many works in the show, a crucial topic is rendered front-and-center. Alita Aldridge’s “Underground Takes a Village” reflects the cooperation needed to make the Underground Railroad viable for enslaved people seeking freedom. And April Anue Shipp ’s “The Oracle of Liberation” depicts abolitionist Frederick Douglass holding red and blue pills—a reference to the 1999 film The Matrix— in which we’re presented with a choice between seeing reality for what it is or remaining ignorant.

In addition to history, Black community, family, and other themes, bold portraiture recurs throughout the exhibition, such as in Viola Burley Leak ’s “Maya Angelou II.” The renowned writer and civil rights activist peers over symbolic representations of her life’s work, including a bird fleeing an enclosure in a nod to her seminal memoir, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings.

“All of the work I make, and the work of my fellow quilters, deals with Black history and material culture,” Mazloomi says in a statement. Through WCQN, along with curatorial projects and in advocacy of the art form, she strives to raise critical awareness of Black quilters’ practices. “This exhibition is our way of saying that our history cannot be erased by any politician or revisionist force; our work will always showcase our triumphs, suffering, creativity, courage, bravery, and genius of my people. Black history is American history.”
We’re Still Here continues through January 7 in Harlem. You might also enjoy Chronicle Books’ recent release , Stories in the Seams: A People’s History of Black Quilts and Their Makers .
Andrada Trapnell: The Delicate Threshold of Vulnerability and Transformation
Andrada reveals how her art forms an emotional bridge between vulnerability and self-discovery. In this exclusive interview, we delve into the liminal spaces of self-reflection, curiosity…

There is something about Andrada Trapnell’s paintings that feels strangely familiar, as though you’ve encountered these moments somewhere before, tucked away in the recesses of your memory, only to have them suddenly return. Looking at her work is a little like reaching inside a jewelry box and pulling out a charm you haven’t seen in years. For a moment, you’re transported. A feeling rushes over you, a memory begins to take shape, and yet you’re not entirely certain where it belongs. Was it something you experienced? Something you dreamed? Or is it a moment that exists somewhere between the two, in liminal spaces?

Her paintings feel like tucked-away worlds, each one waiting to be discovered. And there’s something so intriguing about the way the recurring circles invite you to experience them. From the outside, you might take in the painting as a whole, following its colors, patterns, and abstract forms. But the circle seems to offer another way in. It becomes a portal, a threshold to something different… where the experience of looking shifts and another layer of the story begins to reveal itself.

Maybe this is part of what makes her paintings so compelling. Each one has a story. They invite you to consider the cyclical nature of life, the passage of time, and the curious ways our memories, dreams, and present moments can occupy the same space. It’s as if the mysteries of the natural world have found a home within the details of her paintings.

As Andrada explains, “I seek to distinguish the lines between dreams and reality through different styles and compositions.” A distinction that becomes increasingly difficult to make as you spend time with her work.

Her portraits, often accompanied by animals, carry a dreamlike quality, although there is nothing entirely removed from reality about them. Instead, she invites us into the beguiling abstract passages, leaving room for the subconscious to take over. A face rendered in blue might sits against a field of golden yellow, while an inverted triangle, an unexpected brushstroke, or the particular placement of light leaves you with something more to ponder.
You find yourself looking not only at the individual elements, but at the relationships between them, and what they might be telling you.

Gold leaf, intricate patterns, and layers of color and texture all have a part to play in this visual language. There is an almost delicate, spiderweb-like quality to the way these details connect, each one seemingly fragile on its own, yet serving a purpose within the larger story. Nothing feels incidental. And as those recurring circles draw your attention once again, you begin to wonder whether you’ve been looking through a window, into a memory, or perhaps somewhere much closer to a mirror.
You’ve described your work as distinguishing “the lines between dream and reality.” How do you experience this liminal space when you are creating?

When creating, I am focusing on the part of myself that draws from intuition, dreams, and the childlike curiosity for a world that has been developing and evolving within me over the years. A dream can vividly express a narrative that can bleed into your reality and make you feel that what you experience is even more than real.

Reality is full of wonder and mystery in itself, and if we slow down to take in all the aspects of life and decay that construct this circle of life that we are all embarked upon, we’ll experience a profound appreciation for the art of being, as well as the art of creation.

All of this represents an innate part of my being, which carries me through my dreams and also brings me back to the reality of life. Two realms, both with light and darkness inside. The ‘in between’ stage is the most fluid area of possibility – where two worlds merge. When creating, I am placing the subject in the ‘what if’ and ‘I wonder where’ scenario of this world.

Turner Duckworth dips Maker’s Mark’s new identity in red wax
Five years after its last refresh, the Kentucky bourbon has gone back to the London agency for a global identity pressed, quite literally, from the very farm it comes from. If you love your…
Five years after its last refresh, the Kentucky bourbon has gone back to the London agency for a global identity pressed, quite literally, from the very farm it comes from.

If you love your bourbon as much as I do, then you’ll know every bottle of Maker’s Mark is still dipped in red wax by hand. It’s a slow and messy process any creative can appreciate, especially in a year when Cambridge Dictionary named ‘human’ its word of 2026.

So it makes sense that the brand’s new global identity would go down the same route. Turner Duckworth London has taken stalks of soft red winter wheat, rings of American oak and plants native to Star Hill Farm, the distillery’s home in Loretto, Kentucky, and dipped and pressed each one into that same red wax. What came out of that is a set of fresh marks that sit at the heart of the brand. There’s also an updated colour palette, new photography and custom typography that pays homage to the brand’s family roots.

Sound familiar? That’s because Turner Duckworth has been here before. We covered its first Maker’s Mark identity in 2021 , when the agency built a system around a graphic version of the famous drip. Five years later, the drawing has made way for the real thing. Why illustrate wax when you’ve got access to vats of it?

The typography has its own story, too. It’s inspired by the handwriting of Margie Samuels, who founded Maker’s Mark with her husband, Bill Samuels Sr, and who came up with the bottle, label and wax in the first place. It is Margie’s wit that the brand has always traded on. Well, I never.

Now for a little history lesson. Bill famously burned the family’s 170-year-old recipe to start afresh and come up with a more balanced bourbon. The couple chose Loretto for its proximity to water and grain growers. And Margie decided that every bottle must be hand-dipped – a strategy that literally made its mark. Maker’s Mark calls this streak ‘Perfectly Unreasonable’, the name of its brand platform, and the new identity is designed to carry this idea consistently worldwide, in what the brand describes as a “modern, more minimal way”.

“In a world increasingly driven by speed and automation, we still believe some things are worth making slowly, by hand,” says Chloe Lloyd-Jones, vice president of global brand marketing, Maker’s Mark. “We returned to Star Hill Farm, working with natural materials from the land and our signature red wax to create a visual identity that reflects the ‘Perfectly Unreasonable’ spirit behind our bourbon. The result gives us a powerful way to tell our story around the world, while creating experiences that feel personal and relevant in each market.”

“My grandparents weren’t thinking about ‘branding’ when they created Maker’s Mark. They cared about a hand-made process in service to flavour and design that honours that vision,” adds Rob Samuels, eighth-generation whisky maker and managing director. “That deeply personal approach created some of the most recognisable symbols in bourbon. This new and exceptional work brings that same intention forward, honouring what they created and ensuring Maker’s Mark feels as personal and distinctive today as it did from the start.”

The identity was launched on 17 November and is rolling out across digital, social, advertising and retail, as well as events and experiences. Parts of it have already appeared at events in the US and China and in out-of-home campaigns in Australia and the UK, with more markets to follow throughout 2027.
&Walsh takes a bite out of the moon for Insomnia Cookies
Jessica Walsh and her team have given the late-night bakery’s identity a refresh, and it’s based on the very thing it’s promised since it launched in 2003: a warm cookie at any hour. Milk…
Jessica Walsh and her team have given the late-night bakery’s identity a refresh, and it’s based on the very thing it’s promised since it launched in 2003: a warm cookie at any hour.

Milk and cookies is very much an American thing. I’ve never once been tempted to sneak down the stairs in the dead of night and snack on something delicious. It’s just not in our culture. Nigella Lawson might, god bless her. I can picture her now in her silk dressing gown, the goddess that she is. But late-night treats are not for me. Seeing the new identity for Insomnia Cookies, though, might tempt me otherwise.

The heart of &Walsh’s rebrand is a logo that looks good enough to eat, and it pays homage to the whole premise. Insomnia Cookies is a late-night bakery that Seth Berkowitz started from his University of Pennsylvania dorm room in 2003. It now has more than 375 bakeries across the US, Canada and the UK. Its original identity had a cookie moon. Genius. &Walsh has thankfully kept that but swapped the drawing for the real deal: a photograph of a melted chocolate chunk cookie, half-eaten into the shape of a crescent. Anyone suddenly think of “Half mooooon!” or is that just me?

Yes, it’s a brave move, a photographic logo. Any designer will tell you they’re awkward at small sizes and damn fussy in print, yet here we are. But have no fear, dear readers – &Walsh has a vector version in reserve for exactly those moments. Everywhere else, though, the cookie is on full show.

So why didn’t they start from scratch? One would assume the importance of heritage, certainly. By Insomnia’s own account, it created the warm cookie delivery category, and &Walsh set out to recommit to that rather than reinvent it. So whilst everyone else is chasing trends, the new strategy focuses on a single promise: ‘Always Warm’. Gosh, my mouth is watering just thinking about it.

That brand promise suits Insomnia’s purpose – turning up at your door at any unreasonable hour with something straight from the oven. It’s why the agency didn’t overcomplicate things or try and be clever. When you look at this refreshed logo, you get that instant promise. It’s confident without trying too hard.

Around the moon is a system built on the hours Insomnia operates. There’s a nice late-night purple palette (Premier Inn, anyone?), along with a run of cookie-dough browns. Typography by Julio Zukerman is rounded and chunky. Illustration is also by Julio and Simran Meshram. And there’s a refreshed tone of voice throughout.

Then there’s Insomnia’s menu, which rotates constantly. And every limited-time offer is another opportunity for the brand to show off its new look. To keep it all feeling like one brand, &Walsh designed a tiered system: most launches share the same warm, appetising photography and art direction, while a select few campaigns get a more graphic approach.

What’s really interesting is the sheer volume of the work. Over six months, &Walsh produced more than five photography and video shoots to cover 12 campaigns, from the core range of cookies to seasonal specials. OK, now I want to know about seasonal specials. Photography was by Henry Hargreaves, while Charlotte Omnes and Daniella Khan handled food styling. Motion design is by Pedro Magalhães, Igor Fajardo and Marco Del Pra, and moving elements can be seen across the refresh. It looks so good you can almost see the heat coming off the freshly baked cookies.

“Every decision in this rebrand, the photo moon cookie, the photography, the rounded type, the colours, was built toward the same feeling: warm, late night and confident,” says Carolina Vazquez, art director at &Walsh. “The goal was to make the brand feel fresh without losing what’s always made it Insomnia.”
Given how much I’ll be playing GTA 6 over the coming weeks, I reckon I could be persuaded to enjoy a late-night cookie.
It’s official: creatives are using AI daily, but most aren’t making extra money from it
Envato’s second annual survey of more than 1,000 creatives finds that AI use has become routine, even if they don’t always tell the client. But whether they’re using it well remains an open…
Envato’s second annual survey of more than 1,000 creatives finds that AI use has become routine, even if they don’t always tell the client. But whether they’re using it well remains an open question.

This time last year, many creatives were rushing to adopt AI tools, but nervously. Twelve months later, things have changed a lot. That’s according to Beyond the Hype: The State of AI in Creative Work , the second annual report from Envato , the creative asset and AI toolkit owned by Shutterstock.

Based on a survey of 1,033 creatives across 103 countries and territories, the report reveals what creatives are actually doing with AI. And two big things immediately grabbed my attention. Firstly, more than half of AI users have used it on key client work without telling their client. And secondly, while AI may save you time, most creatives aren’t seeing that turn into actual money.
To unpack these findings and more, I spoke to Hichame Assi, president of Shutterstock, which includes Envato.

Envato first ran the survey in 2025, and Hichame says the reason was simple. The public conversation about AI didn’t match what he was seeing from the working creatives who use Envato. “At face value, the narrative was all hype or doom,” he recalls. “Yet in our community, creatives were quietly working AI into client jobs.” So last year, Envato asked creatives how they were using it.

One finding from that first survey stayed with Hichame in particular. “Almost half were using AI every day, but only about a third felt really prepared for it. That gap felt worth keeping an eye on, so we came back to see what had changed.”
So what has changed in the last 12 months? Well, quite a lot actually. For a start, today 87% of creatives use AI at work at least occasionally, and 58% use it every day.

“AI is now part of the daily routine for most creatives,” says Hichame. “Daily use rose from 49% to 58%, and agentic tools, which we didn’t even ask about last year, are now used regularly by more than a third of AI users. At the same time, active avoidance has grown from 3% to 8%, so not everyone is on board yet.”
But while most creatives are using AI to help them in their work, that doesn’t mean that AI is doing their work, at least not all of it.

The survey split people’s creative work into six stages, from research and admin to editing. At five of the six stages, “directing [AI] closely” was the most common approach. The percentage of creatives who let AI work “with little input” never went above 11%, and at some stages, it dropped to 4%. As for generating assets, only 7% took a hands-off approach.
For Hichame, the biggest surprise in this year’s data concerned the skill that, only a year ago, everyone seemed to agree was essential: prompting.

“Last year, our respondents named prompting as a skills gap and predicted ‘prompt engineer’ as a new job,” he recalls. “This year, though, creatives ranked it last of eight factors, at 19%.” Taste and judgement came first, at 53%. Craft came second, at 49%, followed by the strength of the idea, at 39%.

So what’s going on? Perhaps this is just a sign that models have got much better at understanding natural language and visual references. Consequently, the time when precise prompts were all-important is long gone.

“The tools are going to keep getting easier and more accessible, so knowing how to use them won’t be what sets creatives apart,” says Jessica Walsh, founder of New York studio &Walsh and one of the experts interviewed for the report. What will, in her view, is “being able to recognise great work when you see it [which is] not something you can prompt, or learn overnight.”

One thing that surprised me personally is that nearly six in 10 creatives who work in teams say they have no written AI policy. Even in organisations of 250 or more people, four in 10 say they’ve been given nothing in writing. As Hichame puts it: “The tools moved fast, and the rules didn’t. Most are working it out as they go.” Which brings us to a thorny question: should creatives disclose whether they’ve used AI in their work?
Julie Legrand finds poetry in coffee pots, shells and other things you see every day
The French illustrator and screen printer turns objects from her kitchen and studio into bold, smudged, characteristically simple images. Julie Legrand’s portfolio is full of things you’ve…
The French illustrator and screen printer turns objects from her kitchen and studio into bold, smudged, characteristically simple images.

Julie Legrand’s portfolio is full of things you’ve seen a thousand times and probably never stopped to really look at, let alone draw them. There’s a moka pot drawn in a wobbly black line, a large-scale sunshine-yellow coffee pot on chocolatey brown, a hand holding a shell among pale blue crabs and whelks, and roses in all sorts of guises, from a yellow bloom with ‘ROSA’ scrawled underneath in her own lettering to a tomato-red one floating on cobalt blue. A few simple shapes, a handful of colours and the odd paper dot from a hole punch are all it takes to make a kitchen staple feel like a star. And it’s all so cheerful and homely that we want to put the kettle on, and maybe pin a few of these to the fridge.

The illustrator and screen printer comes from the south of France. “I grew up in the mountains of the Hérault hinterland,” she says, before studying illustration in Épinal, eastern France, and later printmaking in Galicia, Spain. Those roots led her to work with traditional techniques, and are perhaps a key reason why rural life and seaside imagery turn up again and again in her work.

When asked where she finds inspiration, she says: “Primarily from everyday life: objects I find in my kitchen or my studio.” That’s the sort of stuff we all have lying around at home. Her themes are always “rooted in the intimate and the mundane,” and she adds: “I try to convey the memories and poetry associated with them.” Since moving to Sète, the sea has crept into her work, including its plant life, mineral forms and inhabitants. “I like to interpret the landscape through the elements and forms that compose it, rather than by representing the landscape itself.”

Once she has her inspiration in check, she moves on to her process. “I exhaust forms,” she explains, “meaning I choose an object or subject and explore its variations, sometimes over the course of months.” That explains why a coffee pot and rose each show up in so many guises. She starts with photos, sketches, and drawings she’s happy with, then works in collage or with pens, pencils, rulers, and lettering templates, before digitising and editing. The handcrafted feel matters enormously to her, so the paper textures from her collages and the marks and smudges on her drawings all make it through. “Cleaning up a scan is the opposite of my approach,” she says – and we’re glad.

Recently, Julie created a pair of collages for the Slow Down Studio open call, featuring a stem of nodding bell-shaped flowers and a cream rose, both on brown. “It perfectly sums up what I enjoy doing right now: flowers, a subject I find delightful, combined with my signature stylistic approach,” she says. And what is that approach, you might ask? Well: “simple, synthetic forms, a limited colour palette, including brown (my favourite colour), a mix of angles and curves and those small paper circles from my hole punch (one of my favourite tools).” Those little dots scatter around the edges like confetti, and she deliberately avoids over-editing the colours or saturation so the original scan’s “authentic, handmade quality” can shine through.

As for what she hopes people take away from her work, Julie is refreshingly relaxed about it. “There isn’t really a message, other than raising my audience’s awareness of the poetry found in simple things,” she says. She thinks the people who connect with her work appreciate its materiality and “see themselves reflected in the universal motifs I choose to depict.”

Plenty is in the works for Julie, including a personal piece for an upcoming exhibition in Sète, plus fairs and markets in London, Marseille, Milan and Valencia in the coming months. She’s also about to start a screen-printed book with the Berlin-based studio Le Raclet. And while we have you, she’d like us to know she’s “looking to expand my commission work as much as possible (take note!)”, with branding projects and press work at the top of her wishlist. “That would be amazing,” she says.

Why GTA 6 is the year’s biggest campaign for a brand that refuses to sell ad space
Rockstar won’t take a penny for product placement, yet half the world’s brands are currently trying to look like Vice City. On the eve of launch, here’s why I think GTA 6 matters to any…

Rockstar won’t take a penny for product placement, yet half the world’s brands are currently trying to look like Vice City. On the eve of launch, here’s why I think GTA 6 matters to any creative professional.

I’m an enthusiastic gamer. But I skipped Grand Theft Auto V entirely. I just couldn’t join the 230 million people who’ve snapped up a copy since it came out 13 years ago, because I couldn’t play as a woman .
Tomorrow, that changes. GTA 6 unlocks at midnight. One of the lead characters, Lucia Caminos, will be waiting for me. And I’ve cleared my diary for the next week.

If you don’t game, you might think that’s a bit pathetic. Fair enough. But if you’re an art director, illustrator or marketer who’s seen those pink-and-orange sunsets flood your feeds lately and wondered what all the fuss is about – it’s only a video game, surely? Well, no it isn’t. Not really.
Not to be dramatic, GTA 6 marks one of the biggest cultural moments in a century. And that’s hugely rewarding, especially for someone who grew up in an era when we still did things together.

Alas, there isn’t much left that everyone experiences together, all at once. We stream different shows on different nights and scroll different feeds. It’s not like the good old days when we’d wait for our favourite programmes on one of four TV channels or get the bus to Hanley’s Fezzy Park to see the latest blockbuster (and hope we bumped into Mark from the year above). GTA is one of the few exceptions. It’s a single date that tens of millions of people have been anticipating for years.

The numbers are daft, too. The second trailer was watched 475 million times in a day. When Rockstar premiered a 27-minute preview on Netflix in August, it drew 31.1 million views in four days and topped the film chart in 87 of the 93 countries Netflix tracks. Strauss Zelnick, chief executive of Rockstar’s parent company Take-Two, described that premiere as “one of the hors d’oeuvres”. Now we’re all hungry for the main course.
Analysts estimate 15.88 million digital pre-orders, worth around $1.54bn. So yeah, it’s big. But the numbers aren’t why I think creatives should be sitting up and paying attention.
As you can imagine, the most wanted media space on the planet right now is a billboard inside Vice City. Yet you can’t buy it.

Zelnick has ruled out product placement and brand deals altogether, on the grounds that “all the brands are made up”. So you’ll not spot any real fizzy drinks or real trainers. Just the usual Patriot Beer, Sessanta Nove and hundreds of other parodies written and designed entirely in-house.

Naturally, the brands have done their thing anyway. Hyundai, BMW and Burger King are among those dressing their social posts in GTA’s sunset palette. Perhaps they’re hoping to enjoy some of that Vice City glow, too.

I’ve just spent a week in Miami Beach, and it was fun to walk around the city GTA 6 is based on. I spotted the ads for the game everywhere. I especially loved seeing street kiosks carrying ads for the game’s fake brands, double entendres and all. A clever bit of marketing, and my friends at Creative Bloq agree.
In Williamsburg, Brooklyn, there’s a vast mural of Jason and Lucia, hand-painted by Colossal Media – the New York sign painters who’ve worked with Rockstar since San Andreas in 2004.

Then there’s the press. The first on-record interviews about the game didn’t go to a gaming site – they went to Dazed, which put Jason and Lucia on the cover of its autumn ‘New Idols’ issue and dressed them in Vice City’s fictional fashion labels. Just brilliant.

And in Wynwood, Miami’s street art district, 10 new murals have gone up from artists including FAILE, Lady AIKO, Queen Andrea and DENIAL, alongside a deal that gives Miami-Dade residents free entry to the Wynwood Walls Museum through 2028. Rockstar says more than 50 real street artists painted the walls inside the game, too. And no generative AI was used.
What’s in it for the rest of us?
OK, so most of us creatives will never have the luxury of a billion-dollar budget or 13 years for a project. But take away that scale and you’re left with something pretty old-fashioned.
‘It’s going to be scary’: a week on from Adobe MAX 2026, creatives get honest about the future
I left this year’s Adobe MAX Sneaks feeling a bit wary. So I asked creatives what scares them most about their work, listened to what two of Adobe’s most senior people had to say, and ended…

I left this year’s Adobe MAX Sneaks feeling a bit wary. So I asked creatives what scares them most about their work, listened to what two of Adobe’s most senior people had to say, and ended up facing a few of my own fears.

If you’re familiar with Adobe’s Sneaks , you’ll know they’ve earned legendary status at Adobe MAX over the years. It’s an hour or two when the people who build the experimental tools get up and show them off to a live audience, livestreamed to millions of creatives worldwide. A nerve-racking experience, I’m sure... Not just because the whole world is watching, but because anything could go wrong.

Usually, there are loud whoops and almost cult-like, frenzied excitement as Adobe proudly reveals its latest innovations. Not so much this year, from where I was sitting, or indeed the last. Certainly not as much since Adobe started to introduce AI into its suite; maybe the audience was just too stunned to applaud.

For more than a decade, I watched from my desk in Manchester in the middle of the night, scribbling down notes for readers who wanted to know what was coming next. How their working lives were about to get easier thanks to the software they’d spent ages learning. This year, I was right there in the room in Miami Beach, as an editor, sitting with the other British journalists. Terry Crews was hosting, dressed head to toe in a bright pink suit with shiny blue shoes and pink socks. And much like anyone who watched, I’m still processing it.
So what did Sneaks show us?
The tools come straight out of Adobe Labs, and none of them is guaranteed to ship, although some do. And yeah, AI played a leading role. Of course it did. The future is here.

As always, I’m pretty nuanced about these things. It’s not so black-and-white. If Adobe can empower creatives to skip the mundane stuff and focus on their creativity, then brilliant. If it can open the playing field to those who previously didn’t have the means to create, then I’m all for it. The computer, after all, opened the gates to so many more people back in the 1990s, and the internet welcomed even more.
But there are multiple fine lines. Where AI might be useful in one corner, it feels unwelcome in another.

Ten projects took to the stage. Some were very much welcome, and those were the ones that got the whoops. Project Rinse Repeat copies edits you’ve made in one area of an image to another, while keeping everything editable in Photoshop.

Project Link Up lets you drag design elements into a scene and sit back and watch their perspective, scale and style adapt to fit, landing as editable vector artwork. Project Deep Brush , my personal favourite, understands an image’s shape, colour and lighting, so you can quite literally paint light into a scene. All clever, time-saving stuff.

Others were not so welcome. Project Screen Test lets you build a fictional character’s look, voice and personality, and then chat to them. I mean, it was incredible, sure. But is it really necessary? Project Live Set changes a subject, a set or a camera move while the video is still playing.

Project Sight Span turns a single image into a 3D-style space that feels like you can step into it and walk around, framing shots that were never taken in real life. And then Project Sound Bender lets you describe a sound and pick it clean out of a finished mix. Mind-blowing, but I’m not sure the audience was happy.

As I sat there, looking around at my startled fellow attendees, I finally realised how fast things are moving. Casting, set design, location scouting, sound editing... whole corners of the industry flashed past in a few minutes each. I’ve been using AI tools for three or four years now. I’m an adopter, and I’m not going to pretend otherwise. But sitting there in that big conference hall, I felt a bit sick rather than excited.
So, still in Miami, I did what I always do in these situations. I asked you.
What keeps you up at night
I posted a simple question on LinkedIn: what are you most scared of in your work right now? More than a dozen replied, and their thoughts offered some brilliant insight.
OUTSIDE IN: New Exhibition at GraffitiStreet Gallery, Chichester
What happens when art made for walls, rooftops and railway lines comes indoors? OUTSIDE IN brings internationally recognised street artists to GraffitiStreet Gallery, Chichester, exploring…

What happens when art made for walls, rooftops and railway lines comes indoors? This November 20th, GraffitiStreet Gallery presents OUTSIDE IN, a group exhibition bringing together internationally recognised artists whose practices are rooted in graffiti and street art. Exploring the journey from public space to the studio, the exhibition considers how an artist’s distinctive visual language moves between different settings, scales and materials, and how these transitions change the way we experience their work.

A graffiti tag, a mural spanning a building, a canvas contained within a frame and a sculpture within the gallery each create a different encounter with the viewer. Site can amplify or redirect meaning, scale can alter our response, and material can reveal another dimension of an artist’s practice. Yet across these shifts, the symbols, ideas and signature styles that define each artist remain unmistakable. How much of urban art is bound to its setting, and how much travels with the artist?
As the street enters the gallery, OUTSIDE IN invites visitors to discover what changes, what intensifies and what endures.

German artist Case Maclaim , a pioneer of photorealist graffiti, moves between monumental murals and intimate studio paintings, bringing the technical precision and extraordinary attention to detail that have defined his practice into a more concentrated setting.

Spanish duo PichiAvo unite classical sculpture and graffiti, bringing ancient mythology into dialogue with contemporary urban culture. Their distinctive compositions challenge the boundaries between artistic traditions, allowing the language of the street to coexist with the enduring influence of classical art.

South African artist Faith47 , internationally recognised for her poetic large-scale murals, extends her practice into sculpture, exploring how familiar themes and imagery acquire a different physical presence through material and form.

British artist My Dog Sighs transforms overlooked objects and unconventional surfaces into emotionally resonant artworks, while Sweet Toof brings the irreverence of his unmistakable teeth motif into paintings that connect graffiti, portraiture and art history.

Belgian artist Joachim Lambrechts balances spontaneous mark-making with carefully considered compositions, while South African artist Sonny Sundancer explores the expressive possibilities of abstraction beyond his large-scale street practice. Nean Kingdom , whose distinctive imagery has become an instantly recognisable part of his artistic identity, similarly demonstrates how a visual language developed through street art can retain its character in the studio.

Although their approaches differ considerably, each artist offers a perspective on the relationship between artistic identity and environment. Moving between the street and the studio becomes more than a change of location; it creates opportunities to experiment with materials, reconsider scale and develop ideas beyond the conditions in which their practices first emerged.
An Exhibition Across Materials and Disciplines

Alongside the featured artists, OUTSIDE [IN] includes selected artworks and collectables by Banksy, STIK and TOX, bringing further dimensions to the exhibition’s exploration of graffiti and street art.

From the repetition of a graffiti tag to the intimacy of a painting, the exhibition reveals how urban art continues to evolve across disciplines while retaining its connection to the visual culture of the street.

Together, these diverse practices create an opportunity to experience familiar artistic languages in an entirely different context, encouraging visitors to look beyond the surface and consider the ideas, techniques and identities that give each artist’s work its distinctive character.

JM Brea Paints the Moment Before the Crucifixion in Montehermoso
JM Brea has painted La Crucifixión del Cristo de los Remedios outside the chapel of the Santísimo Cristo de los Remedios in Montehermoso, Spain. Made for the town council, the mural stops…

JM Brea has painted La Crucifixión del Cristo de los Remedios outside the chapel of the Santísimo Cristo de los Remedios in Montehermoso, Spain. Made for the town council, the mural stops just before the first nail is driven through Christ’s hand. Brea places the moment of impending violence beside a chapel whose altar holds an image of the crucified Christ.

In Brea’s account of the composition, Christ’s hand rests against the wood of the cross while a nail is held over its palm. The action has not yet happened: the pointed nail and the waiting hand carry the tension. Brea describes the treatment as Baroque in character, a choice tied to the chapel rather than simply to the biblical subject.

The painting also draws on details at the site. Three nails represented at the top of the main altarpiece find an echo in the mural’s single poised nail and the shadow of three fingers across the painted wood, according to Brea. Outside, three granite crosses stand near the chapel. These connections give the work a particular setting: its scene begins on the exterior wall, while the crucifixion appears in the sculpture inside.

Montehermoso’s town council dates the chapel to the 16th century and describes it as regional Baroque in style. The image of the Cristo de los Remedios inside is from the 18th century. The chapel remains associated with the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross and devotions to Christ of the Remedies, making Brea’s subject closely bound to the building’s use as well as its decoration.

The mural is part of Vientos del Pueblo, a literary and cultural route developed with Montehermoso’s schools and local partners. The project links artistic work in the town to education and local heritage. Brea’s contribution is grounded in one place: the chapel, its crosses and the image encountered within.

Eltono painted Composition on Building CSB#33 in Nashua, New Hampshire, in September 2026. The work extends across multiple sides of the downtown Elm Street parking garage, where Beyond Walls curated a public-art project for the city. Its setting gives the composition more than one face: it is encountered around the building rather than from a single viewpoint.

The garage is an unusually expansive support for a wall painting. Eltono’s work occupies several of its exterior elevations, while Leon Keer painted separate sections of the same structure. Across town, Mr. June painted the High Street garage. Together, the commissions form Nashua in Motion, a project developed by Beyond Walls with the city and architecture firm Payette.

Work on the garages began on September 14 and concluded on October 2, 2026. Beyond Walls led the painting phase after preparations for the two structures, with the artists working on active downtown facilities rather than isolated mural walls. At Elm Street, the building’s corners and successive elevations make the painting something visitors encounter in stages as they move around the garage.

That relationship between a work and its surroundings has long been part of Eltono’s practice. In an artist statement published by Beyond Walls, he describes public space as a place of unpredictable conditions that affect what an artist makes. His Nashua painting puts that practice on a conspicuous piece of city infrastructure, though the statement does not prescribe a reading of this particular composition.

French street artist Seth Globepainter has created six murals across the Faroe Islands for We Need Art 2026 , drawing upon the archipelago’s maritime heritage, wildlife and cultural traditions to explore childhood, migration and belonging. Set against dramatic coastal landscapes, working harbours and familiar village architecture, the paintings bring Seth’s distinctive visual language into dialogue with the lives of the people who inhabit these North Atlantic islands.

Through images of children, seabirds and symbolic encounters, the series considers what it means to leave home, to imagine a world beyond it and to preserve the traditions that connect one generation to another.

Puffin: A Meeting Between Two Worlds

In Puffin , painted in Kollafjørður, a young boy wearing traditional Faroese clothing and a puffin mask offers a small sand eel to a puffin wearing a human mask. The figures face one another in an unusual exchange of identities, their shared gesture suggesting an attempt to understand the world from another’s perspective.

The painting takes inspiration from the relationship between humans and nature in the Faroe Islands, where fishing, seabirds and the surrounding waters have long shaped everyday life. Seth approaches that relationship through a reversal of familiar roles, allowing the child to assume the appearance of a bird while the puffin takes on human characteristics.

For the artist, the encounter is concerned with harmony, adaptation and empathy. Rather than portraying people and wildlife as separate inhabitants of the landscape, the exchanged masks suggest the possibility of recognising something of ourselves in another living being.

The mural’s setting reinforces that connection. Painted on a harbour building, with the waters of the fjord and surrounding mountains visible alongside it, the work occupies the environment from which its imagery is drawn. In one photograph, a young child wearing traditional Faroese dress sits beneath the painted figures, creating an unexpected relationship between the artwork and the living culture it represents.

The emotional complexity of leaving home emerges in Taking Flight , where a seated boy watches a young girl rise into the air. Painted on opposing sections of weathered concrete, the two figures are physically separated by a gap in the structure, transforming the existing architecture into an essential part of their story.

Seth connects the painting to the migration of Faroese people who leave the islands in search of employment and opportunities elsewhere. The departing girl becomes a figure of possibility and separation, while the boy who remains watches a departure he cannot prevent.

The artist also draws upon the relationship between Peter Pan and Wendy in J. M. Barrie’s novel, introducing another interpretation concerned with the loss of innocence and the passage from childhood into adulthood. The girl’s flight carries both the excitement of discovering another world and the sadness of leaving something familiar behind.

Positioned among rocky ground, vegetation and residential buildings, the figures appear almost absorbed into their surroundings. The distance between them, emphasised by the physical break in the concrete, gives the painting a quiet emotional force that might have been lost on an uninterrupted wall.

The cruel world of Octopus Wrestling, the most bizarre sport ever which was finally banned in 1976
People really will watch anything, won't they?
One wonders what the editors of Mechanix Illustrated magazine thought when they received a pitch for an article about the writer’s sport of choice, titled ‘Octopus Wrestling is my Hobby’.

In fairness, perhaps it was because the year was 1949. Anything that could keep people’s minds off that thing that ended four years ago was worth a try. Especially considering the emergence of all the horrifying secrets the enemy was keeping. The war was over only in terms of he cessation of conflict, but the world kept going in its shadow for decades. So God help us all, sometimes we just need to stop thinking about the world and start thinking about some freak who wrestles sea creatures for his kicks.

The author wasn’t kidding either. Wilmon Menard wrote about his time in Tahiti, where he assisted local hunters in taking to the water and killing an octopus that Menard said had 25-foot-long tentacles. The absorbing way he wrote about this experience, plus his insistence that it had done amazing things for his mental and physical health, meant that the article became a sensation. So much so that diving clubs in the Pacific Northwest thought this would be a brilliant idea to adapt into a proper sport.

The first thing they did was remove the killing of it all. This wouldn’t be competitive hunting because that would be barbaric , especially considering the quarry and its rarity in parts of the ocean accessible to humans. The first version of this article adapted into a proper sport came from the Puget Mud Sharks Diving Club, where they would mark out an area between 30 and 60 feet into the sea. Then one team would dive down, coax out one of the octopuses just going about its day, then capture it and take it to land.

There, the octopus would be weighed and then released. The divers would then be given points based on the weight of their quarry, which would be doubled if they brought it to the surface without scuba gear. Other diving clubs took this rule set and began using it themselves, and suddenly, clubs would compete in octopus wrestling competitions that would attract crowds of hundreds. If you think people would just watch anything pre-TV out of boredom, you’re actually not quite right.

Perhaps it was morbid curiosity, but people tuned in to keep track of the octopus wrestling in droves. Not only as a flash-in-the-pan novelty either, but in the 1960s, there were World Octopus Wrestling Championships that attracted crowds of thousands in person and hundreds of thousands on TV. People clowned on Marty Mauser in Marty Supreme for his belief that the next big sport was ping-pong, but considering that octopus wrestling was gaining momentum at the time that film was set, maybe he had a point.

However, it couldn’t last for two reasons. For one thing, octopus wrestling was incredibly exciting… if you were 50 feet under the water where it was actually happening. Crowds in person weren’t, and TV technology of the 1960s couldn’t possibly put a camera down there. So normal people got bored of the spectacle real quick. Then the 1970s came, and the other shoe dropped. You see, by that time, the tech had been made to just about film professionally underwater, and Jacques Cousteau had used it to make Octopus, Octopus , a still astonishing documentary about how smart, gentle and all-around amazing our eight-tentacled friends are.

It was a massive hit, and suddenly, octopus wrestling began to be seen as cruel even if the quarry stayed alive after reaching the surface. Which, considering the struggle and the time out of the water, many of them did not. By 1976, the practice was banned, and while some people still try and match the glory days but doing illegal octopus wrestling bouts, they’re shamed on social media at best and arrested at worst.
Just as it should be, to be fair.

Juan Luna: The painter so evil that his paintings were thought to be cursed

It makes sense that for years, people assumed that the great work of art Portrait of a Lady by Juan Luna depicted his wife Paz Pardo de Tavera, especially if you didn’t know the full story behind their relationship.

The subject of Portrait of a Lady is bathed in almost holy white. Dressed in a white gown and relaxing on her bed, she looks at the viewer with a serene expression as she toys with a rosary that provides a spark of red across her otherwise pure chest. The soft-focus colours, teal and light orange bookending the light in the middle, the gentle line work, the overall peaceful feel of the portrait.
It makes sense that this would be how an artist would portray someone they were desperately in love with. Then you hear the other side of the story.

Juan Luna and Paz Pardo de Tavera may have been in love once, but Luna was dangerous. He had a short, easily lost temper and was violent with many people. However, he didn’t start taking that anger out on Tavera until the tragic loss of their three-year-old daughter, Maria de la Paz. Luna lost what little control he had in the aftermath of Maria’s loss. He began verbally and physically abusing her, suspecting her of having an affair and eventually beating a confession out of her at gunpoint.

Of course, there’s no actual historical record or proof that she ever had an affair. Luna was just a violent man who wanted a reason to feel like his abuse and murderous nature was justified. Paz went to her family home to hide from him to hide but it wasn’t enough. Luna broke in and shot Paz and her mother dead. Something Luna was acquitted from in 1893 by arguing that it was a “crime of passion” because of her infidelity.

It’s a testament to the sheer misogyny of the day that even Paz’s brothers testified in favour of the man who murdered their mother and sister because he told them that the woman he murdered had been unfaithful to him.

Thus, Portrait of a Lady soon became an infamous work. A woman depicted by the man who murdered her. It became such a point of conversation that people became convinced that Paz’s spirit haunted the painting. They pointed to previous owners suffering from illnesses, financial catastrophe and death, with the most famous owner being the Filipino First Lady Imelda Marcos. Supposedly, the painting hung in the Marcos residence while her family were overthrown in the People Power Revolution.

It’s a harrowing story. However, that’s all it is, for two reasons. First off, since 1986, the “cursed” painting has been housed in the National Museum of Fine Arts in Manila. 40 years on, everything has been pretty much hunky dory there. Still, that’s not the only major flaw in the story. Howie Severino made a documentary about the life of Juan Luna and, in particular, his time in Paris. While working on the documentary, he found proof that the woman in Portrait of a Lady was actually Angela Duche, a French model he often worked with.

However, this story also doesn’t really need to be “debunked” because it concerns ghosts and curses . Things that don’t exist. So, why did this story exist to begin with? Honestly, I think it’s the reason that stories develop in the first place. We see not only the horrifying end of Paz Pardo de Tavera’s life, but the knowledge that a fate like that is nowhere near as rare for women as we’d hope it to be. The injustice and the fear that reaction sparks within us are the kind we don’t process by simply talking about it, especially at the time.

People of the 1890s in Paris wouldn’t have talked about it as an injustice at all. Again, even Paz’s own brothers felt that she got what she deserved. So, how do people talk about an injustice that they can’t talk about openly? They turn it into a story. So maybe it doesn’t matter that the subject of the picture isn’t actually Paz Pardo de Tavera. If it means people remember her story and, by extension, the story of so many women whose meaningless murders people thought were justified?
Maybe that’s the very meaning of the term “print the legend.”

In addition, deadly Trials await at the brand-new Mall Map, where The Fog meets an eerie, uncanny liminal space.
Adding even more fun is the “Red Band” version of the launch trailer, which you can see below.
A love letter to the series’ most iconic kills, Art’s gameplay delivers on the killer clown’s signature blend of carnage and comedy with a trash bag full of terrifying toys for players to unleash.
A serial killer raised from the dead by demonic forces, Art the Clown is always down for a bloody good time.

With his Power, Bag of Toys , Art reaches into his trash bag for a random selection of weapons including a flail, a flamethrower, a firearm, a beer bottle full of acid, and even that little bike horn. Each successful hit with a toy builds its deadliness, eventually letting Art knock down injured Survivors and execute them with murderous glee. To top it off, each weapon will have its own unique Mini-Mori.

As for perks, Art has three: Funny Business grants a random effect in addition to a temporary haste buff whenever you damage a Generator. These effects can be as helpful as blocking Generators or as wacky as a burst of confetti. Kill Spree ends each Trial with a merry massacre, letting Art unlock the ability to kill remaining Survivors when they have all reached 2 Hook States and all Generators have been completed. Finally, Laughingstock makes Survivors near completed Generators Exhausted and Oblivious.

Countering Art’s mayhem is Survivor Sienna Shaw, who has a few tricks of her own. Best Gift Ever lets you drop items to gain powerful passive abilities. Whenever you take a protection hit, Shared Trauma allows all Survivors within 12m to recover from the Exhausted status while running. After being chased by the Killer, Valkyrie’s Rage lets you turn the tables by unleashing an extra-powerful pallet stun.

Arriving alongside Art and Sienna is The Hartshorne Mall , a brand-new original Map that has been long requested by the Dead by Daylight community. Littered with haunting storefronts and liminal hallways, what was once a friendly space for families to go shopping has been warped by The Entity into a dark reflection of itself.

Answering the long-standing request from the community to explore more liminal spaces in The Fog, this Map invokes a nostalgic, comforting, but also unsettling feeling as the familiar turns into the uncanny. Keen-eyed players may be able to spot some interesting lore drops for beloved Survivor Dwight Fairfield, who experienced a traumatic encounter with The Entity while lost in the mall as a child.
The Dead by Daylight: Terrifier Chapter can be found on PC via Steam and the Epic Games Store , PlayStation 5 and PlayStation 4 , Xbox One and the Xbox Series , and the Nintendo Switch .

‘Mindhunter’: David Fincher Explains Why a Season 3 Won’t Happen at Netflix
Filmmaker David Fincher proved with Se7en that he knew how to tell a gripping serial-killer story, as it is still considered one of the best thrillers of the ’90s. .

Filmmaker David Fincher proved with Se7en that he knew how to tell a gripping serial-killer story, as it is still considered one of the best thrillers of the ’90s. Fincher would return to the realm of serial killers for Zodiac a decade later, which told the real-life story of the serial killer that stalked California and remains unidentified to this day. Against all odds, Fincher arguably made an even better serial-killer movie with his second contribution to the genre.

It makes perfect sense, then, that when Fincher made a TV show about the history of criminal profiling, his Mindhunter on Netflix would be a major hit with critics. Despite both seasons securing critical acclaim, the show only earned a niche-but-passionate fanbase , resulting in Netflix pulling the plug on the program.

Virtually every interview with Fincher or stars Jonathan Groff and Holt McCallany eventually circles back to the fate of the series, and Fincher’s current promotional circuit is no different. Speaking with the Happy Sad Confused podcast, Fincher very directly explained that, while he appreciates the fans of the show, a Season 3 would likely cost another $100 million and the audience never justified Netflix’s spend.

“Every time somebody says to me, ‘Can’t we bring that back?’ I said, ‘Here’s what I need you to do. You need to go out, you need to make 10 million friends, and you need each of them to send me $10, and then I’ll do it ,'” Fincher explained. “I love the fact that people finally love the show. Things have a time and a place, and the best-laid plans led to not an optimal delivery system or schedule. Getting off on that wrong foot put us on the wrong foot for the second season. We were very close to being quadriplegics by the third season.”

Another significant setback for the series was that, after Season 1, Fincher took a step back from the series and allowed a new showrunner to step in. After a majority of the second season was written, Fincher finally got to look at the scripts and didn’t feel like they aligned with the series , forcing the season to start over. This meant it was nearly two years before Seasons 1 and 2.
Fincher explained Netflix’s attempts to compromise:

“That’s when Netflix said, ‘Look, we got to be honest with you, there are two million people who love the show. And the show costs $100 million a season, and it’s basically guys with styrofoam cups in their hands sitting at stainless steel tables getting the rundown. Is there anything you can do, so this audience can grow?’ I said, ‘What do you mean?’ They said, ‘I don’t know, will they ever run after somebody with a gun in their hand?’ I said, ‘No, no, that’s not what it is.’ They were like, ‘We get it, but we have to ask. Can you make concessions to get closer to CSI?’ I said, ‘No, I can’t. I won’t. And I don’t think you really want me to.’ And they said, ‘We don’t, but we don’t know how else we are going to grow this.'”

It’s clear that Fincher still has a passion for the project, but the reality is that the show was always too expensive to justify its viewership. If a world existed where money wasn’t a question, a Season 3 isn’t impossible, but given how much time has passed since Netflix canceled the series, each day makes it even less likely we’ll ever see the series return.
Luckily, the first two seasons are still available to revisit on Netflix.

Mike Flanagan Confirms ‘Carrie’ Season 2 Targeting 2027 Filming, Writers Are “Firing on All Cylinders”
It’s safe to say that Mike Flanagan has joined the ranks of filmmakers like Frank Darabont and Mick Garris as someone who has an innate ability to adapt the works of Stephen King. .

It’s safe to say that Mike Flanagan has joined the ranks of filmmakers like Frank Darabont and Mick Garris as someone who has an innate ability to adapt the works of Stephen King . While some filmmakers only make one foray into bringing King’s works to life, the aforementioned filmmakers have all developed multiple projects inspired by King, with Flanagan adapting Gerald’s Game , Doctor Sleep , and The Life of Chuck .

Given his intrinsic understanding of King, it came as no surprise that Flanagan’s Carrie reboot series on Prime Video would be renewed for a second season . With the filmmaker having teased he envisioned the project having a three-season trajectory, this renewal takes us one step closer to realizing his full vision.

Even though the first season just debuted last month, Flanagan recently confirmed to The Hollywood Reporter that he already has a writers room hard at work on Season 2 and that he’s already completed the script for the Season 2 premiere.

“I turned in the first episode script earlier this morning, which is very exciting. We’ve been working on it unofficially for a while because I had always hoped that it could go this way and wanted to be prepared in case it did,” Flanagan explained. “ We’re gearing up to hopefully go into production next year, and we’ll see how it all shapes up . The beautiful thing is that Carrie’s journey has always seemed to me to have a clear trajectory. And that was something, even though we were never taking for granted that it would happen, it was something that was always in the back of my mind.”

Making Flanagan’s Carrie all the more impressive is the fact that we’ve already seen the events of King’s debut novel brought to life a number of times over the years, leaving us to wonder what would set this adaptation apart from its predecessors. One of the biggest changes is that, rather than dying at the end of the journey, Summer H. Howell ‘s Carrie White survived the experience and is seemingly on a path that would connect her with other women with similar abilities .

“I know it was in conversations that I had with Summer about where she could go and with Steve too — King was very aware and excited about the potential for that ,” the filmmaker continued. “It’s always been in the room with us, but we didn’t really have permission to fully explore it until it was real because you don’t want to jinx it. But we are fully immersed in it. The writers room is firing on all cylinders .”
If the next season were to film early in 2027, it could potentially be released later in the year, though no release date has been confirmed.

Erotic thriller Bone Lake wasn’t the first collaboration between director Mercedes Bryce Morgan and star Maddie Hasson ( Malignant ). The pair previously worked together on Morgan’s feature directorial debut, surreal psychological horror movie Fixation , and the official trailer has arrived ahead of the film’s release.
Quiver will release Fixation on Digital and VOD on December 11 .

Hasson stars as Dora, a young woman undergoing a psychiatric evaluation before her sentencing in an unusual murder trial. But as the tests become more personal and frightening, she begins to question the true motives of her doctors.

Reality doesn’t appear to be reliable in the trailer below, which sees recreations of Dora’s past get more disturbing and strange. It brings Alice in Wonderland to mind as the subconscious becomes a bizarre, terrifying place for Hasson’s character.

Genesis Rodriguez, Atticus Mitchell and Stephen McHattie ( Pontypool , Watchmen ) also star. William Day Frank , who developed the story with Morgan and producer Katrina Kudlick , wrote the screenplay.

Morgan said in her director’s statement, “ Fixation was born from this idea: What if you had to escape the physical manifestation of your own mind? This film follows a young woman who’s been told she’s ‘CRAZY’ her entire life. As the story unfolds, it becomes clear that the men in her life have pushed her to this point so that she feels helpless without them. More now than ever, I feel it’s important to create stories that strip away the ‘woman-is-crazy’ narrative that has been hammered into our brains since we were kids.”

“I’ve always been fascinated by the close link between love and hatred in family dynamics and by patriarchal figures,” Morgan continues. “What was once remembered as a loving childhood memory could later be a source of trauma. ‘Love’ is often used by abusers as an excuse for manipulation and violence.”
Fixation made its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2022 , and arrives next month on Digital.

Manchester man successfully flies to Spain on Ryanair flight using his wife’s passport
You get what you pay for.
A man flew from Manchester to Spain for a stag party using his wife’s passport by mistake, something that wasn’t flagged by staff at Manchester Airport.

Ben Moore told BBC Radio Stoke that the mix-up was only revealed when he touched down in Alicante and began queueing up for passport control. In the interview, he said, “I opened up the passport there and, to my horror, it was my wife’s photo on the passport.”
He then said, “I searched through all my luggage about eight times thinking there’s no way I could have got to Alicante without my own passport.”
Moore initially thought that he’d picked up both by mistake, used his own to get through customs back in Manchester before taking out the other one in Spain.

After all, Moore owns property in Spain and makes the trip multiple times a year. It was possible that he’d made a mistake while on autopilot. However, he realised that the only passport he had in his luggage belonged to his wife. Something that confused Spanish authorities just as much as him after he went to them and explained the situation. A process that Moore said the police officers there were “a little bit intimidating” about.

Moore’s trip ended early, with him being put straight back on a flight to the UK while his friends continued the stag party without him. The flight out from Manchester was operated by Ryanair, who have announced that they’ll be reviewing the matter.
However, they also stated that passenger document checks at the boarding gate are technically not carried out by the company themselves, but by their third-party ground handling provider Swissport.

BBC News reached out to Manchester Airport for comment, who said that the responsibility for checking passports lies with the airlines, as airports only ask for boarding cards from passengers when passing through security.

‘DERELIKT’ and ‘Queen’s Domain’ Bring Low-Poly PlayStation-Era Horror Into the Modern Age
Rather than looking to the future, two recent games have found inspiration in PlayStation-era games, both in look and gameplay, to great success. .
Rather than looking to the future, two recent games have found inspiration in PlayStation-era games, both in look and gameplay, to great success.

DERELIKT , from one-man studio Visuwyg, aims to emulate the early days of console first-person shooters by using Alien Resurrection , one of the first FPS games that used the twin-stick control scheme that’s become standard today, as a template.
The other game, Queen’s Domain , looks to the legendary studio FromSoftware , but mimics the feel of their earlier King’s Field series, rather than copying the combat of Dark Souls as so many do.
Despite using these old games as a starting point, both feel extremely modern, learning from years of game design lessons while still harkening back to an older era.
DERELIKT Turns PlayStation Nostalgia Into Modern Survival Horror

In DERELIKT , you play a new recruit who is deployed to investigate Von Neumann Outpost, a research station on an asteroid orbiting Saturn. Based on the mental state of one of the scientists you talk to, who is muttering to himself about songs and spirals, it seems like whatever they’ve found on that cursed rock is dangerous to everyone around. Once you get there, you find the outpost overrun with strange creatures, some of them clearly mutated from the previous residents of the station .
Not only that, but the remaining survivors are all a bit off, making it hard to know who to trust as you try to put a stop to whatever is happening.

Right off the bat, it’s clear that the game wants you to know that it’s a love letter to the PlayStation. The opening splash screen resembles the classic PlayStation startup movie, right down to the iconic sound. The graphics look like they’re ripped straight out of the past, with big chunky models and wobbly texture warping. The cutscenes even capture the feel of old-school pre-rendered cutscenes, with scanline effects that complete the illusion. It’s such a stark contrast to the high-fidelity AAA games we see everywhere, and it uses it smartly to make the dark corridors of the facility feel like any kind of horror could be hiding in their indistinct shadows.

Aside from the extremely obvious Alien vibes, which are hard for any space horror game to avoid, there are other clear references that the game pays its respects to. Strange glyphs and obelisks play a big part in the mystery behind Von Neumann Outpost, which brings to mind the Marker from the Dead Space series, and the mutated humans reminded me a bit of both System Shock 2 and Half-Life , especially since it has a similar level of graphic fidelity to those classics.

There’s even a flashlight to illuminate the hallways like Doom 3 , though you can wield that and one of the game’s many guns simultaneously . Despite being a pastiche of a lot of different influences, there’s still enough with the characters and the lore that makes it feel like its own thing, making it just the right combination of original and homage.

The actual gameplay is retro at its heart, but not in a way that feels outdated. Shooting in the game still feels responsively modern, even if it is slightly lacking in impact from animation or VFX, but it has a classic survival horror style of ammo management that makes you think carefully about every firefight. There’s a tension in realizing you’re almost out of shotgun shells as a huge worm is spitting acid at you, making you take a moment and breathe before you pop out and take a desperate shot at it in hopes of killing it before your gun empties.

Even though it has that System Shock 2 DNA in vibes, it’s not entirely an immersive sim, but there are elements of it there . As you continue to find strange relics, they open up parts of your mind, allowing you to unlock upgrades and improve your character. It doesn’t feel like it gives you the immersive sim levels of freedom to approach the game with different tactics; it’s still mostly a standard shooter at its core, but it’s nice to have a power curve as you progress.

Nobody’s Ever Asked Me That : Anna Konkle
The co-creator/co-star of Pen15 , whose beautiful memoir The Sane One came out earlier this year, gets deep on therapy, childhood trauma and ill-advised travel.
My guest today is actor, comedian and writer Anna Konkle, whose excellent memoir The Sane One cameout earlier this year.

If you know Konkle from anything, it’s almost certainly Pen15 , the TV show she co-created and co-starred in with Maya Erskine , in which the thirtysomething pair played awkward 12-year-old best friends navigating the perils of middle-school life, acting opposite real tweens.
Konkle and Erskine mined their own respective adolescences to create an inspired comedy that was hilarious and painful in equal measure, and rightly became a cultural phenomenon.

Straight after Konkle finished the second and final season of Pen15 , she began writing The Sane One , which looks at her life through the lens of childhood trauma and the shadow it has cast over her adulthood.

Though there are moments of humor, The Sane One is not one of those light comedic memoirs. Instead, the book is emotionally incredibly acute and insightful, as Konkle details her mother’s mental health issues and her complex relationship with her father, from whom she was estranged for five years, reconciling only shortly before his death. The book also shows the extensive work Konkle has done on herself to process the pain of the past and find empathy for the people in her life, with that growth best exemplified by a remarkable letter she wrote to her father.

My conversation with Konkle was beset by some technical issues, but if anything it kinda bonded us as we talked about such diverse topics as: why each of us tells white lies, her (sometimes reckless) quest for adventure in the Himalayas, how to navigate eating alone, re-evaluating her childhood after watching an old home movie, how Pen15 was essentially a $20 million therapy session, why Al-Anon needs to get the Raya treatment, and much more.
The Sane Out is now wherever you get your books, and it’s terrific. I’ll give a special recommendation to the audiobook, and if you haven’t seen Pen15 , you should go check it out ASAP.

Perturbator and KABBEL Got Into Electronic Music From Gaming
The electronic musicians catch up about their love for video game soundtracks, writing lyrics in English versus French, and more.

Perturbator , aka James Kent, is a French electronic musician based in Paris; KABBEL is the project of the Gothenburg, Sweden-based French electronic musician Gregory Hoepffner. The debut KABBEL album, When The Was Is Over , just came on Perturbator’s label Music of the Void out last month, so to celebrate, the two got on Zoom to catch up about the origin of the project, video game soundtracks, and more.
KABBEL : Thank you so much. It’s all thanks to you, man.
KABBEL : And you saw the potential in it, so thank you. It’s a two-way street.
Perturbator : I’m glad I got to release it because it’s a great album.
KABBEL : I see that you’re going on tour soon. I’m also going on tour at the end of the week, so I thought we could start with some touring related questions.
Perturbator : Is it going to be a long tour?
KABBEL : It’s not very long. It’s just six shows. But for me, that’s already a pretty big deal. [ Laughs .]

Perturbator : That’s pretty cool. I remember my first tour — we have the same manager, Seb, just for the record — it was in his car, and it was a week around France. We would sleep in little hotels and stuff. It was good times. I wouldn’t say I miss it, but it was a very carefree moment. So enjoy it. You know, when you get bigger, you’ll get a tour bus… [ Laughs .]

KABBEL : It’s funny because I’ve toured with obviously way bigger artists and bands than I am, and they always say the same thing: They miss the freedom of just being two or three people in a car or a train and not having all these complicated things to do with all the equipment, the tour bus, and whatever.
Perturbator : The logistics. Yeah, absolutely. I can’t say I truly miss it. I kind of just miss the era. But I’m very happy with the tour bus.
KABBEL : You miss the possibility of what comes next, maybe.
Perturbator : Hey, who knows — maybe one day we’ll have private jets.
Perturbator : How many side projects do you have? And how do you approach them differently from KABBEL?
KABBEL : Well, I have a bit too many of them, to be honest, for my own sanity and health. But I have a lot of talented friends that often invite me into these adventures, and I always say yes.
Perturbator : Are you singing in all of them? Or do you have different roles in them?

KABBEL : It’s always a different role. I’m not always the center of the artistic vision. I’m mostly in service of a vision that sometimes comes from me, and sometimes it comes from other people. I try to approach that as if it was different characters for different movies, for example. So every one of these characters has a different view of the world and a different taste. And that’s how I make decisions, based on these, quote-unquote, “characters.”

Perturbator : That’s pretty cool. I have like something similar, where I have different musical projects. Some of them are solo projects, which is just me with machines and synthesizers, and also bands. But I see them like you — I don’t see characters, but I use those to do stuff that I wouldn’t do in Perturbator, to experiment.
KABBEL : It allows you to push ideas further than you would be allowed in your main project.

Perturbator : Yeah, absolutely. I have a side project where I wouldn’t dare do stuff like that on a Perturbator record. I wouldn’t try to go that far or that experimental. So I use that as a catharsis kind of thing.
