The day 10,000 women marched on Versailles and won the French Revolution
The original cost of living crisis.

If we think the current cost of living crisis is bad (and to be clear, it is), we should spare a thought for 1700s France , where a cost of living crisis got so apocalyptically bad it inspired the French Revolution.

While one can’t help but generalise when talking about a period of history as Earth-shaking as the French Revolution, it is true. One of the key things that turned the opinion of the French working class against the nobility was how expensive bread had gotten. Combined with the rumours that this was not due to a famine or a natural food shortage, but quite simply because Versailles was stockpiling it for themselves, and you’ve got a recipe for a serious regime change.

So, was this true? The history of the French Revolution is a messy one to wade through due to the sheer amount of propaganda on both sides racing around. Was Versailles really just hogging bread for themselves because they thought they had a God-given right to it? Not quite. Turns out that in 1788, destructive hailstorms combined with a brutal winter meant that the national stocks of grain ran low, causing the French government to pay through the nose for foreign imports.

This meant that the government had to place a high premium on grain and bread, which the working class of the nation couldn’t afford. The government tried to take the hit on this, capping bread prices at a more affordable cost and paying the nation’s bakers the subsidy to cover the difference. If we’re to believe the government reports of the time (who often had just as big a problem with Versailles as any of the working class), this nearly bankrupted the entire country.

Thus, the government tried one last roll of the dice. They completely deregulated the domestic grain trade, letting local merchants decide the prices for themselves, thinking class solidarity would mean they’d sell for an accessible price. Deregulating markets has literally never solved anything, though, and that was also the case here. The nation’s merchant class just held onto their grain stocks to increase its value. Considering this was based around food, who would be at the front lines of all this strife?
The class of people in France tasked with buying and preparing food for their families.

It’s true, the people at the forefront of this revolution were women, and on October 5th, 1789, they decided to do something about it. They were fuelled by the rage of not being able to buy more than scraps for their family while Versailles feasted on game and white wine; a riot started in a market in the Faubourg Saint-Antoine district of Paris. It consisted mainly of the city’s women who had been out to market that day and decided that enough was enough.

The riot grew and grew until there were enough people to storm Paris’ City Hall and help themselves to the local government’s food supplies. They didn’t find any there, but what they did find were weapons. This was the turning point for the whole revolution. Their plan (if you could call it that) was to burn down Paris City Hall, at least until the immortal words “À Versailles” were shouted by the known hero of the revolution, Stanislas-Marie Maillard.

This changed the whole makeup of the event. It suddenly went from a riot to a march. The assembled group, mainly made up of between six and ten thousand women, marched 12 miles from Paris to Versailles. How did they get there? Wasn’t there an army or a national guard of some kind to prevent them from leaving Paris? Well, there should have been. However, the mainly working-class members of the National Guard demanded to join the march. They were just as done with this shit as any other member of the working class.

Eventually, the mob arrived at Versailles. They refused to leave until a delegation was brought in to meet with King Louis XVI directly, where the king agreed to their terms. He finally signed the revolutionary decrees his nobility kept demanding he ignore, but it wasn’t enough. Too many people had starved over the past few years for King Louis to just do the bare minimum and be done with it. Especially when people were well aware that the weak-willed Louis could be just as easily bullied out of enforcing these reforms…
One Saliva Bubble: How David Lynch tried to go mainstream
"So, she said to him 'poo-poo on your pee-pee'!"

Considered by many to be the greatest piece of television ever made, Twin Peaks: The Return was a seismic moment even to die-hard fans of David Lynch because it proved one thing that no one saw coming.
His entire career before it had been him holding back.

Yes, baffling movies like Inland Empire , Eraserhead and Mulholland Drive had been Lynch not necessarily on easy mode, but definitely trying to curb some of his more esoteric traits and make his signature style more accessible to others. On the one hand, this is just as well. Twin Peaks: The Return left several people who weren’t high-minded TV critics baffled, confused and bored.

On the other hand, it does ask a tantalising question. What if Lynch tried to actively talk down to his audience and open himself up to making a full-on blockbuster? While his most accessible work, The Straight Story , is also his most low-key and low-stakes, it remains his biggest attempt at a blockbuster alongside Dune . His sole attempt at an adaptation, and one that still alienated several people for all the wrong reasons. What was Lynch’s idea of a film to get butts in seats?

Well, we actually have some idea thanks to his work in the aftermath of Dune . He was in dire straits after that film died a horrible death at the box office, and he was very lucky to get a gritty, somewhat grotesque crime thriller like Blue Velvet off the ground afterwards even at its tiny budget compared to the heights of Dune . Thus, after the success of that film steadied the ship, Lynch was paired with Hill Street Blues showrunner Mark Frost to begin work on the script of his next project.

After the duo initially began work on a shelved Marilyn Monroe biopic, they started work on their idea of a surefire hit, which became One Saliva Bubble . This is a script which really is levelled at the lowest common denominator at points. If you need an example, the inciting incident of the entire film involves a security guard at a military complex saying, “So, she said to him ‘poo-poo on your pee-pee!'”, and laughing so hard that he spits the titular bubble onto a console he’s guarding.

This causes a short circuit in a satellite it’s controlling, which then makes it shoot a laser beam onto a small town in Kansas, causing all of its inhabitants to swap bodies at random. This led to 90 minutes of slapstick fun built around a family man swapping bodies with a psychotic hitman, that Lynch himself described as “out-and-out wacko, dumb comedy”. To be clear, he wasn’t being entirely snooty about this, he said that he and Frost essentially spent the entire writing process thinking of things about the body swap premise that made them laugh and just crammed them into the script one after the other.
Considering they had just finished making Blue Velvet , I can imagine this was a refreshing change of pace.

What’s more, the script was a massive deal in Hollywood. Everyone who read it loved it and was willing to give Lynch a chance after a flop like Dune and a grim little thriller like Blue Velvet could have made him radioactive. Martin Short and Steve Martin signed up to star in the picture; all was set for work on One Saliva Bubble to begin. However, this was when Lynch still had a contract with Dino De Laurentiis’ production company, and six weeks before shooting was due to start, the company filed for bankruptcy.

What brings this full circle, though, is what Lynch and Frost did next. After two Hollywood projects in a row that stalled despite them not only working well together, but enjoying it too, their shared agent suggested they find a project that could work in Frost’s native medium of TV. Frost and Lynch went to a coffee shop in Los Angeles and started work on an idea that would combine the small-town absurdity and broad comedy of One Saliva Bubble with the crime thriller grit of Blue Velvet .
They came away with the pitch, premise and series outline for a little show called Twin Peaks . Not bad for a knucklehead comedy, right?

The beloved movie studio that doesn’t need to make money to survive
A bad sign... But not in the way you'd think.
In any other scenario, this would be a comfortable illustration that the very concept of the movie studio is dead and that billionaires killed it.

Because it should be an absolute crock. A movie studio with over 20 years of experience, six films to its name, and only one of them could be considered a hit. Even then, it was a cult favourite that was a fairly decent hit at the box office upon its release in 2009 and only became a genuine phenomenon with time, a hugely successful home release and a blockbuster theatrical rerelease in the last few years. Ever since then, it’s been diminishing returns at the box office for this studio, yet still they continue.

Not even because all of their movies have an afterlife similar to their debut feature. While they do have other cult hits to their name, a number of their pictures have outright bombed despite being incredibly expensive to make. There doesn’t seem to be all that much interest in their movies, yet they’re still here, taking risks on high-stakes movies. Admittedly, it does help that their CEO is Travis Knight, the son of Nike CEO Phil Knight .

This should make me angry, and in a way, it does. However, it’s not because it’s a clear case of nepotism masking a vacuum of talent. In fact, the opposite is true. Because the movie studio in question is Laika. The makers of some of the best animated movies ever made. And The Boxtrolls and Missing Link , which are, y’know, fine.

However, when they hit, they hit like an absolute train. That debut “hit” I was talking about earlier? Yeah, that’s Coraline . They followed that up with Paranorman and Kubo and the Two Strings . Three masterpieces in a row. Recently, they’ve just made the most epoch-shaking animated spectacular since Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse in the form of their fourth masterpiece, Wildwood . Yet each of them haven’t quite tanked at the box office, but not made anywhere near enough to justify their investment.

Because these films aren’t just expensive, they’re herculean tasks to make. Laika makes stop-motion animated pictures and is committed to the medium , making tactile animated movies that still show things that you would never believe could be done in the medium. However, if they’re so good, why don’t they make any money?

It’s a question that’s bothered me for years. One where the knee-jerk response is the old doomerist sentiment that “people today only want the same regurgitated shit over and over again and original ideas are dying”. Which is a flawed argument for many reasons. For one, that’s always been the case, don’t be a moron. For two, the success of films like Sinners , Obsession , GOAT , Backrooms , Hoppers , Project Hail Mary and The Odyssey shows that ideas that aren’t sequels (even if they are adaptations) can be hits at the box office. So, why don’t Laika movies do the same?

To me, this is the part where their dedication to presenting an untrammelled creative vision comes back to bite them. I believe the high points of their back catalogue are films that could have been mega hits had they been slightly more savvily handled. Coraline , Paranorman , Kubo and the Two Strings and Wildwood are all films that are a little (sometimes much) too violent and scary to be out-and-out kids films, but are also a little too cutesy and sincere to be appreciated by teenagers and young adults.

My theory is that The Boxtrolls and Missing Link were attempts to course correct and go for a younger crowd, but they still were still a little too out there for an audience keen to see Frozen II . Films like this aren’t uncommon, but they need to be expertly handled by a marketing campaign that knows how to target a very specific audience of older children and adults with whimsy in their hearts. As much as I love Laika, I genuinely don’t think they’ve had one of those since Coraline .

However, that quite simply doesn’t matter. Travis Knight might just be the ultimate nepo baby because he is using his generational wealth and clout to get these movies made. The Loneliest Orbit: Why Sci-Fi Needs the Gig Economy, Not Billionaire Fantasy
Daniel Zvereff, director of the new animated feature Moonfish , carefully considers the role science fiction should play in this current moment.

When I was a child, I’d lie in the yard at night, stare at the sky and dream about leaving Earth. My head was full of the rings of Saturn and the red dust of Mars, thinking about worlds where nobody had ever walked. The Apollo missions, the Soviet cosmonauts, the disasters and the triumphs: back then, it felt like proof that no matter how ugly geopolitics got down here, curiosity could still pull us forward together.

Maybe that was a child’s delusion, but our collective relationship with space has since changed into something almost unrecognizable. Over the past 20 years, space has become privatized. If you watch a commercial rocket launch today, the aesthetic is slick: carbon-fiber hulls, tablet consoles and bespoke spacesuits tailored to look good on social media feeds. Private capital sells off-planet travel like a venture-backed manifest destiny, an escape hatch for a ruined planet bought with tech fortunes. Billionaires pay for three minutes of zero gravity, holding up flowers in orbit for multi-camera livestreams cut like fashion commercials. Hollywood mostly plays along. Modern sci-fi gives us clean, digital environments where the actual misery of the void gets buried under good lighting and industrial chic. Characters fly pristine ships, solving crises through sheer heroic grit. It looks great on screen, but it ignores how human labor actually works on a frontier.

Every time people pushed into extreme environments to dig up resources, whether it was on Pacific whaling ships, North Sea oil platforms or in boomtown mines, the story was never about freedom. It was about exploitation: impossible quotas, broken bodies and deadening isolation. Right now, in the new digital frontier, data centers are chewing through power grids and overheating the planet to run algorithmic models. If a company ever sets up a permanent base out in orbit, they won’t be sending the upper class. Space is toxic, freezing and dangerous. The only people out there will be contract workers trapped inside heavy machinery, millions of miles from Earth.

When I started writing my animated feature Moonfish , I wanted to push back against the tech myth. Silicon Valley spent decades promising that a connected world would build an open, utopian paradise. Instead, we got algorithmic surveillance. Moonfish grew out of that frustration: an unglamorous, blue-collar survival story where the only thing keeping a person alive is the memory of home.

During the Cold War, filmmakers understood the importance of imbuing their vision with symbolism critical of their oppressors. In Tarkovsky’s Solaris , Stanislaw Lem’s station isn’t a monument to human genius; it’s a leaky, rusting psychological dump where instruments sit under layers of dust while the crew falls apart from grief. Filmmakers behind the Iron Curtain knew how to smuggle harsh truths through genre. They knew that technology doesn’t fix human nature; it just gives a faceless bureaucracy better ways to control you. Decades later, we live in the world they warned us about. Pretending a privatized orbital space station would run any differently is pure denial.

In Moonfish , the main character is just an off-planet contractor mining rock on an asteroid. He has a simple company rule hanging over his head: hit your extraction quota, or the transport ship leaves you behind. No quota, no pickup. His life is valued strictly by the weight of what he pulls out of the ground. The threat in the film isn’t an alien hiding in the dark, it’s a spreadsheet in a data center back on Earth, checking a box that says his life isn’t worth the fuel cost of bringing him back. Down here, we’re already living that way. Office workers have their keystrokes logged every minute. Gig workers get told that zero stability is just “flexibility and freedom.” A miner forgotten on an asteroid isn’t a sci-fi invention, he’s the direct continuation of a delivery rider pedaling through sleet, or a driver sleeping in a car to hit a surge bonus.

What do 35 years of touring the UK look like to Manic Street Preachers?
Here’s what Nicky Wire remembers best, as told to The Quietus editor John Doran. An excerpt from issue one of SHOWNOTES.

I am very much a homebird, so when it came time for Manic Street Preachers to go on tour I was nervous about it. My Dad had an old grandad’s chair, which he managed to tie to the wall in the back of the hire van, so someone could have a seat on the way to the gig. It was incredibly dangerous. And then on the way back, James would just get in a sleeping bag and lie down in the back of the van, rolling around all over the place as we were driving back home. He can sleep anywhere.

We had such a deep bonding experience on the Motown Junk Tour in 1991. The staff at the venues were just so friendly; you felt that they really cared. I remember getting to the Stoke Wheatsheaf – a magical venue – and we hadn’t had any food for a day and a half. They made us the most beautiful burger and chips.

King Tut’s Wah Wah Hut, Glasgow? The Stoker, Coventry? The Barrel Organ, Birmingham? JB’s, Dudley? Moles, Bath? The Adelphi, Hull? The Leadmill, Sheffield? It was a truly magical tour, I can’t even remember any bad shows.

The greatest one was probably The Buzz Club in Aldershot. What a fucking venue. Who’d have thought if you were in a rock band, going to Aldershot would give you one of the greatest gigs of your life? It was full of squaddies because it’s an army town, and it was antagonistic, but also brilliant. That was on the edge but some gigs could tip over the edge.

We did quite a scary gig at Reading’s After Dark Club. There was a proper firm of football hooligans there. That film The Firm had just been on TV and I don’t know if it had got people excited but it kicked off. James got punched but we stood our ground. There was a real adrenaline rush to it, even if there was a hint of violence at a lot of those early gigs.

What strikes me now is that all of these places were towns and I wonder how many of them have that kind of gig venue left. You can still play gigs in the cities, but to play in these towns was amazing: learning your trade and meeting people. Also realising there are people like you in every town you go to.

Very early doors, Little Chefs were different – they deserve an honourable mention because you could just get a proper meal there. A plate of bacon, egg and chips. We loved going to them but even by the time we started touring they were getting harder to find. And in the services before they improved, all you could find was some dodgy pasty that had been sitting in a fridge for weeks. But I have a theory that bad food equals great music. Show me a band that’s eaten healthy food all of their lives and their music is always shit. Whereas The Fall, those bands in Seattle that just lived on hard drugs and strong coffee, Sex Pistols… they lived on bad motorway service station diets and they made the greatest music. I think if you care that much about your bodily health, you’re shutting off a pathway to creativity.
“But I have a theory that bad food equals great music. Show me a band that’s eaten healthy food all of their lives and their music is always shit.”

If the small venues fed us, it was a bonus to be honest, but from what I remember, there were a lot of really lovely people who did. Even if there was some booze and crisps on the rider we were happy, really. But even if there was no food on offer we could usually find a local chippy, even though those are hard to find these days. Hamburg’s Seasurfer Revisits First Love in Video for “Hush Now” — “Trip” EP Out Now!
Here we are again You look so familiar In this red light… Drop your mask, my friend Someone you loved at seventeen can say your name across a room and… The post Hamburg’s Seasurfer Revisits…

Someone you loved at seventeen can say your name across a room and bring back every little thing you did to look at ease. You remember where you put your hands and the joke you made while you worked up the nerve to ask them to stay. The relief came when they heard the question in the joke and stayed a little longer. It can take years to realize how much you miss being known that well.

At the opening of “Hush Now (The Calling),” Apolonia sings to a familiar face bathed in red light, as king them to drop the mask with the gentle insistence of an old friend inviting you to sit and stay awhile. The track is the lead single from Trip , the four-track EP released November 20 by Hamburg noise-pop trio Seasurfer .

Christian Klepp ’s footage casts the first verse’s red light across the stage. Red and yellow projections sweep the back wall, while green glints in the dark glasses above a ribbed microphone. Maysterwerke cuts from this intimate close-up to wider shots, where amber haze reduces the band to little more than silhouettes.
Watch the video for Hush Now (The Calling) below.

The way the band moves in and out of view has a counterpart in the arrangements Dirk Knight began imagining in New York. “For me, this is the sound of cities,” says the instrumentalist, who recorded, produced and mixed the EP. He keeps the bass and drums fairly still while the guitars and the voices of Apolonia and Kiora drift in and out of focus.

Those guitars have been a constant since Seasurfer’s first two albums on Saint Marie Records and through collaborations with Cocteau Twins’ Robin Guthrie and producer John Fryer. This year the band put them to work on the post-punk of June’s Angels , then let them fill the room on August’s shoegaze-heavy The Noise is ours . On their third EP of 2026, a trip-hop beat gives the guitar chords more room to ring.

You can hear that space in the first bars of the opening track , One . The guitars drone and the drums take their time, leaving room for the strings that Chandeen’s Harald Löwy adds to the arrangement. The higher voices blur into the chords the way they do on My Bloody Valentine’s Loveless . The low lead comes through with the intimacy of someone speaking in confidence. It’s a seductive way to sing about making peace with your own company and the knowledge that we come and go alone.
Watch the video for One, filmed by Ahmed Sarowar and edited by Dirk Knight, below:

That intimacy carries into Hush Now (The Calling) , where a sigh of synths stretches into long, luminous lines and Knight’s guitars bring warmth up from below. Apolonia and Kiora’s voices cascade through the chorus, opening the melody out the way Elizabeth Fraser could on Cocteau Twins’ Heaven or Las Vegas and Milk & Kisses . Apolonia describes the song as a memory of first love, and Kiora hears loss and longing in the words. When the refrain comes round to “I’m by your side,” the reassurance sounds as necessary to the person giving it as it does to the one hearing it.

The guitar comes further forward on “Disappear” , where the opening loop has the woozy repetition of Cocteau Twins’ Otherness EP. The voice has Cranes’ reserve and some of Portishead’s unease. When the drums drop away, the guitar keeps circling long enough for you to stop anticipating the next hit. By the time it comes, the loop has built up a charge that carries into the closing bars.

The drums make you wait for them again on “I See You” . The guitars pile up first, with the soft-edged distortion of Loveless , and the drum machine gives them a trip-hop lilt when it comes in. There’s some of Cranes’ distance in the singing and some of the poise of Siobhan de Maré on Mono’s “Life in Mono.” At under three minutes, the closer rewards a second pass. Follow a guitar you barely noticed the first time through, and you can hear the arrangement shift around it.

“Forever in the Blood Moon” — Berlin Darkwavers Night Nail Head Out on a Ghoulish Commute in Video for…
Thoughts of dread for the living. Pandering with the queen of sorrow. Pandering to the mirrors of no tomorrow.
Thoughts of dread for the living.
Pandering with the queen of sorrow.
Pandering to the mirrors of no tomorrow.

Depression can turn a trip to the corner shop into such a long negotiation with yourself that the place ends up closing long before you’ve picked up your keys. On “Feelings Are Monsters,” Berlin’s Night Nail give that dread seven eyes and seven legs. Brandon Robert counts them off as though taking inventory might make the damn thing easier to deal with.

Once upon a time, Robert was scraping by as a hired bassist in Hollywood, selling other people’s demos on the street, when a bandmate who put great stock in lucky numbers told him to “cheer up.” “It was degrading,” Robert says of those days. “But, we had to eat. Super dark times.”

“I decided that day to never play for someone else’s dream again,” Robert recalls. “I started recording my own music. I learned the hard way that no one tells your story for you. My bandmates actually did support me in my breakaway dream and ended up helping me tremendously with making my first singles and videos. But, I learned it’s really all on you to make it happen and rightfully so.”

That faith in lucky numbers has a sour afterlife in the refrain, where Robert sings, “Luck won’t change your number.” The track opens in a clatter, with bright flecks of guitar sticking out of the noise. Once the drums snap into time, the guitar winds through the sort of uneasy melody The Comsat Angels used to make sound inevitable, while the bassline lays down a gothic rock groove. A little over a minute in, Ruby Mai’s saxophone takes over from Robert’s low recitation. He comes back with his voice raised, then lets it sink in again, deeper, as he draws out his ode to the “queen of sorrow.” A rubbery bass break gives way to another round of counting before the guitar takes the song out.

Director Ilija Gavrilenko and editor Jean De Oliveira keep returning to the band under blue light, with black wisps spreading across the frame. Between those shots, a skull-faced figure in a wide black hat rides a lime-green scooter and lopes around a courtyard carpeted with fallen leaves. It looks like somebody sent a horror-movie ghoul out to run an errand.

Seattle Dungeon Synthpop Project PROFIT PRISON Asks What the Living Owe the Dead in Video for “In Memoriam”
There’s something profoundly rotten about a world where people can disappear, families can be destroyed, and the surviving witnesses are expected to carry on buying groceries and paying…
Though they’d lost control of the outskirts of their town
and I loathe to tell you how it ends
so in silence we bow our heads

There’s something profoundly rotten about a world where people can disappear, families can be destroyed, and the surviving witnesses are expected to carry on buying groceries and paying their miserable bills while history quietly buries the evidence. Human civilization has developed an extraordinary talent for committing atrocities, commemorating the dead, and finding fresh excuses to repeat the process. Somewhere in this grand procession of moral bankruptcy, Seattle’s Profit Prison has found sufficient inspiration to write a disco song about the unbearable weight of collective guilt.

The solo project of Parker Lautensleger, whose musical history includes Anteinferno, Bhereg, Victims Panel, and Excarnated Entity, has spent nearly a decade exploring the more psychologically disturbed possibilities of electronic pop. His latest single, In Memoriam, taken from the forthcoming album Why art thou wroth? And why is thy countenance fallen? , sounds like Bronski Beat wandering into a particularly unpleasant historical reckoning, with electronic pioneer Gershon Kingsley conducting the proceedings from behind an enormous bank of synthesizers.

The arrangement possesses a strange, almost indecent sweetness. Synthesizers trace delicate melodic figures above a measured electronic rhythm, their crystalline repetitions creating the impression of a forgotten European dance record rescued from somebody’s flooded basement. Lautensleger sings with a trembling, distant resignation, his voice occupying the uncomfortable space between Neil Young’s wounded sincerity and the exquisite emotional distress of early synthpop by Das Kabinette, Depeche Mode, and others you might find on the Some Bizzare Compilation. Every syllable seems burdened by information its owner would dearly prefer to forget.

And what dreadful information it is. The lyrics describe a family whose apparently stable existence has been overturned by events unfolding near a border, where some unspecified act of violence has left questions that nobody seems willing to answer. Children inherit uncertainty, the dead receive their solemn acknowledgments, and the living are forced to contemplate the possibility that their own moral identities have been built upon carefully maintained ignorance. The song’s repeated interrogations grow increasingly desperate, suggesting a confrontation with somebody whose participation in an atrocity has become impossible to dismiss. Beneath the delicate electronic flourishes lies the hideous proposition that ordinary people can commit extraordinary acts of cruelty and subsequently spend entire lifetimes inventing explanations for themselves.

In Memoriam ‘s synthesizers maintain their patient, hypnotic progression while the words wander into the ugliest corners of human responsibility. You could conceivably dance to this record, which raises some rather uncomfortable questions about the emotional usefulness of disco. Lautensleger leaves those questions unanswered, however, allowing the music to continue its beautiful, merciless rotations while the accumulated weight of memory threatens to crush everything beneath it.

The video takes on a philosophical matter, as though we’re prisoners in Plato’s cave, watching distorted projections of events whose true nature remains somewhere beyond our comprehension. The road stretches onward, the lights assault our vision, and every image seems to conceal a fragment of some dreadful revelation.

The very British problem of GB Music Radio
GB News has launched an all-British radio station. As nationalistic thinkers so often do, they've oversimplified what it means to be British, and diluted the quality of their output in the…

How do you find common ground between a Guardian reader and a Daily Mail reader? Get them talking about British music. Somewhere down the line, they’ll share some musical common ground, or at least bond over their reverence – despite said reverence likely coming from different places – of the factory of musical greatness that is this strange little island.

For the right wing, perhaps it’s a beacon of what makes Great Britain greater than anywhere else. For the left, our music and culture might be the one thing about this country they can feel proud of in an era of decaying support structures and rampant division.

There’s something ironic, then, about right-wing slop spewers GB News positioning their new all-British radio station as a source of unity. Upon its announcement last month, Chief Revenue Officer Ross Sergeant said: “GB Music Radio gives advertisers something genuinely new: a station built around a single, warm idea that almost everyone in this country can get behind.”

Music should be the great unifier. Can a radio station really do that, though, when it’s had red, white and blue vomited all over it courtesy of arguably the most polarising, untrustworthy and hateful news brand in the country? It’s doubtful. For that reason alone, plenty of people wouldn’t touch it with a bargepole.

In fact, something about its announcement felt ridiculous enough to be satirical, especially with how it positioned its show names, like ‘Great British Drive Home’ and ‘Great British Breakfast’. So this is a station for people who chant ‘Come on Ingerland’ as they wolf down their bacon sarnies in the morning before sitting in their very Bri’ish traffic jam (in a vehicle that is decidedly not British)?

Sergeant added: “British music is a shared passion that cuts across generations, and we look forward to helping brands become part of the soundtrack to our listeners' day, from Breakfast with Paul [Coyte] to weekend mornings with Nana [Akua].” Coyte and Akua are already established names on GB News, the former presenting sports shows before pivoting back to music, while Akua recently went viral for a heated exchange with a guest on a panel last month.

Consequently, 'All British, all day’ once again spits in the face of any sort of unity. There’s no hiding the nationalism behind it, as it turns music into a cultural battleground it has dominance over, wresting it out of progressive hands into something it can call its own.

The arts and culture sectors, particularly music, are overwhelmingly left-wing , and music has for decades been a site of community building and changemaking, from Seventies punk values to recent calls for boycotts and solidarity with Palestine.
More recently, when the right have wanted a piece of this, they’ve even turned to AI-generated figureheads such as Danny Bones, who we investigated on the podcast.

GB Music Radio’s other problem is it tries to make the idea of Britishness far more simple and far less nuanced than it is in reality. Who gets to be considered British? What about mixed-nationality artists? Does AI count?

A spokesperson tells Drowned in Sound: “We celebrate British music in the broadest possible sense. British artists, or groups who are British or have British members. For example we will feature Fleetwood Mac. GB Music already features AI generated content in our hourly traffic AI reports but there are no plans for any fully AI songs."

It’s better that it’s broad, of course. To strip away all but the most ‘purely’ British artists certainly leaves the pool looking about as bland and beige as a plate of potato smileys sans sauce. Looking at what they've played at the time of writing, the playlist includes Lewis Capaldi's 'Survive', Pulp's 'Disco 2000' Kajagoogoo's 'Too Shy', Rainbow's 'Since You've Been Gone', David Bowie and Queen's 'Under Pressure' and Duffy's 'Mercy.' These are all songs you could hear if you whacked on Heart, Virgin Radio and the like. It's not all that different from a lot of middle-of-the-road mainstream radio, except without the variety an all-nationality playlist could offer.

What made the show special is that Lily, Jack and I are from the Isle of Man. I felt like a piece of home was in the room on Wednesday night and there were times where I was trying to not cry a little. It’s weird because I have such a weird relationship with the Isle of Man, but that’s not for here. That’s for elsewhere.

I’ve only been to gigs in the UK but I can honestly say that the crowd at Supersonic were just lovely, and it was a joy to be in such a beautiful environment. People were respectful of personal space and there were no drunken idiots ruining it for everyone. Although the set was just under an hour; it was a perfect set. Every song was delivered in such a perfect and tender way. You felt every song, and connected with every word. Another Kind Of Love shows just how delicate Jack’s vocals are, and where there are moments in the set where Jack, Lily and Joe absolutely tear the roof off the venue (especially during Gnarbone, which was an insane way to end the show)- you just really see how bloody talented this band is, and they truly deserve the world.

The room felt like it was filled with love and just appreciation for the band, and maybe it was extra special because it was the last night of the tour, but it just felt like one of those shows that people will talk about in years to come and those of us who were there will know exactly how lucky we were. It was a truly stunning show, and is up there as being one of my favourites of the year. Lily, Jack and Joe are just exceptional musicians, and it was a real honour to witness their greatness last week. I also felt super proud that a band from where I’m from are playing venues like Supersonic and just being a dream to watch.

At the end of the show, my partner and I went up to the merch stand and Lily spotted my Bushy’s t-shirt. I told her I was from the Isle of Man, and it was one of the most wholesome moments I’ve had. Jack and I had our photo taken together, with our Bushy’s shirts, and spoke about home for a little bit. It was nice to have a piece of home and to meet the band who have again, released one of the best records of the year.

What does access look like for disabled gig goers in 2026?
The average disabled music fan faces spending an extra £99 to attend a gig

Attitude is Everything connects disabled people with music and live event industries, to improve access together. Starting in 2000, the charity has supported industry pros and organisations to help better understand and improve access for Deaf, disabled and neurodivergent people in music.

The charity’s State of Access Report - a report set up to set standards for national progress with disability in music - lays out exactly what that looks like in 2026, and how fraught with problems it can be, alongside the scale of the extra burden it places on disabled fans so they can safely enjoy their night out.
It’s the first report in eight years, and the first since Covid-19. In that time, the volume of the conversation around access in live music has hit a fever pitch.
It's partly out of necessity, given that Covid-19 has been described as a "mass disabling event", and as of 2023, 2 million people in the UK are estimated to be living with long Covid.

This fan-led review echoes similar calls to improve inclusion across music events. 24% of Music Fans Voice respondents disagreed (compared to 58% who agreed) with the statement that live music events currently reflect the demographic diversity of the UK.
There's a disability tax on attending live gigs

The average disabled music fan faces spending an extra £99 to attend a gig, the most common of which (66%) relates to travel or accommodation. Other common access related costs include health or recovery costs (40%), personal assistant or companion costs (28%), higher ticket prices (25%) or food and drink for medical purposes (23%). Sadly, 58% of fans say extra costs have stopped them from attending an event.

The most frequent barrier disabled fans encounter relates to poor or inaccurate access information, which 69.5% of fans say they've experienced. Meanwhile, lack of seating or rest spaces is a barrier for 66.4% of respondents, booking or ticketing systems for 56.1% and staff attitudes or behaviour for 51.6%.
Access is inconsistent across the board

Only 20% of disabled gig goers say they feel they can consistently rely on their access needs being met. Even more starkly, 94% say they expose themselves to some level of risk when they go to a show.
The burden still falls on disabled people to advocate for themselves

72% of disabled gig goers have had to resolve access problems themselves, while 62% report having to explain their needs repeatedly. Just under half (48%) of respondents have said they've supported other disabled fans in the past, while more than half say they've had to leave events early due to access issues.
Fortunately, 58% of those surveyed said that they think access has improved in the last five years, and 61% would describe events as 'somewhat' or 'very' accessible.

"The findings from the survey are shocking, but sadly not surprising. But, by sharing the feedback with the sector, and supporting the music industry to embed access, we aim to improve the experiences for the disabled community, because by removing barriers, we don’t just open doors, we open up an entire industry."

Here’s How to Easily Record Your Entire Family History So No One Forgets Who’s Who in All Those Photos
Up to your eyeballs in old photos, letters and records? These expert tips to document your family history will help you organize everything and connect the dots.

My sister and I were recently hanging out at her place, and the conversation turned to our childhood. I pulled up some old photos on my phone—snaps of pictures that used to live in albums at the center of my parents’ living room. We started taking guesses about when they were from and shared stories about what was happening in them. We both remembered family picnics at the waterfall, our dog Cujo (yes, Cujo), and flying kites in the cornfield across the house. But there were people, places and stories I couldn’t recall at all, like a close family friend’s house we spent a lot of time at; my sister could still describe it in detail.
That’s when it hit me: It had been years since we’d flipped through old albums like that. As physical albums get left behind and older relatives depart, we’re increasingly losing our family history.

I’ve researched bits of my family’s genealogy over the years, but I’ve always run into roadblocks. Like many families in the U.S., our ancestors immigrated several generations ago, and a lot of details were lost or changed along the way. How do you document family history when there are so many missing pieces? By tackling it little by little, says Allison Singleton, the genealogy services manager at the Genealogy Center. “There will be gaps of information you don’t know,” she says. But don’t let that stop you.

That being said, you’ll have a lot more luck if you have a method to the madness. That’s why I reached out to a few experts who do this for a living and could lay it out in simple terms for us. In addition to Singleton, I spoke with Kyle Betit, a senior genealogist at Ancestry; Haleh Shoa, a certified professional photo organizer and the founder of Picturli; and Peter Andrew Wint, the founder of Family Roots.

It turns out, there are a lot of strategies and resources available, and some of them are free. Read on to find out how to document family history , create a family tree and be the detective your clan needs—starting now!
How on earth do you even start this kind of project?
Before you dive into documenting your family’s history, determine your goal. “Knowing where you want to end up tells you where to start and how much you need to gather,” Shoa says.

Next, collect supplies. Shoa says you’ll need several plastic bins, colorful index cards for categorizing batches of photos, an archival pencil, a 2TB or 4TB external hard drive for storage, nitrile gloves for handling photos, and a notebook or spreadsheet for tracking.

Then, gather the documentation you already have and group it into categories. Think of this like taking an inventory. “Put like with like,” Shoa says. “The albums, the slides, the negatives and the VHS tapes should each have their own piles.” In addition to photos and videos, include things like old letters , newspaper clippings, obituaries, birth and death certificates, and recipe cards. “These items are full of clues about your family history,” Singleton notes. After you’ve grouped everything, you’ll dig into each category. (More on that below.)

Keep in mind that you don’t need to do everything at once. “Start small—with one photograph, one document, one family story, one person or one question—and see how your research progresses,” Singleton advises. After all, you don’t want to get overwhelmed before you even really start!
How do you create a family tree?
To create a family tree, gather and cross-check details about your family, and designate a place to keep it all organized. Follow these steps to get started.
Building your tree online allows you to save and share it virtually, and on some platforms, you can turn on collaborative permissions so relatives can contribute in real time.

If you’re looking for a free and simple platform that’s particularly good for beginners, Shoa recommends Family Echo. You can also create a basic free tree in FamilySearch, Canva, Ancestry and MyHeritage. Just be aware that free trees may have limitations, and access to some records and services may require a paid subscription.

How to Navigate Grief During the Holidays in Ways You’ll Actually Find Helpful
When the season feels anything but merry, these expert tips will give you a game plan to make it through—even when that feels impossible.

No matter what time of year you’ve lost someone, navigating that grief during the season devoted to joy, togetherness and sparkle can become a challenge unto itself. When my 82-year-old mom died the night before Thanksgiving three years ago, my grief became permanently imprinted into the holidays. Ever since, I’ve swung between wanting to eat cookies by the fire with Santa and scream through the streets with Krampus.

The holidays haven’t felt the same since, and admittedly, I even feel a little dread around this time of the year. I’m not alone. According to American Psychiatric Association’s Healthy Minds poll from 2025 about holiday-related concerns, nearly half of adults polled felt worry over grief and missing someone . The reality is that the best parts of the season can lead to some of the worst feelings of loss.

There is no easy answer here, unfortunately, but experts do have a few suggestions to help people handle grief during the holidays . For that advice, I spoke with Raman Mohabir, PhD, a licensed professional clinical counselor and the founder of Good Mourning Mental Health Counseling, and Tess Clarkson, an end-of-life doula and the creator of the Your Best Goodbye workshop.
Read on to find out how to get through the holidays after a loss , find special ways to honor your loved ones and maybe even enjoy the season again.
Why are the holidays particularly hard after a loss?

First of all, it’s not your imagination: The holidays are harder. And the first notes of a familiar holiday song or the scent of a special dish can really feel like a gut punch. “The holiday season can further magnify grief because it is a time often marked with moments meant to be spent with family and loved ones, which can further highlight the absence of the person who has died,” Mohabir says . On top of that, you may feel guilt, anger or resentment for not feeling celebratory, and your grief can feel darker against all the sparkle.

How it hits can also depend on the kind of loss. Grief isn’t only about death, Mohabir notes. It can also include “ambiguous losses, such as the anticipatory grief associated with the decline of a loved one facing a terminal diagnosis, or loss due to divorce, deployment, incarceration or a miscarriage.” Those losses can be especially lonely during the holidays. “These ambiguous and disenfranchised grief experiences can complicate the holiday season as well, especially if the loss is not acknowledged or supported by others,” she says.
Whatever kind of loss you’re carrying, feeling as if you’re living a different holiday than everyone around you can be alienating.
Should you still celebrate the holidays after a loss?

It really depends on you. “There is no correct answer or moral obligation to how an individual should navigate the holiday season,” says Mohabir. A lot of it boils down to how you feel and who will be around you . Spending time with people who share your loss, or who are simply supportive, can be a real comfort and worth the effort. Spending it with people who aren’t supportive can do more harm than good, whether they’re friends or family.

“It is important to assess the quality of the support around you and what you need when gathering with others,” Mohabir says. Time alone counts too. “Choosing solitude and privacy can be restorative and healing as well,” she adds.

If celebrating feels like too much this year, try a gentler approach: “observing” the season or focusing on getting through it rather than celebrating it. “Maybe it is not putting up the tree or getting out the menorah,” Clarkson says. It’s also not all or nothing; Show up for dessert, pop by Christmas morning—”it’s about having more serenity without the performance of the holidays,” she says.
How should you approach the holiday season after a loss?

Start by listening to yourself rather than to your list of obligations. This Junk-Drawer Staple Could Save Your Home in Case of Flooding, According to a New Study
A new study found that a surprisingly effective and cheap household tool blows sandbags out of the water when it comes to flood protection.

Flooding often brings to mind springtime thunderstorms and late-summer hurricanes, but this year, El Niño is serving up a nasty winter across much of the United States. Heavy rains and flooding are in the forecast for huge swaths of the country, leaving many wondering what they would do if water was bearing down.

Sandbags have been the go-to for centuries, but if you’ve ever tried to use them, you know they are a pain: heavy, labor-intensive and often not available when you need them. But now, researchers looking for inexpensive ways to help homeowners fight flooding have stumbled across something that blows sandbags out of the water.

Britain’s University of Hull released the surprising findings in a new report, and we have the results ahead. It turns out that something you no doubt have rattling around in your junk drawer or garage toolbox works better than sandbags—a lot better. Read on to learn an effective (and cheap) way to protect your home during a flood.
What junk-drawer staple can save your home from flooding?

That’s according to a new report called Testing the Performance of Low-cost, Temporary Property Flood Resilience (PFR) Solutions . The university teamed up with Flood Re, a partnership between the U.K. government and insurers, to pinpoint inexpensive ways for homeowners to protect their homes during a flood.

The results were amazing: Duct tape reduced water leakage 97% to 98% compared to a plain closed door. The much less common synthetic rubber tape (aka putty tape) did even better, with a 99% reduction. Even the worst-performing tape, yellow plastic tape, kept out 80% of simulated floodwaters during testing. And every single tape tested did better than sandbags, which reduced water intrusion by only 70%.

“Sandbags remain a symbol of flood protection , but these tests turn that assumption on its head,” said Jonathan Kassian, head of flood resilience at Flood Re. “What we have found is that some relatively simple and affordable products can do a much better job of keeping water out.”
Why does this work better than a sandbag?

For one thing, sandbags are porous, and they’re not designed to keep out water completely. Think of them more as a diversion tactic or obstruction, as opposed to tape, which can actually seal an opening through which water can flow.

In this study, researchers found that when placed in flood conditions of 0.2 meters (about 8 inches), sandbags leaked water at a mean rate of 584 liters per hour per meter, or 47 gallons per hour per foot. They were more effective in deeper water, but still only prevented, at most, 70% of water leakage . Sandbags are also heavy, time-intensive to deploy and difficult to place correctly.

Tape, on the other hand, is cheap and easy to store. It can be applied directly across gaps and conforms to irregular surfaces and openings where water can seep in. After the storm, cleanup is easy because tape is safely disposable, unlike sandbags, which absorb dangerous floodwater contaminants. And remember: Duct tape was more than 97% effective.
There is one caveat. Researchers concluded that how the tape was applied was “critical.” We’ll give you those details next.
How do you do this properly?

First, it’s important to understand that this was a research study about the effectiveness of certain barriers under testing conditions, not a how-to manual of using tape to stop a flood. But scientists were encouraged by the findings. Here are recommendations from the report:
Use a strong, wide tape. For duct tape, researchers recommend a width of 100 mm (roughly 4 inches).
Apply it to the flood-facing side. Tape performed best when it was applied on the outside of the door.

Cover vertical joints first. Tape the sides, making sure the vertical strip is attached to both the door and jamb and extends to the threshold. Then do the threshold and corners, overlapping the vertical strip.
Apply to clean, dry doors. To get the best adhesion, tape the door before wet weather arrives .
Make sure there are no openings. Avoid folds, press out any air bubbles and cover gaps.

Vaughn Tan | Longreads | November 24, 2026 | 3,989 words (17 minutes)

Back in 2003, I was in the early stages of researching how the distinctive visual style of Japanese plating and dish design influenced plating outside Japan, and wanted to analyze photos of fine-dining dishes in industry periodicals like Art Culinaire . Back in the early 2000s, this was easiest to do in libraries. At the time, I lived in Cambridge, Massachusetts, so I wound up in the collection of historical cookbooks and culinary materials at the Schlesinger Library.

One afternoon, Barbara Haber, then the Schlesinger’s curator of books, stopped by my desk with something for me: Japanese Cooking: A Simple Art by Shizuo Tsuji, published in 1980 with an introduction by MFK Fisher. I knew of Fisher through her essays on eating and her translation of Brillat-Savarin’s The Physiology of Taste , but not for anything related to Japanese food. Barbara mentioned that many boxes of Fisher’s collected papers had recently arrived at the library. The papers were still uncatalogued, but was I interested in looking at them?

I didn’t know then that I was beginning a 20-year detour. As I went through these boxes over the next few months, my original research project faded away. I found myself more and more drawn to the Fisher archive boxes, and to the story that emerged as I read through years of her correspondence and other documents, including letters about her trip to Japan to research the introduction she wrote to Japanese Cooking ; letters about the book she wrote to journalists, writers, and editors across the US; and draft manuscripts of Japanese Cooking , with her comments in red pen, which had crisscrossed the Pacific between California and Osaka. The story that emerged was of a secret campaign Fisher waged between 1979 and 1982, which was instrumental in the seemingly sudden transformation of Japanese food into fine dining in America.
The Fisher I uncovered in those boxes was someone else, and her role in making Japanese food into fine dining in America remains almost entirely unknown.

Fisher’s campaign worked well because it was largely invisible. The publishers of Japanese Cooking didn’t know that any of this was happening. Ruth Reichl, who wrote the foreword to the 25th anniversary edition in 2005, had no idea Fisher had done any more than write the introduction when I spoke to her earlier this year. (Fisher had gifted her a copy of the book before Reichl’s first trip to Japan in the early 1980s.) Yet Fisher not only shaped the book itself, she also systematically put it in front of everyone who mattered in the American food world—people whose endorsement could not be bought, and whose reasons for endorsing the book were, as I later realized, largely Fisher’s own.

In 2003, I wasn’t sure what to do with my discovery. It didn’t fit any story I knew how to tell yet. And although it made sense to me back then that no one had uncovered this evidence before—Fisher’s campaign was visible only through forensic analysis of an uncatalogued archive, and left no traces in the places people normally look—in the years since, it has remained largely unexamined, even though Fisher is an extensively examined writer. Her reputation has grown considerably over the past two decades and, in the UK especially, she is now frequently invoked as the great American food writer.

Until the late 1970s, Japanese food wasn’t just exotic to the American public, it was fundamentally alien. That Sinking Feeling: A Race Against Time to Save a Pregnant Woman from a Car Submerged in Freezing Waters
A dazed pregnant woman drives into an ice-cold pond. Amid a sea of bystanders, one man takes action to save her life.

Shedly Apollon was awakened by a sound she couldn’t possibly sleep through: that of her car splashing into a pond … with her in it. Add in the rush of cold water pooling beneath her feet, and suddenly Apollon was fully alert, if disoriented. She was also fearing for her life. Actually, two lives. Apollon was in her 34th week of pregnancy on that cold morning this past February in Stuart, Florida, when she awoke to the reality that she was trapped in a sinking car .

Apollon, of nearby Port St. Lucie, had been on her way to a prenatal massage gifted by her fiancé, Woodly Sully. It was a birthday present. (Yes, this happened on Apollon’s 29th birthday.) Apollon had been struggling during her third trimester with preeclampsia, and as she drove to the massage, she began to feel woozy. She pulled her silver 2019 Hyundai Elantra over to the shoulder of Interstate 95, called Sully to let him know what was happening, drank some water, ate a little food and waited for the dizziness to subside.

After it did, about 10 minutes later, she got back on the road, but what happened next is a blur. Her car’s safety systems were beeping, telling her she was veering outside her lane, although in her haze-filled mind she was driving perfectly straight. She tried to pull over again, but started passing out. “I thought the car was in park,” Apollon recalls, “but in reality, it was still in drive.” And she drove off the right side of the road, straight into the pond.

When she came to seconds later to the sound of the splash, she unsnapped her seat belt and hit redial on her phone, then screamed to her confused fiancé, “I’m in a lake!” Within seconds, the call dropped. She and her unborn baby were all alone in a car that was listing, front driver’s side first, into a body of water.

Around this time, 29-year-old sport fisherman Logan Hayes of Sebastian, Florida, was driving down the same stretch of I-95 in his pickup, remarking to his friend and boss in the passenger seat, Chase Cornell, about how unusual it was that traffic was light and that they were running 20 minutes ahead of schedule on their work errand. “Something’s gonna happen,” Hayes joked.
Sure enough, Hayes soon saw brake lights ahead of him. And then the reason for the sudden slowdown: the Elantra, barely floating in the water.

Other cars had pulled over, but so far nobody had gotten out to help. So Hayes, also a professional surfer and confident swimmer, crossed from the far left lane across two other lanes, cutting off every car in his way, then pulled onto the shoulder and leaped out of the truck.
“Hey, is someone in that car?” he asked a bystander.

Hayes ran 50 yards down the highway, then a few more feet to the water’s edge, his eyes fixed on the Elantra. He was shedding clothing every step of the way. Off came his hat, his sunglasses, his shirt, his fishing boots, his sweatpants, his socks … until all he had on were his board shorts.

The outdoor temperature was in the mid-40s when Hayes hit the water around 8 a.m., and the pond was colder than that. But Hayes was surging with adrenaline and didn’t feel the chill as he dove in , trying to cover the distance as quickly as he could. He was underwater for a couple of seconds, then came up and took a few more strokes, and he was at the car.

With the vehicle tipping forward and to the left, the rear passenger door was the only one not submerged. Treading water, he pulled on the door handle, and it flew open. Scared and still struggling to get her bearings, Apollon was jolted by the sight of Hayes floating just outside her suddenly wide-open back door. “You have to get out of the car right now!” he yelled to her.
“You need to!” he urged. “You need to get to me.”

Apollon saw she’d have to crawl over the console between the seats—not easy to do in a car listing in the opposite direction, especially as her instinct was to move delicately and protect her belly. She swung her legs around so her feet were pointing toward Hayes. Now lying on her side, she pushed with her arms and slid up the console, inching toward the back seat, gravity working against her at every turn.

God!” has come flying out of your mouth as you resist the urge to stomp away from the table.
You’re an adult. You run meetings, pay bills, have kids of your own. So how did you end up 12 again in less than 30 seconds?

If it makes you feel any better, you’re in good company … and there’s plenty you can do about it. Why do we revert to our childhood selves when we’re with family for the holidays?

Short answer: You’re back with the people who knew you at 12, and part of you is still stuck in that phase. Yes, even all these years later. “The holidays evoke such strong, visceral regressive emotions in all of us,” Mayer says. “These intense emotions have been imprinted inside us since we were toddlers, so we can’t help but re-experience them throughout our lives.” His name for it? Imprinted regression.

Seiter calls it role regression. “It is also a subtle form of a trauma response—whether it’s big T or little t trauma—where our bodies remember the old roles and scripts we played in our families,” she says. “For example, you might become the responsible one again as you do all of the chores, or the baby, who finds themselves asking for help that they don’t need, or the rebel, breaking the hidden family rules.”

But why do we slip into those parts, even when we know better? “We learned when we were young how to protect ourselves from harm, and our body still has the feeling that we need to play out our adaptations, even when we are adults and no longer need to,” Seiter says.
And no amount of personal growth makes you immune. As Seiter points out, the spiritual teacher Ram Dass famously said, “If you think you’re so enlightened, go spend a week with your family.”
How do we let this happen in the moment?
“Let” is doing a lot of heavy lifting there. There’s a confluence of things happening that contribute to this perfect storm of family drama.

Your family pulls you back into these roles. “It is important to understand the power of families,” Mayer says. “As a coping mechanism, families place members in such categories, and often they are immovable.” No matter what you’ve accomplished since you moved out, he explains, “the power of the family forces you in that role.” In fact, if you’ve become more educated, accomplished or social than the rest of your family, keeping you in your childhood role may be how they cope with the difference.

Big events exacerbate issues. It’s not just holidays. Weddings and other family gatherings can trigger this regression too. “It is just that the holidays come around predictably and regularly,” Mayer says, “and these other events don’t.”

Family pecking order can influence how this all plays out. Mayer notes that research hasn’t backed up the famous birth-order personality types . But some families do develop their own patterns around who’s oldest or youngest, and those patterns are “idiosyncratic to families, not any biological imperative,” he says.

Slights sting more when they come from family. “Our relationships with our parents and siblings are our first attachment relationships,” Seiter explains. “When we were young, our very survival depended on these people. I hadn’t meal-prepped in months. There was a Netflix show I’d been meaning to watch, chores were piling up, and my partner and I hadn’t had much time for a quiet night together. Between work and everything else on my schedule, I was struggling to find time for much of anything.

The change in seasons wasn’t helping. By the time I finished work, it was already dark outside, and whatever motivation I had left seemed to disappear with the daylight. I was tired, had plenty to catch up on and somehow felt guilty about wanting to spend what little free time I had relaxing.

So when I came across cozymaxxing, a social media trend that encourages people to make their time at home as comfortable and enjoyable as possible, the timing couldn’t have been better. And when I learned that some of the ideas behind it overlap with an established treatment for seasonal depression, I wondered if there might be more to it than an excuse to stay home.

To find out, I spoke with a psychologist who’s spent decades researching winter depression, then gave cozymaxxing a try for three evenings. Read on to find out how my cozy little experiment went—and why you’re going to want to hop right on this cozy train.

Cozymaxxing means deliberately making your surroundings and activities as comfortable and relaxing as possible. Think: candles, blankets, warm drinks and spending an evening doing whatever sounds good to you.

The trend gained attention in 2025 through videos of cozy living-room setups, cooking, reading and movie nights. As of November 2026, more than 500 Instagram posts feature the #cozymaxxing hashtag, with some videos racking up as many as 3.4 million views.

Dictionary.com named maxxing its 2026 Word of the Year, recognizing the growing number of trends dedicated to optimizing everything from appearance (looksmaxxing) to sleep (sleepmaxxing). Cozymaxxing is a funny addition to the bunch, considering how little effort it asks of you.
Why is cozymaxxing such a good idea?
Cozymaxxing may help improve your mood by giving you something to look forward to during a season that can leave you feeling tired and unmotivated.

Kelly Rohan, PhD, a psychology professor at the University of Vermont who studies seasonal depression, says it’s common to notice changes in your mood and energy as the days get shorter. Some people barely feel the difference, while others develop seasonal affective disorder (SAD), a form of clinical depression that typically occurs during the fall and winter. Many of us fall somewhere in between, feeling more tired, sleeping longer or noticing changes in our appetite.

Shorter days appear to be a major reason why. According to the National Institute of Mental Health, people with SAD may experience changes in serotonin and melatonin, chemicals involved in regulating mood and sleep. These changes can also throw off the body’s internal clock , although researchers are still figuring out exactly how it all works.

Rohan has spent 25 years studying cognitive behavioral therapy for winter depression. One technique she uses is called behavioral activation, which encourages people to get out and do something they normally like, even when they aren’t feeling up to it. “Anything that one can do to approach and embrace the winter season and find some joy in it is probably going to be helpful for well-being and mental health,” she says.

She’s even encouraged patients to try things that sound a lot like cozymaxxing, including taking warm baths surrounded by candles. Rohan says it can help to find things you genuinely like about winter, similar to how you might look forward to gardening, swimming or spending time outdoors in the summer. She also points to Scandinavian traditions like hygge , which encourage people to embrace the colder months by making their homes warm and inviting.

Of course, cozymaxxing hasn’t been studied as a treatment for depression. But Rohan’s research offers a good reason to make some plans for those dark winter evenings—even if your plans don’t involve leaving the house.

Fresh vs. Frozen vs. Canned Vegetables: Which Is Better? (Hint: It May Not Be the One You Think!)
One of cooking’s biggest debates has an answer—and we have it below. Read this before your next trip to the grocery store. The post Fresh vs. Frozen vs. Canned Vegetables: Which Is Better?

We were always taught—or maybe we just assumed?—that fresh produce was always the best choice. That it’s the healthiest, the best-tasting, the whole nine yards. But remember this summer, when fresh produce was trying to kill us? And what about all the soups and casseroles and holiday dishes we’re making right now that call for frozen or canned veggies? Why are we so obsessed with fresh?

Samantha Peterson, a functional medicine dietitian and personal trainer, has a theory. “Fresh feels closest to nature. We see crisp lettuce and bright peppers in the produce section and immediately read them as healthy, while anything in a bag or a can feels ‘processed,’” she says. “That word has been used so broadly that it now scares people away.”

Should it? Or should we stop being so snobby about our veggies and start feeling good about them in whatever form they come in? Of course, it’s complicated … but we’re here to make it easy for you. Read on as we settle the fresh vs. frozen vs. canned debate once and for all.
What’s at the root of the fresh vs. frozen vs. canned veggie debate?

As noted above, most people believe fresh equals healthy. But the word fresh just describes how a vegetable looks, not how long ago it was picked, which is the real marker of how many nutrients it contains when it reaches your plate, Peterson says. Veggies develop nutrients while they’re ripening, she explains, so those that are picked too early are starting at a deficit. But once they’re picked, the clock starts.

“Vegetables keep ‘breathing’ after they’re picked, and delicate nutrients like vitamin C and folate start to break down with time, heat and light. Leafy greens like spinach are especially sensitive,” Peterson says. “So how far a vegetable traveled, and how long it sat in a warehouse, a store and your fridge, matters as much as how it was grown.” Put another way, a fresh veggie that has been off the plant for more than a week is going to contain fewer nutrients than one that was frozen the same day it was picked.

Of course, there are other factors besides nutrient content that determine whether you want a fresh, frozen or canned vegetable. Things like taste, cost, seasonality, waste and more all play a role too, as you’ll see below.
What are the pros and cons of each type of vegetable choice?
OK, it’s the moment of truth. Here’s what you need to know before your next trip to the grocery store.

Pros: If you can get your hands on in-season, just-picked fresh veggies , you can’t beat them for nutrient content, flavor and texture. “Fresh is the only option that gives you real crunch, which makes it ideal for salads, slaws, crudités and snacking,” Peterson says. Many vitamins and minerals, such as vitamin C, are sensitive to heat, so eating fresh veggies ensures that you are getting the full possible amount of those vitamins from the food.”
You also have full control over how the veggies are prepared. “There’s no added salt, sauce or seasoning unless you add it,” Peterson notes.

Cons: The biggest downside to fresh produce is its short shelf life. “Most of us have opened the crisper drawer to find a bag of wilted spinach we had big plans for,” says Peterson. “Fresh produce goes bad quickly, and tossing it wastes both food and money.”

Speaking of cost, both the price and quality of fresh veggies are going to vary widely depending on the time of year. “A winter tomato is often pale, mealy and more expensive than a summer one,” Peterson says.
And since fresh veggies are (usually) whole and raw, they take more time to prepare than their frozen and canned counterparts.

Pros: Frozen vegetables are loaded with nutrients. “They’re typically picked at peak ripeness and frozen within hours, which locks in their nutrition at its high point,” Peterson explains. “Research comparing the two has found frozen vegetables are often nutritionally similar to fresh, and sometimes higher than fresh produce that’s been stored in the fridge for several days.”

Thousands of Units of Toothpaste and Mouthwash Are Being Recalled Due to Unwanted Hormones Found in Product…
More than 51,000 units of toothpaste and mouthwash products made for children and adults are being recalled.

When you think about product recalls, toothpaste and mouthwash probably aren’t the first things that come to mind. We’re used to hearing about recalls involving food , cars and household products, but everyday oral care items can make the list too.

That’s what happened recently with thousands of toothpaste and mouthwash products made for children and adults. They’re being recalled after testing uncovered hormone contamination, according to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

The voluntary recall involves 51,762 units of six ORL Organic Oral Care products distributed nationwide. The FDA notified ORL Labs after testing found hormones in samples of the products, according to its enforcement report.

The recall began Oct. 12 but was classified as a Class II recall earlier this month. That designation means the products may “cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences,” according to the FDA’s recall definitions.
Which toothpaste and mouthwash products are included?
The recall covers the following products from ORL Organic Oral Care. All of the items have expiration dates between September 2026 and August 2028.

The FDA report says samples contained progesterone, estradiol or dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA). It doesn’t identify the amounts found or explain how the cross-contamination happened. It’s the second toothpaste recall as of late, too.
The report also doesn’t specify what consumers should do with products they purchased. Anyone with questions can contact ORL Labs at 844-675-5227 or email orl@orlcares.com.

These Holiday Cooking Mistakes Could Put Your Family’s Safety at Risk
The American Red Cross is advising Americans to follow these easy safety rules in the kitchen this holiday season.

The holidays are supposed to be about good food , time with loved ones and enjoying a little holiday tradition. But before everyone gathers around the table, there’s something to keep in mind: A few common cooking mistakes can put your family and home at risk.

The American Red Cross is reminding Americans to take extra precautions this holiday season, especially in the kitchen. After all, Thanksgiving is the leading day of the year for home cooking fires. With busy kitchens, multiple dishes cooking at once and distractions everywhere, it’s easy to overlook something that could become dangerous.
Simple Thanksgiving cooking habits can help prevent fires and hazards
It doesn’t take a major mistake for a fire to start. That’s what makes kitchen fires so sneaky and dangerous. Here are some safe-cooking tips to keep in mind this Thanksgiving.
Turn off the stove: The Red Cross recommends staying in the kitchen whenever you’re using the stovetop or oven. If you need to step away, even briefly, turn off the appliance first.
Avoid loose clothing: Be careful about what you’re wearing too. Loose clothing and dangling sleeves can easily catch fire.
Keep tabs on flammable items: Paper towels, oven mitts, wooden utensils, food packaging and curtains should stay away from hot appliances.
Establish a “safe cooking zone”: If you have children or pets, the Red Cross says to keep them at least three feet away from cooking areas.
Get a fire extinguisher: Be prepared for potential problems. Have a fire extinguisher nearby and know how to use it before an emergency happens.
One final safety note about frying turkeys

Thanksgiving and Christmas meals often feature turkeys, so turkey fryers deserve extra attention. Anyone preparing a fried turkey should keep the fryer outdoors, away from the house, garage and other structures. It should sit on a flat, stable surface, and the turkey must be completely thawed before it goes into the fryer.

Once you have your holiday cooking plan ready, the Red Cross recommends downloading one of its free safety apps , which offer customizable weather alerts for holiday travel and first-aid help (including for pets!). It’s also good to keep up with current recalls , so you know what you’re serving for dinner is safe.
The holidays should be a time for making memories, not dealing with an emergency. A few smart moves in the kitchen can go a long way toward keeping everyone safe.

Kylie Kelce Reveals the Kelce Family’s Surprising Thanksgiving Tradition
Forget the turkey! The Kelce brothers grew up with a very different Thanksgiving menu, and Kylie has found a way to keep the tradition going for their four daughters.

Kylie Kelce recently revealed that when she first started dating her now-husband, former Philadelphia Eagles star Jason Kelce, she discovered his family had a rather unconventional Thanksgiving tradition. While most Americans were carving up turkey, the Kelces had something entirely different on their plates.

During the Nov. 19 episode of her Not Gonna Lie with Kylie Kelce podcast, the 34-year-old talked about the family’s holiday food preferences while playing a game involving popular Thanksgiving main courses.

“The Kelces were not a turkey family, okay?” Kylie explained. That goes for Jason and his younger brother, Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce. “I don’t know what was happening in their house. I’m not going to pass judgment or assume anything. They were not a turkey house.”
Kylie Kelce reveals what the family ate instead of turkey
So what was on the menu instead? “They would do pork chops. They would do other types of protein,” she revealed.
Fortunately, there was another holiday staple the family could agree on. “But they also are smart human beings, and they love ham,” Kylie continued.

After marrying Jason, Kylie began incorporating some of his family’s preferences into their own celebrations, although turkey eventually earned a place at the table. “So when Jason and I got together, and we started holding holidays and hosting, we ended up hosting with ham. Now, of course, we have a turkey on Thanksgiving , and I want leftover sandwiches,” she said.
Kylie and Jason Kelce’s family life
Beyond their holiday traditions, Kylie and Jason have their hands full raising their four daughters, Wyatt, 7, Elliotte, 5, Bennett, 3, and Finnley, 1.
The couple, who married in 2018, have been raising their children in the public eye, particularly as the Kelce family’s fame has grown in recent years. They’ve even gotten quite good at it.

During the Nov. 5 episode of her podcast, Kylie spoke with Fixer Upper star Joanna Gaines about balancing their family’s privacy with giving their children a normal upbringing. “We’re not hermits,” Kylie explained, emphasizing that she doesn’t want her daughters to miss out on everyday experiences just because their parents are famous.

But she also acknowledged that public encounters can sometimes be confusing for young children, especially when strangers approach them as though they know them personally. “Just because someone knows mom’s name does not mean that mom knows them,” she said, sharing one of the lessons she’s taught her older daughters.
If there’s one thing the Kelces have made clear, it’s that they’re not afraid to do things a little differently—which includes holiday meals.
