This Beloved Star Trek Actor Reveals His Secret Cancer Battle—And the Alarming Symptom He Spotted First
Jonathan Frakes opens up about his private bladder cancer battle, revealing the alarming symptom that led to his diagnosis.
Star Trek star Jonathan Frakes is opening up about a frightening health scare that he kept private until now.

The 74-year-old actor and director, best known for playing Commander William T. Riker on Star Trek: The Next Generation , revealed that he was diagnosed with bladder cancer after noticing an unusual symptom while attending a fan convention in Phoenix.
Frakes shared his experience during the Nov. 21 episode of his Dropping Names podcast, where he was joined by his surgeon, Dr. Ramkishen Narayanan, to discuss his diagnosis and treatment.
Jonathan Frakes reveals the first sign of his bladder cancer

Frakes recalled discovering something unusual while getting ready for breakfast at his hotel during a convention with his Star Trek co-star and podcast co-host Brent Spiner. “My pee was pink,” he explained. “I was unnerved and I started to read about it.”

Initially, Frakes considered whether something he’d eaten could explain the discoloration, but Spiner encouraged him to contact his doctor. Just days later, a cystoscopy revealed tumors. “We discovered there was cancer in my bladder,” Frakes recalled.

Narayanan explained that visible blood in the urine, particularly without pain, should never be ignored. “So when it’s painless blood that you see with your eyes, that’s always a red flag, no matter, you know, where you are,” he said.

Frakes underwent surgery three days after the initial examination to remove the tumors. “At the end of it, he says, I think we got it all,” Frakes recalled. Fortunately, the cancer had not invaded the bladder muscle, allowing him to avoid a more extensive operation that could have required removing his bladder. He completed six weekly rounds of treatment.
Why Jonathan Frakes decided to share his cancer diagnosis

During his treatment, doctors also discovered that Frakes had a significantly enlarged prostate. An MRI showed no suspicious signs of prostate cancer, and he later underwent surgery to address the condition.

Despite everything he’d experienced, Frakes initially kept his bladder cancer diagnosis to a close circle of loved ones. “I haven’t talked about my cancer with anybody outside of our family,” he recalled telling his surgeon during a follow-up appointment.

Narayanan encouraged him to share his story in hopes of motivating others to seek medical attention when something feels wrong. And it’s personal for Frakes, too, who has advocated for pancreatic cancer awareness since losing his brother, Daniel, to the disease in 1997.
Now, he’s hoping his own experience will serve as another reminder of the importance of recognizing potential warning signs and getting checked promptly.

Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and several adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” will almost certainly come near the top. At first glance, that story of a man paying…

Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and several adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” will almost certainly come near the top. At first glance, that story of a man paying a visit to an old friend who lives with his twin sister in their family’s grand house — each of the latter three well advanced into a different process of deterioration — might seem too short, as well as too light on conflict to translate into a conventional screenplay. Yet it’s also full of cinematically irresistible images, from the somehow ruinous yet wholly intact titular mansion to the bloodily wretched sister throwing herself upon the terrified brother who entombed her alive while their ancestral home collapses around them.

Of the twenty or thirty versions of “The Fall of the House of Usher” so far made for the screen, the most celebrated remains the one Jean Epstein directed in 1928. Officially designating it as one of the “great movies,” Roger Ebert calls that picture’s vision of the great hall “one of the most haunting spaces in the movies. Its floor is a vast marble expanse, interrupted here and there by an item of furniture that seems dwarfed by the surrounding emptiness. An odd staircase rises from one distant corner. It is not impossible that this vision, in one of the best-known French surrealist films, inspired the designers of the great hall of Xanadu in Citizen Kane .”

The avant-garde filmmaking duo James Sibley Watson Jr. and Melville Webber (in collaboration with e. e. cummings, who contributed to the script) could hardly manage the same scale of production design for their own short adaptation of Poe’s story , which happened to come out the same year.

But the resulting Expressionist take on the material has also been highly acclaimed, and through this YouTube playlist of Poe films , you can experience not just both of them, but also other adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” by idiosyncratic Czech animator Jan Švankmajer and B‑movie powerhouse Roger Corman . Sensitive to Poe’s sensationalist appeal and air of transgressive decadence, Corman ended up directing an eight-film “Poe cycle,” nearly all of which star Vincent Price.

It’s fair to say that no film actor is more closely associated with Poe than Price, a link Tim Burton celebrated in animation at the beginning of his career. Price even played the writer himself in An Evening with Edgar Allan Poe , a special from 1970 in which he recites “The Sphinx,” “The Cask of Amontillado,” “The Pit and the Pendulum,” and “The Tell-Tale Heart.” That last, the most screen-adapted Poe story of them all, also appears on the playlist in various forms: an early D. W. Griffith feature , the directorial debut of Jules Dassin , an animated short narrated by James Mason , a British psychological thriller , and a transposition into modern-day New Orleans . And if you haven’t had enough Poe after watching through all 25 of these films, consider watching the recent, well-received Fall of the House of Usher miniseries on Netflix — an entertainment platform that satisfies much the same appetites Poe’s stories have been feeding for nearly two centuries.

For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and cash rewards that come with prestigious prizes like the Nobel. Cornell historian of science Margaret Rossiter coined the term “The Matilda Effect” to describe sexist bias in the sciences. Rossiter’s work and popular reappraisals like book-turned-film Hidden Figures have inspired other women in academia to search for forgotten female scientists, and to find them, literally, in footnotes .

When systematic discrimination limits opportunities for any group, those who do receive recognition, the exceptions to the rule, must often be truly exceptional to succeed. There has been little doubt, both in her lifetime and in the many decades afterward, that Marie Curie was such a person. Although forced to study science in secret at a clandestine “ Floating University ” in her native Poland—since the universities refused to admit women—Curie (born Marie Salomea Sklodowska in 1867) would achieve such renown in her field that she was awarded not one, but two Nobel Prizes.

Curie and her husband Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Antoine Henri Becquerel, discoverer of radioactivity, in 1903. The second prize, in Chemistry, was hers alone in 1911, “in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element.” Curie was not only the first woman to win a Nobel, but she was also the first person to win twice, and the only person to win in two different sciences.

These are but a handful of achievements in a string of firsts for Curie: denied positions in Poland, she earned a Ph.D. in France, awarded the degree in 1903 by the Sorbonne , the same year she won her first Nobel. “Her examiners,” notes the site Famous Scientists , “were of the view that she had made the greatest contribution to science ever found in a Ph.D. thesis.” Three years later, after Pierre was killed in an accident, Marie was offered his professorship and became the first female professor at the University of Paris.

Curie succeeded not in the absence of, but in spite of the sexist obstacles placed in her path at nearly every stage in her career. After she received her doctorate, the Curies were invited to the Royal Institution in London. Only Pierre was permitted to speak. That same year, the Nobel Committee decided to honor only her husband and Becquerel. The Academy relented when Pierre protested. Curie fell victim to a wave of xenophobia and anti-Semitism (though she was not Jewish) that swept through France in the 1900s, most famously in the so-called “Dreyfus Affair.”

In 1911, the year of her second Nobel, Curie was passed over for membership in the French Academy of Sciences . It would take another 51 years before the first woman, Marguerite Perey, a former doctoral student of Curie, would be elected to that body. That same year, Curie was persecuted relentlessly by the French press, the public, and her scientific rivals after it was revealed that she had had a brief affair with physicist Paul Langevin, one of Pierre Curie’s former students.

But no matter how many men in positions of power wanted to deter Curie, there always seemed to be more influential scientists and politicians who recognized the supreme value of her work and the need to help her continue it. After her second Nobel Prize, her native country finally recognized her with the offer to direct her own laboratory in Warsaw. Curie turned it down to focus on directing the Curie Laboratory in the Radium Institute of the University of Paris, which she founded in 1914, a major achievement and, again, only a small part of her legacy.

Curie is known, of course, foremost for her exceptional scientific work, but also for opening doors for women in science all over the world, though much of that door-opening may only have happened decades after her death in 1934, and much of it hasn’t happened at all yet. Behold the Most Detailed Painting in History: The Ghent Altarpiece
These days, if you want to see a particular painting, you can almost certainly pull it up online in seconds. In more and more cases, the resolution of the image will be so high that you can…

These days, if you want to see a particular painting, you can almost certainly pull it up online in seconds. In more and more cases, the resolution of the image will be so high that you can zoom in and in and in: such a level of detail is unavailable in a museum, of course, but also difficult to access even if you owned the physical artwork in question. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured such luxuriantly digitized paintings as The Night Watch , Girl with a Pearl Earring , and The Garden of Earthly Delights . But there’s at least one celebrated work of Dutch masters whose viewing experience can never truly be replicated on the internet: the Ghent Altarpiece , also called the Adoration of the Mystic Lamb , by Hubert and Jan van Eyck.

After watching the video from The Gaze above, you’ll surely want to take as close as possible a look at the online Ghent Altarpiece , seeking out such highlighted details as the individual hairs on Adam’s beard, the realistically awkward expressions on the faces of the angel chorus, and the identifiable crucifixion scene pinned to a pilgrim’s hat.

But that may only stoke your desire to make a pilgrimage of your own, to Belgium, where you can see the real thing carefully placed in St. Bavo’s Cathedral. In the early fifteenth century, when that institution was called St. John the Baptist’s Church, its warden was the wealthy merchant Jodocus Vijd. Having endowed a new chapel, Vijd also commissioned the van Eyck brothers to create an altarpiece spectacular enough to secure him a spot in the afterlife. The result was one of the earliest masterpieces of oil painting.

Even apart from that designation (to say nothing of its being the most stolen work of art in history ), it has enjoyed an impressive afterlife of its own. Of the many who have traveled to behold it in situ at St. Bavo’s, some have no doubt sought the ecstasy of faith that can only be felt in a true holy place. But others have been thrilled, whether they were aware of it beforehand, by all the attention the artists put into integrating the work with its surroundings. The light within its images, for example, is painted in such a way as to match the light streaming into the cathedral itself. Those who look closely at the gem worn by the foremost singing angel will see a reflection of the very room meant for the altar. By the time their eyes meet the knowing gaze of the sacrificial lamb, they’re all but guaranteed to have a religious experience — though whether its nature is Christian, artistic, or otherwise will depend, as it does with all enduring art, on the individual viewer.

The Aristotelian notion of “man” as a “rational animal” has seen its share of detractors, from the Cynics to Bertrand Russell to nearly the whole of Poststructuralist thought. Leave it up to Oscar Wilde to compress the debate between intellect and passion into a pithy aphorism: “Man is a rational animal who always loses his temper when he is called upon to act in accordance with the dictates of reason.”

We no longer need clever verbal barbs to refute too-optimistic assessments of human behavior. Economics is catching up: we have the language of neuroscience and psychology, which consistently tells us that humans decidedly do not behave rationally very often, but are driven by bias and biology in inexplicable ways . And for over a hundred years now, we’ve known that the clockwork Newtonian view of the physical universe turns out to be a much messier and indeterminate affair, as does the universe of the human mind.

Why, then, has so much economic theory operated with a kind of dogged Aristotelianism, insisting that the units of capitalist society, the workers, managers, investors, consumers, owners, renters, speculators, etc. behave in predictable ways? We have case after case showing that intelligence and critical reasoning often have little to do with success or failure in the market. In such cases, however, one often hears the “madness of crowds” or other clichés invoked as an explanation.

To illustrate, market reporters and business writers have seized upon the story of Isaac Newton’s spectacular rise and fall in the so-called “ South Sea Bubble ” of 1720. We find the story in Benjamin Graham’s 1949 classic The Intelligent Investor , a widely-read book that attributes the irrationality of market systems to an anthropomorphic entity named “Mr. Market.”

Back in the spring of 1720, Sir Isaac Newton owned shares in the South Sea Company, the hottest stock in England. Sensing that the market was getting out of hand, the great physicist muttered that he ‘ could calculate the motions of the heavenly bodies, but not the madness of the people .’ Newton dumped his South Sea shares, pocketing a 100% profit totaling £7,000. But just months later, swept up in the wild enthusiasm of the market, Newton jumped back in at a much higher price — and lost £20,000 (or more than $3 million in [2002–2003’s] money. For the rest of his life, he forbade anyone to speak the words ‘South Sea’ in his presence.

The quotation in bold may or may not have been uttered by Newton, but the events Graham describes did indeed happen. As the Wall Street Journal ’s Jason Zweig relates , University of Minnesota professor Andrew Odlyzko found that “Newton had shifted from a prudent investor with his money spread across several securities to a speculator who had plunged essentially all of his capital into a single stock. The great scientist was chasing hot performance as desperately as a day trader in 1999 or many bitcoin buyers in 2017.” (Odlyzko estimates Newton’s losses at closer to $4 million.) Perhaps it was not a metaphorical “Mr. Market” who cost Newton up to 77% “on his worst purchases,” nor was it widespread “wild enthusiasm”—the mass movement of passion that Enlightenment philosophers so feared.

Perhaps it was Newton himself who, Elena Holodny writes at Business Insider , “let his emotions get the best of him, and got swayed by the irrationality of the crowd.” Maybe it’s more accurate to say Newton succumbed to greed when the bubble expanded. “Throughout history,” Barbara Kollmeyer writes at Market Watch in her interview with author Richard Dale , “people—especially those at the top rung of society—have been greedy and gullible participants in financial bubbles. And a century before the South Sea Bubble , hundreds of wealthy investors lost their shirts in the Dutch Tulip Bulb craze. )

What Makes Notre-Dame Cathedral a Masterpiece of Gothic Architecture
And even upon learning that the most famous of all French cathedrals had been badly damaged rather than completely destroyed, it still felt as if something irreplaceable had been lost. It…

Most of us remember where we were when we heard that Notre-Dame had burned down. And even upon learning that the most famous of all French cathedrals had been badly damaged rather than completely destroyed, it still felt as if something irreplaceable had been lost. It made no difference whether we’d actually been to the place, as I hadn’t at the time. When I did finally make it to Paris four years later, Notre-Dame’s restoration was still underway, and construction walls prevented anyone from seeing much of anything at ground level, let alone entering. Yet crowds still gathered to take pictures in the square outside, apparently finding that proximity to such a civilizational landmark was enough, even in its partially ruined and inaccessible state.

Even without a chance to step inside, experiencing Notre-Dame’s surroundings on the Île de la Cité, as well as the greater urban context of Paris, certainly deepens one’s understanding of the beauty of the cathedral itself. So does visiting other, less widely known examples of the form, as shown by architecture-and-history YouTuber Manuel Bravo in his new video above .

Ordinary tourists in Paris may make a beeline for Notre-Dame, but they’re hardly likely to find their way out to the other medieval cathedrals in Saint-Denis, north of the city, much less all the way out in Laon. Though glorious in their own way, they’re perhaps even more valuable in providing the context of Gothic church architecture in which Notre-Dame made such a mark.

As Bravo explains it, Notre-Dame’s façade represents “the moment in which Gothic façade achieves its most balanced synthesis. The experiments and innovations of Saint-Denis and Laon are absorbed, disciplined, and unified into a composition in which no element appears arbitrary or independent from the whole.” Among its most influential appreciators was Victor Hugo, in whose time much of Paris’ Gothic architecture was being demolished. His romantic evocations of the medieval built environment in Notre-Dame de Paris (in English, The Hunchback of Notre-Dame ) helped save the much deteriorated titular structure, which received an ambitious renovation under Eugène Viollet-le-Duc between 1844 and 1864. That project went beyond period accuracy, adding such non-original details as the gallery of chimeras perched high enough to remain visible during the latest restoration work. Visitors today may notice that the interior doesn’t look exactly like it used to, but some will appreciate that even a monument like Notre-Dame must change with the centuries.

The Amazing Inventions of Ancient Greece: From Plato’s Alarm Clock to Ancient Flamethrowers
“It’s a sunny morning in ancient Greece. Students have started gathering in the Academy, but their famous teacher Plato is nowhere to be seen.” The great philosopher has, it seems…

“It’s a sunny morning in ancient Greece. Students have started gathering in the Academy, but their famous teacher Plato is nowhere to be seen.” The great philosopher has, it seems, “overslept and missed his own lecture.” The sun and the sound of early-rising animals may have failed Plato that day, as the story goes, but never would he let it happen again — at least after he got the mechanism worked out for the first alarm clock in history. Its design involves a series of containers linked by pipes through which water flows at a steady speed all night long. When the water accumulates in the penultimate, sealed vessel, air is pushed out through the flute embedded in its wall, producing something like birdsong.

Plato’s water alarm clock is just one of the pieces of advanced ancient Greek technology explained in the new video above from Lost in Time , a YouTube channel whose look at ancient Roman technology we posted here on Open Culture last year.

Most of the others were invented for less gentle purposes: we have a nasty-looking flamethrower on wheels meant to breach stone fortresses; a “machine gun” able to fire arrows much more rapidly than any bowman; a nine-story-tall proto-tank fully stocked with catapults and soldiers ready to swarm a city; and a gigantic claw, designed by no less a mind than Archimedes, able to grab and overturn invading warships. Yet as formidable as they sound, evidence of just how all these machines of war worked — and just how well they functioned in actual battle — remains scarce.

Much clearer are records of the Diolkos , recently mentioned here when we featured the megaprojects that even ancient Rome couldn’t pull off . Among those endeavors was a canal across the Isthmus of Corinth, which would save ships having to take the long way around the Peloponnesian peninsula. Or rather, it would save them having to be dragged by a couple hundred slaves over the Diolkos , a paved trackway built in the sixth century BC. Using ramps and winches, ships could be shifted onto a wheeled cart that ran in grooves the whole way, making the whole system a precursor of the railroad, or perhaps an inverted ancestor of the ferry still used to transport railway cars across the Strait of Messina . Like the Romans, the Greeks also considered digging a canal, but to do so might have violated the intentions of Zeus, a better excuse not to build infrastructure than some of those we hear in the twenty-first century.

The Psychedelic Animated Video for Kraftwerk’s “Autobahn” (1979)
Ah, yes, “Autobahn.” From the moment the door slams and the ignition starts, prog rockers and pre-new wavers know a journey is afoot.

Ah, yes, “Autobahn.” From the moment the door slams and the ignition starts, prog rockers and pre-new wavers know a journey is afoot. Though Kraftwerk had already made three albums, and the band members still looked like well-meaning, bookish hippies, 1974’s “Autobahn” is considered Year Zero for the denizens of the Electric Café, the four German robots who made human music with machines.

This cel-drawn animation by Roger Mainwood was made in 1979 to promote “Autobahn,” after most of the culture had caught up with the song, and it’s now bopping around pop culture again. By that last year of the ’70s, Omni magazine was a year old, music was sifting through the shockwaves left by Bowie’s Low and Heroes , analog was flirting with digital, and the world was ready to drive on that long, electric highway.

Mainwood’s protagonist is part alien, part human, and he begins looking around in awe in his hip goggles, then sets off for a run straight out of a Muybridge loop, only to wind up floating, flying, sailing and swimming through a landscape indebted to Peter Max, Push Pin Studios, underground comix, and 1930s modernism.

Mainwood had just graduated from London’s Royal College of Art Film and Television School, and was commissioned by John Halas, the Hungarian immigrant who became known as the Father of British Animation, for Kraftwerk’s record label. The label wanted to put out one of the first music Laserdiscs. (Halas, by the way, directed a very UPA-influenced short called “Automania” in 1963 ). According to Mainwood, he still doesn’t know if the band liked the short or even if they watched it.

Mainwood avoided any direct representation of driving or automobiles, much to his credit, which may be why the film holds its fascination. The animator continued in his field, winding up a producer of several classics of British animation, including The Snowman and the chilling When the Wind Blows . As for the meaning of “Autobahn,” we’ll let Mainwood have the last word:

Thinking back to my thought processes at that time, I remember wanting to specifically not have conventional cars in the film. I wanted a sense of a repetitive journey, and alienation, which I took to be what the music was about…hence the solitary futuristic figure, protected by large goggles, moving through and trying to connect with the journey he is taking. The automobile “monsters” are deliberately threatening (I have never been a big fan of cars or motorways!) and when our “hero” tries to make human contact (with different coloured clones of himself) he can never do it. In the end he realises he is making the repetitive and circular journey alone but strides forward purposefully at the end as he did in the beginning. All of which sounds rather pretentious…but I was a young thing in those days!

While the term ‘Friendsgiving’ is new, the tradition has been around for decades – found family and…
A food studies scholar provides some tips for throwing the perfect Friendsgiving gathering.

One of my favorite holiday memories is of a Friendsgiving my husband and I hosted in our tiny two-bedroom house in Atlanta. We didn’t have a dining room. We barely had space to fit a foldout table in the living room. I think one of us sat in an office chair because we didn’t have enough seating. But having our friends gather in our home, no matter how small, made me feel proud.

I planned the menu for weeks, grocery shopped far in advance, and spent days prepping. As a young adult hosting my first holiday, I felt a lot of pressure to get it right. But I also reveled in the freedom to make it what I envisioned. I deviated from traditional family dishes, made impressive magazine cover desserts, and bought linens and dishware to create a tablescape.
While I knew I couldn’t recreate the grandness of my grandma’s family gatherings, I wanted this one to reflect my taste.

My inclination to host a gathering that honors the holiday while making the presentation my own may feel familiar. While many people grow up with certain familial obligations around holidays, entrance into adulthood may grant you some liberties from them, or at least some agency on whether to participate in the production of the event.
If you’re looking to assert that agency, Friendsgiving is the perfect holiday.

As a food studies scholar researching how food traditions are shared and preserved, I am interested in the idea of a holiday that centers friends over kin. I think this is why Friendsgiving, a term that emerged only in the early 2000s even though people had been participating in the concept long before, endures as a sanctified gathering.

Modern American dinner parties still have roots in the Victorian era , when a formal gathering was steeped in etiquette and tradition to demonstrate class and propriety and to create social connections to improve one’s status. And while some form of social connection is still likely the main reason for gatherings today, dinner parties can take on many forms, often with the intention of sharing the labor involved.

In her book “ Eating Together: Food, Friendship, and Inequality ,” sociologist Alice P. Julier interviewed people of various classes, ages, incomes, sexualities, ethnicities and genders about mainly non-kin gatherings around food. Different forms of gathering require different amounts of labor – sometimes paid labor – and the labor between couples and friends is often negotiated. But she found that women often still took on the bulk of the work in the planning, communication or execution of an event.

Within these circumstances, the women often navigated this labor in ways that worked for them or fit their ideas around work, femininity and hospitality. As a young woman, I wanted to emulate the holidays I had experienced, hosted by my mother and grandmother, and was happy to take on the labor involved. However, the beauty of a Friendsgiving is that this labor can be shared and divided in accordance with capacity.

Friends who don’t enjoy cooking can provide drinks or snacks, while those – like me – who spend their days scouring food magazines can try out a new recipe. The key is being honest about the time and money you are able to spend and fit the gathering to the needs of the group.

No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.

When Jorge Luis Borges Co-Wrote a Surreal Sci-Fi Noir Film: Invasión (1969)
“La ciudad es más que la gente.” So declares a character called Don Porfirio in Invasión, the debut feature by Argentine director Hugo Santiago. The line is the film’s most memorable, not…

“ La ciudad es más que la gente. ” So declares a character called Don Porfirio in Invasión , the debut feature by Argentine director Hugo Santiago. The line is the film’s most memorable, not least because of the reversal it pulls on our expectations. Saying that a city is really its people must have been a somewhat banal observation even in 1969, when Invasión came out, but saying that a city is more than its people still sounds contrarian enough to be intriguing. It’s even more compelling coming from Don Porfirio, a mastermind whose intensely abstracted manner and refined literary diction will remind some viewers of no figure so much as Jorge Luis Borges — and as well he might, since Borges co-wrote the script.

Another major contributor to Invasión ’s screenplay was Borges’ longtime friend, occasional collaborator, and junior colleague in letters Adolfo Bioy Casares . Anyone who’s read about their relationship (as detailed in Bioy Casares’ tome of published diaries, simply titled Borges ) knows how deeply entangled it was with the streets of Buenos Aires, where both of them were born and raised. And anyone who knows Buenos Aires will recognize those streets onscreen in this film, despite the title card that calls it Aquilea. Echoing the name of Achilles, it offers a clue as to Borges and Bioy Casares’ classical inspiration for this project, which transposes the city under siege of Homer’s Troy into mid-century Latin America, where a small group of resistance members organize against an arriving army of menacing white-coated invaders.

Though Borges wasn’t exactly one for topicality in his own ficciones , it wouldn’t be wholly unreasonable to make an allegorical reading of the film. It’s set in the year 1957, when Argentina was ruled by Pedro Eugenio Aramburu, one of several dictators in the country’s twentieth-century history. It came out during the dictatorship of Juan Carlos Onganía Carballo. And the 1976 military coup that put Jorge Rafael Videla in power banished it to an official non-existence, seen only in the most underground screenings. It wasn’t until the nineteen-nineties that Invasión was rediscovered and made whole out of partial prints found in France, the country to which Santiago had long since decamped. Now it can be seen on YouTube in one version with optional English and French subtitles, and another, higher resolution version with French subtitles only.

Viewers today may be quick to notice the obvious budgetary limitations, manifest in odd-sounding foley work and theatrical death scenes, but the cinematic vitality of its mixture of film noir, Nouvelle Vague , political thriller, and even science fiction remains undeniable. (With the chases and explosions it manages, it may even partially qualify as an action movie.) So does the atmosphere of the real locations — the streets Borges and Bioy Casares walked, as well as cafés, rail yards, and the climactic football stadium — that constitute its alternately stately and desolate setting. It would be clichéd to say that the city itself becomes a character, but it would also prompt us to ask, which city, Buenos Aires or Aquilea? As with so many other questions about Invasión , there is no one answer.

Given recent history, the prospect of hundreds of young men meeting on Facebook, then traveling from around the country to a central U.S. location might sound like reasonable cause for alarm. Yet a convention fitting that description had nothing to do with political violence but, rather, a celebration and appreciation of the name “Josh” (full disclosure: this writer did not attend). The gathering of the Joshes in April 2021 in Nebraska could not have been more peaceful, including its finishing battle royale, conducted with pool noodles.

The Joshes had no concern for proper pool-noodle-wielding technique, if there is such a thing. But groups of people who gather around the country to stage medieval-style battles in live-action role playing (LARP) games with weapons both real and fake might benefit from pointers.

So, too, might those who choreograph sword fights on stage and screen. Where can serious historical re-creators learn how to wield a real blade in historically accurate combat? One resource can be found at Wiktenauer , a wiki devoted to collecting “all of the primary and secondary source literature that makes up the text of historical European Martial arts (HEMA) research.”

The Fior di Battaglia (“Flower of Battle”) —an Italian fencing manual by Fiore de’i Liberi dating from circa 1404—offers richly- and copiously-illustrated demonstrations of medieval Italian longsword fighting techniques. In the original manuscript, seen here and at The Getty , “the illustrations are inked sketches with gold leafing on the crowns and garters,” notes the Wiktenauer entry. They dominate the text, which “takes the form of descriptive paragraphs set in poor Italian verse, which are nevertheless fairly clear and informative.” So clear, indeed, the brooding young men of Akademia Szermierzy—a Polish group that recreates medieval sword-fighting techniques—can more than convincingly mimic the moves in the video at the top.

Once they get going, after some requisite pre-fight rigmarole, it’s impressive stuff, maybe already familiar to modern fencers and certain members of the Society for Creative Anachronism , the LARP-ing organization of amateurs recreating everything from the Middle Ages and the Renaissance. But for those who think all live-action role-playing is the equivalent of the Battle of the Joshes (or off-brand Nazis running through the streets in homemade armor), the sheer ballet of historical sword-fighting may come as a surprise — and maybe inspire a few more people to pull on the doublet and hose. Mogging is the word of the year – but men have been doing it since Shakespearean times
The male drive to assert dominance stretches back centuries, but what’s striking is how closely today’s posturing mirrors early modern ideals of manhood.
The Collins English Dictionary has selected “mogging” as its 2026 word of the year.

The Collins website says that the word originated with the acronym AMOG – or “alpha male of the group” – which is often associated with bodybuilding forums and, more recently, the toxic culture of incels and the manosphere . But mogging has now entered mainstream language with its meaning slightly repurposed: to describe someone who is outperforming, outshining or upstaging someone.

While the verb is often used in reference to physical looks, it can also be applied in other contexts. Alex Beecroft , managing director of Collins, explained that the selection of mogging demonstrates how “each generation leaves its mark on language”, with the term seeing a 210% increase in usage in 2026.
The male drive to assert dominance stretches back centuries, but what’s striking is how closely today’s posturing mirrors early modern ideals of manhood.

The Oxford English Dictionary contains four historic meanings of the base verb “mog”. The earliest meaning and usage comes as early as 1674, referring to card games “to exchange a card with the dealer”. A later usage means “to move on, depart, decamp”. By the mid-1800s, two new possible meanings emerged : “to walk slowly but steadily” and “to shift (a person, animal etc.) to cause to move on (esp. quickly)”.

What unites these historic meanings is the connection to movement or performance. For many men in the early modern period, the demonstration of superiority through action and movement was a key method to showcase, or perhaps fittingly, “mog” others.

New research by theatre historian Eleanor Rycroft explores this link between movement, gender and social power. Rycroft examines theatrical works by playwrights such as Shakespeare and Ben Jonson alongside historical conduct books and household management guides, revealing just how much cultural capital was attached to a man’s posture and stride.

How-to guides and etiquette books from the time told men and women how to behave, labelling certain traits as respectable and others as improper. In the 1566 English translation of Ortensio Landi’s Delectable Demaundes and Pleasaunt Questions (1566), readers were shown how to outdo other men in wit and conduct. Yet in doing so, the text also exposed the cracks in this ideal, revealing how precarious that masculine status truly was.

In his influential Book of the Courtier (1528), courtier and diplomat Baldassare Castiglione defined this quality as a “certain nonchalance, which shall conceal design and show that what is done and said is done without effort and almost without thought”.
Sprezzatura in Shakespeare and asserting manhood
Castiglione was first translated into English by Sir Thomas Hoby in 1561, and the concept of sprezzatura heavily influenced early modern English culture.

In many early modern plays, characters demonstrate the importance of asserting a mastery of manhood and, with it, upstaging others. While Shakespeare does not use the terms sprezzatura or mogging in any of his works, many men attempt to outperform or outshine other characters to assert or affirm their manly status.

In Much Ado About Nothing (first performed 1598), the “merry war” between protagonists Beatrice and Benedick – a rapid-fire exchange loaded with insults as the two characters shield their true feelings for one another – is often a source of audience amusement and laughter. However, this “skirmish of wit” points to the different expectations on men and women for Benedick across the play text: to match and ideally best Beatrice’s skill in wordplay so as not to emasculate himself.

Beatrice seems to be aware of these dynamics of masculinity, noting that Benedick “gets nothing” from their verbal exchanges – after their last encounter, “four of his five wits went halting off, and now is the whole man governed with one”. These scenes of verbal sparring might be understood as a trial of masculinity, testing Benedick’s skills in rhetoric and wordplay.

A more direct trial is captured in the penultimate scene of Shakespeare’s Henry IV Part 1 (first performed in 1597), which depicts the showdown between Prince Hal, who will eventually ascend to be Henry…
Behold the Gloriously Cheap 1970s Italian Knockoffs Inspired by Star Wars
When the first Star Wars movie came out, in 1977, cinema was the better part of a century old, yet it had never produced a popular-culture phenomenon on such a scale. Covering the resulting…

When the first Star Wars movie came out, in 1977, cinema was the better part of a century old, yet it had never produced a popular-culture phenomenon on such a scale. Covering the resulting explosion of public enthusiasm, the contemporary media initially struggled to find ways to describe the picture itself. “A cowboy movie set in space, that’s Star Wars ,” pronounces the announcer in a TV news clip included in the new Nerdwriter video above . “It’s old-fashioned escapist entertainment, pure and simple.” That may have been all the Italian film industry needed to hear. The “spaghetti westerns” of the previous dozen years had proven that it could profitably master an American genre; surely it could do the same with a similar one.

Among the results, alas, one looks in vain for A Fistful of Dollars , or even a Navajo Joe . Nerdwriter creator Evan Puschak goes over various instances of shameless imitation that characterize the Italian Star Wars clones, but you don’t have to take his word for it; you can, in fact, find some of these movies on YouTube.

Luigi Cozzi’s StarCrash , for example, stars David Hasselhoff, The Spy Who Loved Me Bond girl Caroline Munro, and a Christopher Plummer putting in one of his most grandiosely villainous performances ever; Aldo Lado’s The Humanoid , an even more shameless knock-off, credits its director as “George B. Lewis.” Nor was Italy the only country cashing in on the Star Wars craze: Puschak also shows clips from the Japanese film Message From Space by no less an auteur than Battle Royale director Kinji Fukasaku.

Though many of these second-rate (at best) space operas made money, and some have even retained a certain charm nearly 50 years later, they all come up against the fundamental stinginess of the Cinecittà production model. “The truth is that you can’t imitate Star Wars with a low budget,” says Puschak. Despite all that’s been said about the myriad ways in which it taps into the power of universal myth, “the spectacle, the immersion induced by its groundbreaking special effects, was just as vital to the experience as the story and the characters.” Hard as it may be for today’s young viewers to believe, there was a time when moviegoers weren’t all that discriminating about the realism, or even the plausibility, of the visuals onscreen. After Star Wars , for better or for worse, they’d never overlook visible wires, unsteady lip-sync, or flat matte paintings so easily again.

How Leo Tolstoy Became a Vegetarian and Jumpstarted the Vegetarian & Humanitarian Movements in the 19th…
After a dramatic conversion, Tolstoy rejected his social position, the favored vices of his youth, and the dietary habits […]

Leo Tolstoy is remembered as both a towering pinnacle of Russian literature and a fascinating example of Christian anarchism, a mystical version of which the aristocratic author pioneered in the last quarter century of his life. After a dramatic conversion, Tolstoy rejected his social position, the favored vices of his youth, and the dietary habits of his culture, becoming a vocal proponent of vegetarianism in his ascetic quest for the good life. Thousands of his contemporaries found Tolstoy’s example deeply compelling, and several communes formed around his principles, to his dismay. “To speak of ‘Tolstoyism,’” he wrote, “to seek guidance, to inquire about my solution of questions, is a great and gross error.”

“Still,” writes Kelsey Osgood at The New Yorker , “people insisted on seeking guidance from him,” including a young Mahatma Gandhi, who struck up a lively correspondence with the writer and in 1910 founded a community called “Tolstoy Farm” near Johannesburg.

Though uneasy in the role of movement leader, the author of Anna Karenina invited such treatment by publishing dozens of philosophical and theological works, many of them in opposition to a contrary strain of religious and moral ideas developing in the late nineteenth century. Often called “ muscular Christianity ,” this trend responded to what many Victorians thought of as a crisis of masculinity by emphasizing sports and warrior ideals and railing against the “feminization” of the culture.

Tolstoy might be said to represent a “vegetable Christianity”—seeking harmony with nature and turning away from all forms of violence, including the eating of meat. In “ The First Step ,” an 1891 essay on diet and ethical commitment, he characterized the prevailing religious attitude toward food:

I remember how, with pride at his originality, an Evangelical preacher, who was attacking monastic asceticism, once said to me “Ours is not a Christianity of fasting and privations, but of beefsteaks.” Christianity, or virtue in general—and beefsteaks!

While he confessed himself “not horrified by this association,” it is only because “there is no bad odor, no sound, no monstrosity, to which man cannot become so accustomed that he ceases to remark what would strike a man unaccustomed to it.” The killing and eating of animals, Tolstoy came to believe, is a horror to which—like war and serfdom—his culture had grown far too accustomed. Like many an animal rights activist today, Tolstoy conveyed his horror of meat-eating by describing a slaughterhouse in detail, concluding:

[I]f he be really and seriously seeking to live a good life, the first thing from which he will abstain will always be the use of animal food, because, to say nothing of the excitation of the passions caused by such food, its use is simply immoral, as it involves the performance of an act which is contrary to the moral feeling—killing.

[W]e cannot pretend that we do not know this. We are not ostriches, and cannot believe that if we refuse to look at what we do not wish to see, it will not exist.… [Y]oung, kind, undepraved people—especially women and girls—without knowing how it logically follows, feel that virtue is incompatible with beefsteaks, and, as soon as they wish to be good, give up eating flesh.

The idea of vegetarianism of course preceded Tolstoy by hundreds of years of Hindu and Buddhist practice. And its growing popularity in Europe and America preceded him as well. “Tolstoy became an outspoken vegetarian at the age of 50,” writes Sam Pavlenko , “after meeting the positivist and vegetarian William Frey, who, according to Tolstoy’s son Sergei Lvovich, visited the great writer in the autumn of 1885.” Tolstoy’s dietary stance fit in with what Charlotte Alston describes as an “increasingly organized” international vegetarian movement taking shape in the late nineteenth century.

Like Tolstoy in “The First Step,” proponents of vegetarianism argued not only against cruelty to animals, but also against “the brutalization of those who worked in the meat industry, as butchers, slaughtermen, and even shepherds and drovers.” But vegetarianism was only one part of Tolstoy’s religious philosophy, which also included chastity…
East Germany exiled singer Wolf Biermann. They only made his message louder
Fifty years ago the GDR withdrew the citizenship of the prominent leftwing dissident. It turned him into an international symbol – and cemented his place in history

November 16 marks 50 years since one of the most notorious examples of artistic censorship from the 20th century: the East German government’s stripping the citizenship of dissident singer-songwriter Wolf Biermann .
Far from quashing Biermann’s voice, this act of political exile amplified it, and cemented his place in history, underscored by a new documentary about his life story.

It is a lesson others should have done more to heed. Earlier this year, US billionaire Robert Kraft and other stadium owners banned Macklemore from their venues over pro-Palestinian remarks the singer made during his support slot on Ed Sheeran’s tour.
But in trying to silence the rapper, Kraft and his cohort unintentionally amplified his message .
The story of Biermann can tell us much about how attempts to quash the political expression of musicians have spectacularly backfired.
From East German darling to dissident
Biermann, born in 1936, became a prominent figure within East German left-wing dissident artists and intellectuals in the late 1960s. But he wasn’t always an outsider.

As the West German immigrant son of a Jewish communist killed in Auschwitz, and a mentee of Bertolt Brecht, Biermann was initially the darling of the East German press, and held a candidate membership of the Socialist Unity Party (SED).

When his lyrics became critical of the SED, however, the Stasi (secret police) began a campaign of harassment that escalated over more than a decade. It included performance bans, sabotage, intimidation, round-the-clock surveillance, bugging, reports from more than 200 Stasi informants , and even a veiled death threat.
Yet this persecution amplified Biermann’s voice and gave him an international platform.
The making of an international symbol
Western governments adopted Biermann as a potent symbol in the cultural Cold War. He acquired famous fans, including Joan Baez and Allen Ginsberg.
Numerous organisations awarded him prizes. CBS gave him a record deal, and West Berlin radio stations frequently broadcast his music into East Germany.

These broadcasts made some remarkable converts. Gerulf Pannach, a young songwriter and then Stasi informant , first heard Biermann’s music while working as a border guard. He befriended the singer, renounced the Stasi and began writing his own critical lyrics.
Pannach convinced Christian Kunert, the keyboardist of the beloved rock band Renft , to take an anti-state position in 1974.

Kunert, in turn, introduced writer and social psychologist Jürgen Fuchs – who would go on to become a prominent East German dissident – to Pannach and Biermann. He also converted his Renft band mate Thomas “Monster” Schoppe to the cause.
Closer to home, Biermann’s former stepdaughter, young rock singer and future queen of punk Nina Hagen , introduced her bandmates to Biermann.

Biermann’s inner circle was, for a time, paradoxically protected by their fame as dissidents. Aided by Western media, they flouted state controls in ways average East Germans wouldn’t dare. While the state maintained tight surveillance of Biermann’s circle, they seemed hesitant to arrest them.
But those more loosely associated with Biermann often found themselves caught in the crossfire of multiple Stasi operations to harass and crush dissidents.
This included band members of Renft, who helped Pannach bypass his performance ban and perform Biermann’s songs, and publicly denounced East German border policy.
As a result, members of Renft were repeatedly summoned and questioned by the authorities. Then the band was banned. In September 1975, a local licensing board told Renft they “no longer exist”.
Taboo themes in Pannach’s lyrics were the pretext for the ban , but declassified Stasi documents suggest the state ultimately targeted them as proxies for Biermann.
The regime accidentally elevated a popular East German rock band to anti-state legends.

A further attempt to neutralise Renft through conscription and a tax investigation converted the band’s thus far apolitical founder, Klaus Jentzsch, into a gifted anti-state organiser. With Biermann’s help, he coordinated a transnational multi-media campaign.
When Animals Were Put on Trial in Medieval Europe
Most of us twenty-first-century urbanites have a fairly sentimental view of farm animals, precisely because so many generations have gone by since they’ve been part of our daily lives. (In…

Most of us twenty-first-century urbanites have a fairly sentimental view of farm animals, precisely because so many generations have gone by since they’ve been part of our daily lives. (In South Korea, where I live, the agricultural past remains just within living memory. Perhaps that’s why so many restaurants in Seoul advertise their meat with pictures of the animals it comes from, sometimes dressed in chef’s garb and cheerfully serving up the very dishes they’re about to become.) Things were different in medieval Europe, where animals were both a necessity and a potential danger. History records many instances of serious harm done to humans by horses, bulls, and especially pigs, who seem to have had a particular tendency to turn on children.

Today we would describe the killing of a child as an inhuman act, a term that, in these cases, applies more than figuratively. As for the fate of the violently offending animal, we might imagine that it would be summarily slaughtered, but between the tenth and eighteenth centuries — and especially in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries — it might well have been brought into a courtroom first. Though other creatures had already been subject to legal proceedings for quite some time, “the earliest recorded pig trial took place in Fontenay-aux-Roses, just outside Paris, in 1266,” writes Alexander Lee at History Today . “By the early fifteenth century, however, they had become established practice throughout Normandy and the Île-de-France,” eventually spreading beyond the border to Italy, Germany, and the Low Countries.

“As contemporary students of the Corpus iuris civilis knew, it was a basic principle of Roman law that animals could not be culpable,” Lee adds. “Lacking reason, they were incapable of harboring criminal intent and hence could not be guilty of a crime.” But in un-Roman northern France, “the administration of secular justice was still largely the concern of local seigneurs and was governed predominantly by custom rather than statute.” Thus sustained, animal trials served purposes beyond simple punishment. “For medieval people, the world was created by God in a very logical way, with animals created first, in order to serve and help human beings who were created in the image of God,” says University of Liverpool medieval European monster expert Damian Kempf, quoted in Popular Science by Anne Ewbank . In that worldview, trying and executing a pig could “restore what was broken.”

Unlike domestic animals, according to Sonya Vatomsky at JSTOR Daily , destructive mice, beetles, snails, weevils, and other vermin would be sent to ecclesiastical tribunals. “Despite being unlikely candidates for Catholicism, such creatures were punished with excommunication, not execution,” she writes, since casting them out of God’s domain would allow humans to exterminate them with peace of mind. Vatomsky also quotes economist Peter T. Leeson’s theory that the Catholic Church tried more animals when people got lax about tithing, with the aim of “bolstering citizens’ belief in the validity of Church punishments for tithe evasion.” Putting animals on trial may now strike us as grotesque, but like any alien-seeming episode of history, it also reveals the beliefs on which a past society operated — a mode of analysis that gets one wondering how far the modern United States is from giving them the right to sue.

‘I am wretchedly sad’: Bertha Monash’s letters and women on the first world war home front
The letters Bertha wrote to her father John Monash reveal the agonising struggle of women on the home front.
Bertha Monash – the daughter of battle commander John Monash – was 21 at the outbreak of the first world war, and an eager participant in Australia’s war effort.

Together with tens of thousands of other Australian women, Bertha’s voluntary patriotic work involved knitting socks, sewing shirts, organising fundraising events, making warhorse bandages and assembling comfort parcels to send to the front.

But her most regular patriotic work saw Bertha volunteering for the Red Cross as a civilian orderly in a south Melbourne rest home for returned wounded soldiers. Determined to support the war effort however she could, she wrote to her father, “it’s all a woman can do in these times”.
My new research into the letters Bertha wrote to her father reveals the agonising struggle of women on the home front to remain committed to the war effort and not be overwhelmed by its costs.
Bertha’s patriotic work was built upon an intense emotional battle. With her father, two cousins and many friends at the front, the war represented a time of relentless fear, loneliness and sadness.
When her friend Harry was killed in action, she expressed herself desolately to her father:

I am wretchedly sad […] Oh this wicked wicked war! All for pure greed & these fine young lives must be the cost. We all think we can sympathise sufficiently with those who lose dear ones, but it’s not until the sorrow hits right home that we can possibly realise what it really means.
Such open expressions of pain were, however, rare. For the most part, Bertha worked hard to disguise her emotions:

it wouldn’t benefit anybody to show my discontent, so I always smile & try to appear happy, as I’m one of those who believe happiness is reflected, & that by appearing bright & brave, others round me are influenced. But what shows on the surface is not always felt beneath, & sometimes, I could just cry & cry, for wanting you back so badly!
We see in Bertha’s letters a determination to prioritise her father’s emotional state above her own. Following the Gallipoli landings in April 1915, Bertha wrote,
with all the anxiety & sorrow we are feeling, we know that the time you are experiencing must be far, far worse in every way, & my sympathy goes out to you.

Meeting loss and tribulation with stoicism was seen as women’s duty. Some newspaper articles of the time even stated that women on the home front had a responsibility to be cheerful as this would affect the outcome of the war .
Patriotic work was an excellent outlet for the anxiety and grief Bertha was suppressing.
It meant supporting the war effort – to which she remained dedicated, despite the suffering it caused – while keeping herself too busy to dwell on her sorrows:

I could never be satisfied in being idle, as long as the war lasts […] I fill up every single minute of my time […] [otherwise] I start thinking & brooding & get unhappy at once. Unless I am absolutely tired out with work, I simply can’t sleep, so it’s always best to keep going.
That emotional burden only grew heavier as the war progressed. In an effort to stave off her terrible anxiety, Bertha filled her days more and more with patriotic work, revealing to her father,
[I] just keep on working till I drop, it’s the only way to forget.
Instead of “ waiting and weeping ”, as the saying went, Bertha’s was a case of “waiting and working”, both to contribute and to cope.
Behind the men fighting and dying on the battlefields was an unofficial army of women like Bertha, steadfastly labouring for the war effort while endeavouring to navigate the pain it caused.
By the time the war ended on November 11 1918 , Bertha, now 25, was physically and emotionally depleted.
Rather than greeting the armistice with great excitement, Bertha told her father she felt only “a deep & whole hearted thankfulness that this longed for time has really come”.
The ones who have lost & suffered least are those who get most excited & demonstratively enthusiastic, while there are many sad hearts, – & there will be, till the end!

Buried is an ambitious and intriguing investigation into the activities of the Queensland Native Mounted Police.

First Nations people please be advised this article speaks of racially discriminating moments in history, including the distress and death of First Nations people, and uses potentially distressing terminology.

Buried is an ambitious and intriguing investigation into frontier conflict and the Queensland Native Mounted Police, by three academic writers. It meshes the techniques of archaeology with methodologies of history and, to a lesser extent, anthropology, a process the authors call “historical archaeology”.
Buried: Archaeology, frontier conflict and the Queensland Native Mounted Police – Heather Burke, Lynley A. Wallace and Bryce Barker (Sydney University Press)

The Queensland Native Mounted Police operated from 1849 (prior to Queensland’s separation from New South Wales) until 1929. It employed both white male officers and Aboriginal troopers and was involved in what appears to be colonial Australia’s most ruthless killing machine, resulting in the possible violent deaths of more than 40,000 traditional Aboriginal peoples across the vast colony of Queensland for roughly 80 years.

Cross-disciplinary ways of reading the colonial past and racial conflict are not new. Yet it’s salutary to remember how, at the outset of this new scholarship in the 1960’s, established professional historians were often the most evasive and resistant to this approach.

When, as a young History honours student back in 1965, I began researching colonial frontier struggle (including the Native Mounted Police), it was the concerted work of anthropologists (such as D.J. Mulvaney and Catherine and Ronald Berndt) who provided the best knowledge pathways towards authentic foundational stories. Another anthropologist, W. E. H. Stanner , used the 1968 ABC Boyer Lectures to discuss Australia’s “cult of forgetfulness, practiced on a national scale” when it came to race relations.

Two years later, in 1970, the remarkable anthropologist/administrator, C. D. Rowley produced the historical, nationwide, frontier study, The Destruction of Aboriginal Society – a 400-page work of deep research rarely mentioned today. Published historians of the frontier were not even on the scene at this point. Rowley presented almost 100 critical references to the Native Mounted Police in this work, concluding the force “offered the perfect niche for the sadist”.

Surprisingly, Buried does not reference this central work, even though Rowley referred to a ground exploration at Bedourie in mid-1965 in far south-west Queensland, where eight Aboriginal skeletons and several .32 calibre cartridges were uncovered by an oil survey team.

Buried, however, takes a different archaeological course. It does not examine Native Mounted Police field activities and there is only one page reference to monthly patrols, where collisions and “dispersals” frequently occurred, in a volume of over 300 pages. The authors, (whose work is aided by the research of three others), explain: “Importantly we did not set out to excavate massacre sites” due, apparently, to their elusive nature.

Of course, dispersal sites do not easily announce themselves – that is to be expected. Yet, as recent archaeological work in Western Australia at massacre sites and a prison for Aborigines at both Forrest River and Rottnest Island has shown, such investigations at places of oppression and conflict are not impossible to excavate with some success. These were places where group killing had occurred and where buried bodies were discovered.

In Buried, however, archaeological methodology is applied only to the Queensland Native Mounted Police base camps themselves. Twenty-six camps were surveyed across four years (2016-2020) and eight were excavated. The outcome of thousands of kilometres travelled “by plane, four-wheel drive, quad bike and foot” — not to mention the hard and exacting labour of the digs themselves as well as the substantial funding expended overall, has uncovered a strange, at times disappointing and often mundane bounty.

Centuries before TikTok, this 1579 bestseller gave readers their daily dose of ‘brain rot’
People were hooked on bite-sized life hacks as far back as the 1500s.

First you are shown a new hack to keep wine from spoiling. Then a dog lovingly devoted to its owner. Immediately in tow there are methods to repair broken glass and remove acne, a tip for weight loss, a cake recipe and an astrological reading of your future. But this is not your TikTok or Instagram feed – it’s the contents of a book written nearly four-and-a-half centuries ago.

The English writer Thomas Lupton’s book A Thousand Notable Things was first published in 1579. True to its title, it collected roughly 1,000 short passages ordered randomly, one after another. A seemingly endless stream of household “life hacks” , sensational stories and recipes, it offered answers for just about everything.

Trouble sleeping? Rub your forehead with a mix of white poppy and henbane seeds. If you find yourself bewitched, leave a mercury-filled quill under your pillow. And have you heard the folklore that claims when a robin red breast finds a dead human, they cover its face in moss?

Flitting through eclectic, attention-grabbing short-form content may be the de facto mode of media consumption in the 21st century. But how-to books like A Thousand Notable Things suggest that our ancestors’ preoccupations were not entirely different.

Lupton understood the wide appeal of such easily digestible material. In a revealing preface , he argued that imbibing many passages of “strangeness and variety” was preferable to being “fed too long with one food” by reading entire books.

It proved a winning formula. A Thousand Notable Things enjoyed at least 33 editions, remaining in print from the time Sir Francis Drake was circumnavigating the globe until 1827, the year the first known photograph was taken.
Its success belonged to a burgeoning taste for “books of secrets” , recipe-like instructional texts that taught everything from cosmetics and alchemy to brewing and beekeeping .

Originating in Italy, and published throughout the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, the most popular of these works were continually translated and reprinted throughout Europe. They are now recognised as exerting genuine influence on contemporary scientific culture.

Whether providing alchemical routes to the philosopher’s stone or the recipe for a nutritious stew, books like A Thousand Notable Things thrived on the promise of revealing hidden “secrets” about nature’s inner workings.

Of course, there was no guarantee that everything Lupton suggested would work: whether sleeping on your right side during pregnancy really meant the baby would be female, or that dreaming of eagles flying overhead was necessarily a sign of imminent good fortune. Sheer efficacy alone wasn’t the point. The appeal lay in the wonder, curiosity and amusement that accompanied practical instruction.

If some passages sound absurd or downright dangerous to modern ears (henbane and mercury are highly poisonous), consider that much of Lupton’s material was cutting-edge in its day. His most cited source was Antoine Mizauld , a Parisian medical professor and advisor to French queen Marguerite de Valois.
Even though the vitality of astrology, occult science and ancient medicine waned over the book’s 250-year lifespan, the deeply human concerns it addressed proved enduringly popular.
We know that contemporary readers found Lupton’s eclectic material engaging thanks to their annotations in personal copies, precious few of which remain today.

One survivor from 1612, now in the Glasgow University Library , is marked with small crosses at passages on lameness, heart trouble, ulcers, meat eating and stomach problems. We might speculate that its owner was managing symptoms of dietary issues or gout. So too are gout cures underlined in a copy owned by the 17th-century book collector Frances Wolfreston .

Another reader pencilled crosses next to 38 predominantly medical passages in their 1706 copy , including remedies for head and toothaches, burning eyes, shortness of breath, sore throat and insomnia.

Others were more selective. One copy in the Wellcome Collection is marked only occasionally, including at an anecdote about a German farmer who died with terrible pain in his side. A surgeon cut him open to find large pieces…

Why Jared Diamond’s leadership book on prophets, coaches and kings is flawed but fun
Like Guns, Germs and Steel, this book is ambitious, provocative and imperfect. It’s also difficult to put down.
Jared Diamond is back. Since Guns, Germs and Steel and Collapse were published a generation ago, Diamond has been synonymous with sweeping explanations for complex historical problems.
His latest book, Profits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings: (When) Do Leaders Matter? tackles another ambitious question: when do leaders make a difference?
Diamond assembles examples from politics, business, sport and religion. The result is an accessible, highly readable book.
Review: Profits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings: (When) Do Leaders Matter? – Jared Diamond (Penguin Books)

The book is strongest when it explores leadership as a relationship between individuals and circumstances. Diamond avoids the extremes of either “ great man ” theory (about history being shaped by exceptional individuals) or structural determinism (all about systems, with individual talent or effort playing a lesser role).
Instead, he argues a middle position: leaders do matter, but only under particular conditions.
Another key attraction in this book is its range. Beyond obvious figures, such as British wartime leader Winston Churchill, Diamond introduces readers to an eclectic cast of world leaders.
The Pulitzer Prize-winning author’s ability to weave different examples into a compelling narrative remains one of his greatest strengths.

Historians like me may have some quibbles with Diamond’s approach. But this book is not written for them. Instead, it’s designed to encourage further exploration about history and society – and on that front, it succeeds.

Diamond’s central device is what he calls the “Hamlet test”. Would the same outcome have occurred if a particular leader had never existed? Or, could anyone else in Elizabethan England have written Hamlet?
This is a form of counterfactual history: asking what might have happened under different circumstances.
Counterfactual history isn’t new. Historians have debated its usefulness for decades, with most very cautious of this approach.

While a conventional history can be checked against the evidence, counterfactual histories are impossible to verify. They can be entertaining thought experiments, but historical circumstances contain far too many dependencies to predict the outcome with any real meaning.

The book’s second major weakness is its choice of case studies. Although Diamond successfully highlights several neglected figures, those selected are almost always interesting or unusual. This makes for engaging reading – but it also introduces sample bias.

If we only study exceptional leaders, we should hardly be surprised when they appear to have influenced history. Everyday, mediocre and unremarkable leaders can often tell us most about whether (and when) leadership actually matters.

Diamond’s comparison across politics, religion, business and sport initially seem refreshingly interdisciplinary. However, the book largely treats leadership as a single phenomenon, rather than an industry-specific occupation.

The skills required to manage a multinational corporation differ from those needed to lead a religious movement, govern a nation state, or coach a winning basketball team. Leaders emerge through industry pipelines, succeed according to different criteria and face different constraints.
A religious leader is typically a member of their faith. A chief executive usually spends decades developing industry expertise. A coach usually played their sport.
Success for each is measured in a different way.

This becomes important when Diamond draws on “natural experiments” – studies where two groups are exposed to experimental and control conditions by external factors – to supplement his counterfactual biographies.

Natural experiments are extremely useful when a clearly defined intervention affects one group, but not another. While the studies drawn on by Diamond meet these criteria, their findings are less convincing when applied to the general question of: “do leaders matter?”.

Diamond’s central concept of “making a difference” is vague. His book is an assemblage of circumstances in which leaders are seen to matter if they had an outcome – any outcome – on the course of history.
AI won’t ever make a historically accurate film – but it could help archaeology create better stories
The evidence we have from Troy is incomplete so it’s impossible to create complete historically accurate images from it.

Tech billionaire Elon Musk was up in arms about the recent adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey by director Christopher Nolan, which he heavily criticised for its diverse casting and accused of lacking historical accuracy. Claiming he wanted to show that artificial intelligence could bypass traditional Hollywood studios and deliver a story “historically accurate and true to the art of Homer” at a fraction of the cost, he set his AI Grok Imagine to the task.
On October 23, the platform posted the first seven minutes .

As archaeologists and art historians, we’re not here to review the film for its artistic quality or even its historic accuracy. Instead, we’re here to point out the real problem with the whole endeavour: the promise of historical accuracy failed before the first frame was even rendered.

Contrary to what many of you might assume, as historians we think Musk’s underlying idea – bringing together everything archaeology and history have to offer and using AI as a tool to explore and work with that knowledge – is a genuinely exciting one. We see considerable potential in that approach: a system spanning excavation reports and object databases might reveal patterns no single scholar can hold in mind, such as how ceramic styles spread. The problem is turning that into a film that claims to be historically accurate.
Any attempt to produce a complete, coherent visual narrative would inevitably require AI to go beyond the evidence and invent what we do not know.

Archaeology is inevitably working with a fragmentary record: only a tiny proportion of the past survives in the ground, and only a fraction of that is ever excavated. For instance, open the boxes in the Troy depot and you’ll find spindle whorls and loom weights; however, you won’t find the cloth they made. Everyone at Troy wore textiles but the textiles are gone.

So, like the textiles, everything that cannot be recovered directly from the archaeological record has to be interpreted and explained through hypotheses, however well-founded they may be scientifically. There will always be gaps, uncertainties and competing interpretations.
AI, by design, would inevitably fill these gaps.

Suppose Grok Imagine was given everything the Troy Project holds: a century and a half of excavation, thousands of plans, pottery drawings and photographs, plus the small-finds catalogue. It would generate connections, details and entire scenarios where the historical and archaeological evidence offers no firm answers.
Generative AI is built to produce complete images, even when there are visible gaps. These gaps are often filled with influence from other existing media like film sets, games, paintings.

This is precisely where the problem lies: additions by AI may be plausible, even convincing. Some sceptical reviewers concede that some of those seven minutes pass for real. But convincing is not accurate, and the space between the two is where archaeology lives.

The Odyssey is also an interesting target for accuracy. It’s a poor witness to the past : shaped centuries after the palaces its about fell, it is a palimpsest of Mycenaean memory and iron age worldview – not a snapshot. Odysseus, Helen and Circe are not people archaeology could confirm. However, there is a lot of creative media about the world these characters are believed to have inhabited.

Back to those textiles. A model trained on that record would inherit our ignorance along with our knowledge. It will hallucinate or imagine because it must paint every pixel. It will draw on all the evidence, media and more connected to the themes and history to render a finished cloak, dyed and draped. This rendering will look like a convincingly accurate garment where the honest research answer is “fibre known, colour unknown”.
What survives is not what happened

None of this makes AI useless. A system spanning excavation reports and object databases might reveal patterns no single scholar could see – such as how ceramic styles spread . But every such pattern would first be a pattern in the record, not a picture of the past.
