King Arthur and Ramayana: ancient stories that speak to the moral dilemmas of today’s leaders
Although separated by centuries, these two epics pose dilemmas that separate the morality of the husband from the duty of the leader.

Across the vastly different worlds of ancient India and medieval Britain, two legendary rulers face the exact same impossible choice: sacrifice their love or shatter the moral foundation of their kingdom? It feels strikingly familiar in an era where modern heads of state are still forced to choose between personal loyalty and institutional justice.

The ancient Hindu epic Ramayana (attributed to Valmiki, 750-500BC) tells the story of Rama, prince and eventual king of Ayodhya, and his struggle to rescue his wife Sita after she is abducted by the demon-king Ravana. More than two millennia later, T.H. White’s The Once and Future King (1958) retells the Arthurian legend, his round table and the tragic love triangle between him, his queen, Guenever and the greatest knight of his realm, Lancelot.

Although separated by centuries, these two epics arrive at the same disturbing question: should the king let his queen burn? It is a dilemma that separates the morality of the husband from the duty of the leader.
This article is part of Rethinking the Classics . The stories in this series offer insightful new ways to think about and interpret classic books and artworks. This is the canon – with a twist.

After rescuing Sita and slaying Ravana, Rama initially rejects his wife. However privately certain he is of Sita’s loyalty, as a king, he must reckon with the public morality of his realm. Is a woman who has lived in another man’s captivity fit to be the queen? Furious, Sita demands a test by fire herself. She pleads with the god of fire not to let her burn if she has remained faithful to her husband and walks into the flames unscathed.

Queen Guenever, on the other hand, really is unfaithful to Arthur. As a husband, he has long made peace with her and Lancelot’s relationship, as he loves them both dearly. But when the other knights of Arthur’s court catch them red-handed in adultery, Arthur can no longer look away. As king, he is duty bound to submit to and uphold the public morality of his kingdom. He orders that Guenever be burnt at the stake. What makes the dilemma even greater for both kings is that both are bringers of a moral code to their respective realms.

Arthur dedicates his entire reign to implement his extraordinary political experiment of replacing “might” with “right”. He replaces brute force with a system of justice that binds even him. To this end, he creates his famous Round Table, recruiting knights who use their valour and strength to help the weak, thus transforming power from an instrument of oppression into that of law and order.
Rama too, is a great political innovator. Upon his ascension to the throne, he establishes Ram-Rajya – a utopian state of righteousness and equality before law.
When faced with the impossible choice between breaking moral codes or letting their queens burn, they decide to uphold the morality of their kingdoms at great personal cost.
It is of little consequence that Lancelot rescues Guenever and that fire itself refuses to burn Sita. Both kings must endure terrible suffering for their choice. T.H White’s Arthur laments:

What is right? […] What is wrong? If Lancelot does come to rescue her, he may kill those innocent fellows of the guard, which I have sent to burn her. They have trusted me and I have put them there to keep him off, because it is justice. If he saves her, they will be killed. If they are not killed, she will be burned. But burned to death, […], in horrible burning flames – and she is my much-loved Gwen.
Valmiki’s Rama is forced by the god of fire to justify himself not just to Sita but to the three worlds of the heavens, the earth and the netherworld. He pleads:

Before the three worlds, Sita needed to be purified. She had dwelt for a long period time in Ravana’s inner quarters. Had she not been purified, virtuous people would have told me that I am foolish and driven by desire. I know that Sita is single-mindedly devoted to me and that her mind is only on me. However, I am devoted to the truth.
Ultimately, Arthur’s “right” would have burnt Guenever alive were it not for the “might” of Lancelot. And it is precisely Rama’s Ram-Rajya that leads to the unfair treatment of Sita.
David Jones falls into administration – and its outdated business model explains why
Department stories used to be the place to be seen shopping. Without bold changes in how they’re run, there will no longer be stores like David Jones.
After 188 years, department store David Jones has been put into administration over unpaid rent at some of its 38 Australian and New Zealand stores, as well as long-term financial woes.
The administrators are expected to manage the business, likely closing some unprofitable stores, until a new owner can be found. The future of its more than 5,600 employees is still unclear.
Voluntary administrators McGrathNicol said on Thursday that David Jones’s physical and online stores would keep trading for now, while the business is restructured.
So how did a once prestigious store – which until 2011 boasted “There’s no other store like David Jones” – get to this point?
For months, there has been growing speculation about David Jones’ future. Consumer group Choice recently warned people to use their gift vouchers sooner rather than later.
The combination of poor sales and major brands exiting the store has left the retailer in a precarious position.
Just over a week ago, it was revealed that David Jones had secured A$10 million in emergency funding to buy stock ahead of its crucial pre-Christmas sales.
From one Sydney store to many

As a researcher writing a book on the history of Australia’s department stores, I’ve watched for years as David Jones has struggled to reconcile its glamorous past with an increasingly difficult present.
Welsh-born immigrant David Jones opened his first store, David Jones and Co, in central Sydney in 1838. His goal was to sell
the best and most exclusive goods […] that embrace the everyday wants of mankind.

Working with a London-based buyer, Jones had a direct link with the latest trends and fashions. His business flourished and new departments were added. By the beginning of the 20th century, David Jones had become a department store.
The modern department store model emerged in the 19th century. In addition to operating different departments managed by their own team, this model relied on a mass market.

Large sales enabled stores to acquire an expanding range of goods at discounted rates. These were sold on to consumers at competitive prices, which stimulated mass sales. It was an enormously profitable loop.
The department store’s success also reflected their unique selling proposition, especially around customer service, convenience and exclusivity.
Department stores once prided themselves on their capacity to deliver an elevated level of service to customers that smaller competitors simply could not emulate.

Convenience was another key offering. In a world of small, dispersed stores, shopping could be a tiresome activity. Long before the arrival of shopping centres, department stores housed everything under one roof, providing an easier and more comfortable shopping experience.

A third element was exclusivity. By having exclusive rights to major brands, department stores differentiated themselves from other competitors. Stocking a particular brand also enabled them to position themselves as arbiters of style.
A weakening grip on customer loyalty
But the foundations of the department store’s unique selling proposition have progressively weakened.
From the 1960s, the self-service model of retailing disrupted the department store’s capacity to maintain its historical level of service.

As shoppers served themselves, staffing levels fell. Casual workers replaced full-time staff. While many customers found themselves missing the old levels of service, the trend towards casualisation continued.
The convenience derived from shopping at a department store was also undermined by more recent innovations.

With ample car parks and rows of specialist shops under a single roof, the suburban shopping centre offered even greater convenience to shoppers. Then came online shopping: often cheaper, and even more convenient.

The department store’s exclusive hold on brands was also undermined by many brands deciding to open their own stores. While department stores countered this shift by creating in-store “concessions” – a store within a store – the move seemed to recast department stores as mere clearing houses.

Plagiarism is a kind of theft, but it is also a question of honour
The essay has been virtually obliterated as a form of assessment by the promiscuous use students make of AI. These students are plagiarists.
Any concept that has a history, philosopher Michel Foucault tells us, cannot have a fixed definition.
Plagiarism is a concept with a history, as the subtitle of Roger Kreuz’s Strikingly Similar: Plagiarism and Appropriation from Chaucer to Chatbots reminds us. But it might be close to perennial.
Review: Strikingly Similar: Plagiarism and Appropriation from Chaucer to Chatbots – Roger Kreuz (Cambridge University Press)
As a term describing literary, artistic or intellectual theft, “plagiarism” is derived from one of the epigrams of the ancient Roman poet Martial :

Quintianus, I commend you my little books – that is, however, if I can call them mine when your poet friend recites them. If they complain of harsh enslavement, come forward to claim their freedom and give bail as required. And when he calls himself their owner, say they are mine, discharged from my hand. If you shout this three or four times, you will make the kidnapper ashamed of himself.

The Latin word for “kidnapper” Martial uses is plagiario , which gives us the English term “plagiarism”. Other Roman writers, like Cicero , already familiar with the phenomenon of literary theft, used different terms like furtum (a trick) and surripio (taking something secretly), which cover a range of connotations.

Much ink has been spilled over the question of whether the ways we understand plagiarism are continuous with the classical notions that gave us the term, or whether there has been a rupture (or several).
The most often cited candidate is the Statute of Anne (1710), the first effort by a government anywhere to codify copyright and make it enforceable under the law.

Copyright, the argument goes, emanates from the rumbustious commercial culture of Restoration England. It encourages us to think about literary texts as a form of capital, valuable for their ability to generate income for their creators and their creators’ descendants.

Medieval and early modern attitudes towards appropriation differed from later ones. Witness the massive profusion of Aristotle’s ideas throughout medieval philosophy, for instance, or Shakespeare’s avid lifting of plots from historians Holinshed and Plutarch .
But, equally, who would deny the enormous ingenuity that transformed Aristotelianism into the Summa Theologica of Thomas Aquinas, or the chronicles of Holinshed into King Lear?

There is an important slippage here, the one telegraphed in Kreuz’s subtitle: from plagiarism to appropriation. Renaissance philosopher Francis Bacon railed against the “idols of the theatre”, his name for dogmas derived from ancient philosophy, assented to only for their antiquity. But Bacon was not accusing anyone of passing off Aristotle’s texts as their own.

Inspiration, allusion, influence, all the textual chains that make up a tradition or a culture: these are complex. They take time and patience to disentangle. Yet plagiarism, as literary critic Christopher Ricks is at pains to remind us , is simple: it is an act of dishonesty. And it has been deprecated as such at every stage of literate culture.

The Statute of Anne did not invent a new understanding of plagiarism grounded in copyright, though it was responding to the new salience of literary theft, as the world of print made the practice easier and, seemingly, more widespread. The great threat to authors’ livelihoods at this time was the pirated edition, rather than theft in the sense of fraudulent attribution (although this took place as well).

Far from representing a rupture with the classical tradition, copyright accentuates a dimension of plagiarism present from the start. It adds a literal theft to the moral injury that Martial’s “kidnapping” characterises as a metaphorical theft.

Ricks underscores another facet of Martial’s tenacious metaphor. The plagiarist does not deprive the originator of the work itself, in the way a thief deprives its owner of the stolen object. In Ricks’ words, the plagiarist “hopes to gain honour from a dishonourable practice”.

Mink braves bears to find food, wins award
U.S. Forest Service rangers award the tiny, hungry mammal the 2026 On a Mission Award.

In a break from tradition, the park rangers at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded one of their 2026 Anan Bear Awards to a completely different animal species. For its tenacity in finding food, a small mink ( Neogale vison ) walking around Anan Creek wins the On a Mission Award.

“This little mink was a frequent visitor at the trailhead and the beach in Anan,” the rangers write . “It seemed unconcerned by nearby humans, completely focused on the small crabs and other nibbles it could get ahold of. It was on a mission to eat!”
Meet the bears of Anan Creek
Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the annual Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears (and a lucky mink) spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area also includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises ), hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan , 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears ( Ursus americanus ) and eight brown bears ( Ursus arctos) . Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish and survive the long winter ahead. And also like the fat bears of Katmai , every bear here has their own antics and quirks.

In addition to the bears and mink, numerous other animals call Tongass home . Bald eagles ( Haliaeetus leucocephalus ), the Alexander Archipelago wolf ( Canis lupus ligoni ), and the Sitka black-tailed deer ( Odocoileus hemionus sitkensis ). Importantly, all five of North America’s Pacific salmon species are found within the forest—Chinook salmon ( Oncorhynchus tshawytscha ), coho ( Oncorhynchus kisutch ), pink ( Oncorhynchus gorbuscha ), sockeye ( Oncorhynchus nerka ), and chum ( Oncorhynchus keta ). These five fish species help feed the bears and other mammals and birds who gather here.
The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org ’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

Bald eagle Kaydee spotted back at Shadow’s nest
Turkeys may be getting all of the bird hype this week, but plenty is still going on in the reality show that is the bald eagle ( Haliaeetus leucocephalus ) world.

Just before the sun rose over Big Bear Valley in southern California on Monday morning, Friends of Big Bear Valley’s (FOBBV) cameras picked up the sounds of eagle chortles throughout the area . The sounds continued as the sun came up over the nest that typically belongs to an internet-famous bald eagle dad named Shadow and his late partner, Jackie .

“Eagles vocalize for many different reasons. It could be to communicate territory, a danger warning, mating, food necessity or merely social contact. Their tone is that of a whistling chatter-like chirp, making it easy to differentiate them with their distinctive, high pitched sounds,” FOBBV writes .

The cameras also picked up two unknown soaring eagles, and some ravens scrounging around in the nest. By Monday afternoon, two bald eagles followed each other onto the Lookout Snag, a tree near the nest. While it is not clear which eagles were there, a familiar face was spotted just before sunset. Kaydee, the four-year-old banded female eagle who has been seen near Shadow since August, swooped onto the nest for the first time in several days.

“Kaydee made a welcome visit to the nest. She poked around a bit, before showing us some beautiful closeups, then exiting through the back porch,” FOBBV says. “We can all agree what a welcome sight it was to see Kaydee. It’s a gentle reminder that if we just wait, there are new surprises each and every day.”

We still do not know if Shadow and Kaydee will mate this season. Shadow has recently been spotted with another female eagle nicknamed Big Beautiful Visitor (BBV) by some fans. Any eggs are generally laid in January. Viewers can follow Shadow, Kaydee, or any other eagle couple that takes over the nest via a 24/7 livestream.

Kaydee, formerly known as KD1 , is a banded female bald eagle that has been spotted in Big Bear Valley following the death of Shadow’s former partner, Jackie. She was born in 2022, about 70 miles away from Big Bear Lake in the Prado Basin between Anaheim and Riverside, California. Coincidentally, her parents are also named Lucky and Ricky like Jackie’s parents, but they are a different eagle pair.

Kaydee was banded as part of the Orange County Water District’s work to track the eagles born in the area. These bands help biologists track and monitor the birds over time. Kaydee currently has a black spot on her head, but that may not be permanent. It’s possible that not all of her white feathers have come in or it could be tree sap or dirt. She also has two small bands on her legs. One is a small metal band, while the other is a lavender band with “KD1” on it.
Kaydee is almost five years old, so she is just about ready to mate.

Jackie and Shadow became official in 2018. FOBBV’s nest cameras documented Jackie and Shadow’s life together, offering us a direct look into the brutality and beauty of nature. They successfully raised chicks in 2019 (Cookie and Simba) and 2022 (Spirit). The pair’s eggs failed to hatch in 2023 and 2024. In 2025, Jackie laid three eggs that all hatched in early March. However, a strong snowstorm dumped up to two feet of snow and battered the nest with strong wind and only two of the chicks ( Sunny and Gizmo ) survived.

In January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers, who died from cancer in February.

On July 17, Jackie was found injured on the ground near Dana Point Park, California. Cell phone video from a witness confirmed that she had an altercation with two other subadult eagles. She successfully fended off the other eagles by turning over and using her talons, but could not fly far away.

She was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center for care, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia . Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center said that she was in unstable condition on August 9 .

Clam discovered living inside of a sea urchin’s throat
The deep-sea duo has an unusual arrangement.

The fact that a new clam species ( Vaticinaria gulicola ) was discovered where the sun does not shine may be the least interesting thing about this bivalve. V. gulicola lives inside of a deep-sea urchin . The clam appears to have made a little home for itself inside the urchin’s oesophagus, the tube that runs through the center of the urchin’s body and into the intestine. A study recently published in the journal ZooKeys details this highly unusual partnership.

An international team of scientists conducting a deep-sea survey of the Great Australian Bight discovered the clam. The survey studied the seafloor at depths of 656 to 16,404 feet deep and uncovered 66,721 invertebrates representing 1,267 species. About a third of these species are believed to be new to science—including this quirky clam.

They found V. gulicola along the abyssal seafloor at depths of about 13,000 to 16,400 feet. At this depth, sunlight cannot penetrate the water column . During these deep trawls, the team found clams equipped with threads for attaching to a host, but did not see any hosts. Additional searching revealed more clams lodged inside thin, slippery tubes. They analyzed the DNA of these tubes and discovered that they were the oesophagus of the urchin Carnarechinus clypeatus.

“We were absolutely stunned to find this bivalve living inside the throat of a deepwater sea urchin,” Paul Valentich-Scott , a study co-author and marine malacologist at the Santa Barbara Museum of Natural History, said in a statement . “A Russian scientist [Alexander Mironov] originally thought these clams were being eaten by the sea urchin, but we later determined that it was actually living inside the oesophagus.”

Mironov had noticed clams inside the urchin’s gut as far back as the 1970s and 1990s. The team also found related clams living inside of a specimen of the same urchin that was collected during the Challenger Expedition (1872 to 1876), where they had gone unnoticed for over a century.

Most clam species that live with other animals cling to the outside of their host. Endocommensalism , or living inside of the host, is more rare. The new clam’s genus Vaticinaria is only the second clam genus of its superfamily known to live this way.
“Endocommensalism is extremely rare in galeommatids and all bivalves,” Valentich-Scott added. “Most commensal bivalves attach to the outside of their host. This new species lives inside its throat.”

This new clam shows no obvious adaptations to life inside a host. It is about 0.74 inches long, which is large for its group, and has a shell that closes fully. The species name gulicola comes from the Latin word for “throat” and “inhabitant.” Much about the clam remains unknown and will require further study.

“We know very little about this new species or its sea urchin host,” said Valentich-Scott. “The host sea urchin has never been collected intact, so we really don’t even know what it looks like. We have no idea how this bivalve can live inside the throat of the urchin, or what it eats.”

The team suspects that the clams can feed off the nutrient-rich sediment that the urchin eats, but this hasn’t been studied. Further deep-sea sampling should reveal more about this clam and other unusual creatures of the deep-sea.

Ancient Egyptian curse found in 3,400-year-old trash heap
An incantation against the snake god Apophis was used against foes, poisons, and bad weather.

A well-known ancient Egyptian curse is not only older than historians thought—the curse that called upon the sun god’s wrath upon one’s enemies was much more commonly employed than experts assumed. However, the new evidence concerning the “Apophis ritual” wasn’t recently discovered in an excavated spellbook. According to a study published in the Journal of the Egyptian Language and Antiquities , archaeologists learned the latest details from postage stamp-sized papyrus fragments left in 3,400-year-old trash piles.

Prior to finding the 40 charred remnants, the only documentation of the Apophis ritual was a ritual manual dating back to the late fourth century BCE. Egyptian priests originally designed the spell to aid the sun god Ra against Apophis, his eternal foe and the snake god of chaos, fire, and darkness. Others later adapted the ritual to curse enemies of the pharaoh and counter problems associated with the serpent like inclement weather and poisons. But although researchers initially assumed the Apophis ritual was reserved for religious leaders, the papyrus fragments retrieved from temple ruins at Thebes have dramatically expanded its audience.

“They show that the ritual was much older than the one surviving copy from the fourth century [BCE] might suggest,” Fredrik Hagen , an Egyptologist at the University of Copenhagen and study co-author, said in a statement . “Already 1,000 years earlier, during what we call the New Kingdom, it was an integrated part of Egyptian culture.”

While additional analysis of the fragments revealed that such rituals were widespread in ancient Egypt, Hagen explained that additional contextual references to the Apophis incantation indicate it was a “common feature” in daily life.

“We know that literate people, including those who were not priests, had access to magical rituals and functioned as magicians and healers,” he said. “It is clear that people approached scribes for help in performing magic, both for protection and for attacking others.”

The existence of the remnants are surprising in their own right, given what the ritual required. Their charring is only part of the necessary curse protocols—prior to burning the written spells, practitioners stepped on the papyrus, stabbed it with a knife, and even spit on it.

“For the ritual to be successful, the materials had to be destroyed by fire, so we are extremely fortunate to have found any of them in a condition that still allows them to be recognized and studied,” said Hagen.

Wild turkey feathers can change color
All it takes is a little genetic mutation.

As most people in the United States know—especially around this time of the year— wild turkeys ( Meleagris gallopavo ) are large, broadly dark-colored birds with iridescent feathers and bald necks and heads. But not all turkeys are alike. Some of these boisterous birds have color phases , or non-traditional arrangements in their feathers, or plumage.

“Color phases are caused by genetic mutations that affect production of melanin, the pigment that causes the dark coloration in a wild turkey’s plumage,” Michael Chamberlain , National Wild Turkey Federation Endowed Chair, tells Popular Science .

There are four general turkey color phases : smokey gray, erythristic, melanistic, and leucistic. Smokey gray turkeys don’t have brown pigments in their plumage, and can look white from a distance . Leucistic turkeys have white feathers because they lack melanin production in their plumage, but their heads, beards , and legs appear more normal and red.

Melanistic birds are essentially the opposite. The genetic mutation causes an overproduction of melanin, so the turkey is darker-colored and almost totally black. Erythristic turkeys have an overproduction of carotenoids (types of pigments behind orange, yellow, and red colors) that prevent the production of melanin and also make their feathers more reddish.

How common these different color variations are is still a question, because experts have just started to track their occurrences. Leucistic birds appear to be present throughout North America, while melanistic birds—the completely black ones—seem to be more rare.

“It’s unknown how odd plumage affects survival or reproduction, but it’s logical to assume that lighter colored birds and particularly leucistic and smoke phase birds would be obvious to predators,” explains Chamberlain, who is also known as the Wild Turkey Doc . However, “the relationship between odd plumage and survival or reproduction has never been documented in the literature.”

But if you come across a picture of a gorgeously-colored bird that looks like a turkey-shaped peacock, chances are that you’re looking at the only other turkey species: the ocellated turkey ( Meleagris ocellata ). These fantastical looking animals are the wild turkey’s tropical cousin and only exist in the Yucatán Peninsula, and were domesticated by the ancient Maya .
Feel free to talk turkey with these and other fun turkey facts this Thanksgiving .

What are those weird things on a turkey’s beak?
It's called a snood and it's actually quite sexy—at least for female turkeys. The post What are those weird things on a turkey’s beak?

When a tom turkey is relaxed, the fleshy growth above his beak is short and stubby, like a little unicorn horn. But when he struts to attract mates or establish dominance, blood rushes into the growth, known as the “snood.” The snood then swells and lengthens until it drapes over the turkey’s beak like a long pink earring. Turkey hens have snoods too, but theirs are smaller. So why would a male bird grow something that looks so impractical?

Dr. Richard Buchholz , a professor of biology at the University of Mississippi, is the best person to ask. Features of bird anatomy that seem more decorative than useful, which biologists call “ornaments,” have long fascinated Buchholz. For his master’s degree, Buchholz studied the yellow-knobbed curassow, a South American bird with a bright yellow knob on its bill and a crest of curly feathers.
[ Related: How did Thanksgiving turkeys get so darn big? ]

When it came time to choose a PhD topic, his advisor suggested a more common bird: the wild turkey. Buchholz wasn’t keen. “I don’t wanna be the turkey guy,” he told his advisor. Still, he gave it a try. More than three decades later, he’s still studying them. And his research has shown that turkey snoods have at least two functions: seduction and status.
The fleshy growth on a turkey’s beak is actually quite attractive

It turns out that snoods are tools of seduction. In a 1995 study by Buchholz that used both live male turkeys and decoys, females showed a distinct preference for males with longer snoods and wider skullcaps . (The skullcap is the smooth patch of bare skin on top of a tom’s head.)

This was surprising because male turkeys have several ornaments, including a beard that grows from their breast area, iridescent feathers, and a tail fan similar to that of a peacock. Yet females seem to care more about the snood and skullcap.
Lady turkeys are discerning birds. In some trials, females were choosing between two males whose snoods differed by “just a couple millimeters,” Buchholz says—and they still went for the longer one.

He found a likely reason for this preference in male turkeys’ guts. Males with longer snoods had fewer coccidia in their digestive tract. Coccidia are single-celled parasites that damage the lining of the intestine and can be fatal in young animals.

Buchholz thinks that snoods are indicators of health, allowing females to assess a male’s quality as a mate just by looking at them. Oldest known quasar formed 630 million years after the big bang
The Euclid space telescope broke a record it previously set in July.

Only four months after setting its own record , the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Euclid space telescope has outdone itself yet again. In a study published today in the journal Astronomy and Astrophysics , ESA researchers announce the discovery of the most distant—and therefore oldest— quasar ever observed. The object now classified as J1504+6252 formed just 630 million years after the big bang , making it 40 million years older than the quasar Euclid spotted in July. Euclid’s new image is equivalent to viewing J1504+6252 as it existed about 13.1 billion years ago, when the universe was only five percent its current age.

A quasar is the result of a galactic core’s supermassive black hole inhaling cosmic gas and dust while simultaneously spewing tremendous amounts of energy. During this comparatively brief phase in a galaxy’s lifecycle, the nucleus can actually shine brighter than the entire system itself. But even such a luminous object like quasar J1504+6252 can be hard to spot when it is located deep within space-time.

However, Euclid excels at finding these and other elusive objects . The ESA launched its space telescope in 2023 to examine the mysterious realm of dark matter and dark energy . Despite estimates that these forces account for about 95 percent of the universe, astronomers still know very little about them. Identifying subjects like quasars allows researchers invaluable opportunities to learn more about dark matter and dark energy, as well as their roles in the early, formative eons of the cosmos.

J1504+6252 is so young and gargantuan that it’s confounding astronomers. Based on their initial assessments, it’s unclear how a quasar with a mass equivalent to about 360 million suns even formed so early in cosmic history.

It also has the largest redshift on record. Redshifting occurs when light waves stretch towards the infrared spectrum as they travel through the universe. The greater the redshift, the older its source is. In barely 1.5 years, Euclid has flagged 31 quasars, including 12 beyond a redshift of 7.

J1504+6252 is the first quasar to possess a redshift beyond 8. Despite its age, J1504+6252 is devouring material at a comparatively slow pace. This implies it attained its size during unprecedentedly fast growth spurts early in its life—a feature that challenges existing models of black hole formation.

Astronomers have nicknamed the quasar Dún Aonghasa to honor its age and location. The actual Dún Aonghasa is a prehistoric clifftop fort in Ireland overlooking the Atlantic Ocean. Like the ancient structure itself, J1504+6252 is situated at the edge of the visible cosmos. That said, astronomers expect Euclid to find multiple more quasars beyond redshift 8 in the years to come.

The machines stand just over three feet tall, and roll autonomously along preprogrammed routes through the station’s underground concourses between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m. Once full, they trundle back to the station’s garbage collection area on their own.

An accompanying illustration of Shinjukuma , the station’s bear mascot, shows passengers which bins are for general trash and which are for plastic bottles. It’s all very Japanese.

JR East officials are hoping these bins on wheels will help relieve some of the burden on garbage collectors who struggle to keep up with trash generated by the millions of people passing through every day. Houston , Baltimore , Pittsburgh , and Oakland are among the many cities in the United States already putting robot cleaners to work scrubbing and mopping airport floors.

Making these robots seem cute isn’t just for attracting selfies. It’s also a self-defense strategy. Humans have a mixed track record when it comes to sharing space with robots. In 2024, the New York Police Department retired a 400-pound, egg-shaped surveillance robot from patrolling subway lines after facing pushback from privacy activists and concerned citizens, some of whom felt uncomfortable near the lifeless, imposing monitor. Years earlier, a friendly hitchhiking robot called HitchBot made it about two weeks into its trip across the United States when it was found vandalized and beheaded in Philadelphia .

The invention’s speed comes from a novel compound steam engine that allows highly pressurized air to expand throughout numerous chambers not once but twice. This air first flows through the robot’s valves, then recirculates through wider, lower-pressure sections in its legs. The team’s creation maintained its efficiency and speed in multiple environments, including gravel, grass, mulch, and concrete. It even handles sandy surfaces and can work underwater.

“The key challenge was to implement a time-tested solution (the compound steam engine) in a soft running robot that can be printed in a single piece out of a single material,” explained Zhai. “We see this as a step towards complex and powerful robots that can be printed on the desktop using inexpensive materials.”

Their current version of the robot is still limited by its power source, and the tethered hose that delivers the pressurized. That said, they plan to design future variants requiring less air. This would hypothetically allow them to attach a portable power source like a compressed air cartridge, as well as enable more complex controls and maneuvering.

These prototypes are more than oddball experiments, too. Without any onboard electronics, similar robots could have an advantage while operating in highly irradiated environments, dangerous conditions, and even outer space.
Wasps recognize faces—and it keeps them from killing each other
The insects use a special group of brain cells for facial recognition.

Wasps can recognize faces. But don’t worry. They may not be telling human faces apart the way that cows can . The stingy insects tell their nestmates apart by recognizing different color patterns on their faces, so they know the difference between mama wasp and papa wasp or a friend versus a foe. A study published today in the journal Cell details how they use specialized brain cells to pull this off.

“These wasps that perform facial recognition have neurons similar to those in our own brains that are doing very similar things,” Christopher Jernigan , a study co-author and neuroethologist at Wake Forest University in North Carolina, said in a statement . “These groups of neurons are all firing, and each neuron has a slightly different preference for one face or another.”

The team studied the northern paper wasp ( Polistes fuscates ). These roughly half-inch long bugs are found from southern parts of Canada through Florida and Texas. Their name comes from the paper-like nests made of hexagonal cells that they often construct under building eaves and on the ceilings of porches. Paper wasps also have silk that shine under UV light, giving these nests a secretive fluorescent glow.

Female northern paper wasps use facial recognition to remember another wasp’s place in the nest’s hierarchy . Once this hierarchy is established, recognizing faces helps maintain social order, without a constant battle for dominance.

Wasps may be using a method for facial recognition that’s similar to how primates (including humans) tell faces apart, even though both methods evolved independently. Even with brains about the size of a single rice grain, Jernigan said that wasps are “able to do this incredibly complex task of remembering and recalling individuals.” They do this by spotting the differences between the color patterns on one wasp face versus another, with the help of specialized neurons.

Wasps can also perform something called social eavesdropping . When two wasps fight to establish dominance in the nest hierarchy, one wasps can watch the two unknown wasps quarrel. Once that spectator wasp sees one of them, it will know whether or not it needs to fight for dominance.

“They will treat the winner of that fight independently in a third interaction differently than they would the loser,” Jernigan explained. “Despite having these small brains and relatively simple vision, they have these really complex social lives that revolve around this specialized ability to recognize each other.”
According to the team, understanding this facial recognition could help us understand human brain systems as well.

“This system, hopefully, holds the potential to help us understand our own brains as we study the circuit connections and the role of experience in giving rise to identity recognition,” Jernigan said. “It’s really remarkable that they have this kind of really human-like or primate-like ability that you wouldn’t typically expect for an insect. And I think it’s almost unbelievable that they have some of the similar kind of neural computations for doing a similar task as we do. It takes a tremendous amount of neural connections to do something similar in a primate.”

How Humans Are Helping Golden Jackals Conquer Europe
By unintentionally protecting jackals from larger predators, people are aiding in the expansion of a remarkably adaptable canid.

The golden jackal isn’t always the color of gold; its coat ranges from creamy beige to a rusty brown with black striations. It is, however, living in a golden age—thanks in part to the ubiquity of humans.

Native to Eurasia, golden jackals in Europe have historically been confined to the southeastern tips of the continent, mainly the Balkan countries. Over the past century, though, Canis aureus has slowly started colonizing new areas of Europe, with a steep acceleration over the past two decades. Golden jackals are expanding their range, reaching as far west as Spain and as far north as the Arctic. Scientists say the expansion represents one of the most dramatic changes in the range of a species in today’s world. New research, including genetic analysis, is revealing what’s driving the jackal’s spread and the part people play in the animal’s success.

One factor that has contributed to golden jackals’ expansion is anthropogenic climate change, which has decreased snow cover and probably revealed more suitable canid habitat. The habitat fragmentation that comes with farming and urbanization is another likely influence, since golden jackals prefer a patchy environment. The species also adapts readily to human-altered landscapes and can disperse hundreds of kilometers in search of new habitat. And, not least of all, researchers suspect that humans cleared the way for them by extirpating wolves across much of Europe in the 18th and 19th centuries.
“The fact that they did not have any competitor made it easier,” says Jennifer Hatlauf, a wildlife ecologist who manages the Golden Jackal Project in Austria .

Today, researchers estimate that around 150,000 golden jackals inhabit 23 European countries, populating a range that’s 46 percent bigger than it was in 2016 . But wolf populations are growing, too; Europe hosts roughly 23,000 wolves today, compared to an estimated 12,000 as recently as 2012.

To better understand how humans, a growing wolf population, and the expanding golden jackal population interact, Hatlauf and a large team of researchers collected and analyzed data on the presence of golden jackals from all around Europe between 2001 and 2017. The information mainly came from playback surveys: Researchers played a jackal call from a speaker and listened for the response of real jackals, identifying the presence of individuals. The team then paired this data with data on wolf and human presence.

Their recently published analysis shows that the presence of wolves is the main factor limiting the expansion of jackals—a result that strengthens the hypothesis that the decline of wolves in past centuries likely opened the door to the jackal expansion. The team also found that human settlements create a shield that deters wolves and offers a refuge for jackals.

The “human shield” hypothesis isn’t new. Researchers have long known that prey or smaller predators take advantage of human presence to escape large predators. For example, some bear mothers with cubs find refuge from adult male bears by moving close to human settlements, especially during the mating season, when the males would try to kill offspring. Prey animals, such as wild turkeys, also seem to find safety near human-inhabited areas.

In places where wolves are absent, the data shows, jackals tend to stay away from humans, likely to avoid deadly encounters with our species. But where wolves are rooted in the landscape, jackals remain within humans’ proximity. “The jackal is three times smaller, so there’s simply no chance for a jackal if you have a core area of wolf populations,” says Hatlauf. That same life strategy is probably going to apply in other areas that jackals will reach in the future as they expand even farther, she adds.

“The work is excellent,” says Luigi Boitani, chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Large Carnivore Initiative for Europe, who wasn’t involved in the research. The idea that the wolf’s extirpation played a role in the jackal’s expansion and that human presence shapes the relationship between the two species has long crossed scientists’ minds, Boitani says, but no one was able to prove it with actual data until now.
Hummingbirds often use their bills for fighting, but some species’ outsized appendages are equally useful in finding food.

Despite their diminutive size and zany colors, many hummingbird species are downright ferocious when they encounter one another at a food source. That’s likely because of the demands of their lightning-fast metabolisms. In flight, a hummingbird may flap its wings 62 times per second, and some species have heart rates that top out at over 1,200 beats per minute. Hummingbirds’ small bodies have a high surface-area-to-volume ratio and they lack insulating down, so they also lose heat quickly. They must consume two to three times’ their body weight per day in high-sugar flower nectar.

Given that flowers bloom only for a short while, that makes each meal more like a high-stakes operation than a companionable feast. Even at feeders with abundant nectar supplied by humans, hummers of both sexes often joust—chasing and stabbing at each other with long, sharp bills, among other aggressive tactics and displays. The shining sunbeam ( Aglaeactis cupripennis )—on the left in this image by conservation biologist and photographer Maxime Aliaga—is no exception. Researchers tracking the species in the Andes Mountains of Peru and Ecuador found that it regularly defended flowers within its territory from hummingbirds of both its own and other species, including sword-billed hummingbirds ( Ensifera ensifera ) like the one pictured on the right.

Sword-billed hummingbirds, for their part, aren’t slouches. They wield their beaks—which are longer than their bodies—exactly as their name suggests. But the primary purpose of the species’ outsized appendage may be to get food, rather than defend it.

Scientists believe that the sword-billed hummingbird’s unique morphology evolved in tandem with long-tubed passionflowers. That subgroup within the Passiflora genus, called Tacsonia , contains more than 60 species with flower nectar tubes 6 to 14 centimeters (2 to 5 inches) long. That’s a close match with the sword-billed hummingbird’s beak, which can reach up to 11 centimeters (4 inches). The birds and flowers also overlap in range, with 37 Tacsonia species pollinated exclusively by sword-billed hummingbirds. They are the only hummingbird species with the correct proportions to deposit pollen grains on the stigmas of these dangling, downward-opening flowers, poking into them from below to drink nectar.

In intact cloud forests, this highly specialized mutualism is a boon to both plants and pollinators. But in fragmented forests, it becomes a vulnerability: Research suggests that sword-billed hummingbirds don’t frequent deforested areas. Scientists speculate that may be partly because the long-tubed passionflowers that they observed in these zones often lose their nectar to “robber” species like bees, which drill into the flowers from the side, skipping pollination and draining the hummingbirds’ food source. With the connection to the passionflowers’ primary pollinator severed, at least four species of the plant have likely gone locally extinct in landscapes fragmented by forest-clearing. Those passionflower species that have evolved shorter nectar tubes, though, are more resilient. They can rely on other hummingbirds and bats for pollination, even when the habitat becomes less suitable for sword-billed hummingbirds.
Searching for a Bird Lost to Science
A researcher grapples with the value of his efforts to document a secretive species in Papua New Guinea.

Our luck turns during a smoke break. It is hot and dry for Papua New Guinea, and we are resting on the shoulder of a gravel road, bags and cardboard biscuit boxes scattered on limestone bedrock. The boxes, in rough shape from travel, are printed with a cartoon of a man named Henry Wopa, whose bulging muscles advertise that his eponymous product is enriched with vitamins and protein. This has made the brand a staple in parts of Melanesia where deforestation has hurt food security, including here on New Britain, an island four times the size of Puerto Rico that accounts for a majority of PNG’s raw log exports . Still, the biscuits are bland and difficult to swallow without coffee, which is running out. I am hungry, but not hungry enough for more Wopa. Instead, as my colleagues squat in broken shade rolling cigarettes, I scan the canopy, ragged from decades of selective logging.

There are 10 of us in total: six Sengseng-speaking Arawe and four outsiders, including me—an evolutionary biologist from Montana—gathered to search for a poorly known bird called the New Britain bronzewing ( Henicophaps foersteri ). This large, glimmering pigeon, endemic to its namesake island, was last confirmed alive through a specimen collected by ornithologist-turned-author Jared Diamond in 1972. The bronzewing has been seen occasionally in the years since but was never again collected and has never been photographed. This is cause for some concern. As Joe Wood, an expedition member who manages international conservation programs for the Toledo Zoo & Aquarium in Ohio, put it: “It would be nice to check in on it.”

But how, exactly, do you check in on a handful of shy birds in tens of thousands of square kilometers of forest? By asking around, to start. Jason Gregg, a graduate student in my lab at Montana State University and the expedition’s leader, has spent years thinking about how to incorporate local ecological knowledge into biodiversity surveys, along with spending many hours interviewing our Arawe crew members. About half say they’re familiar with the species—known locally as kau—but communicating across gulfs of language and culture about a bird of which there are no photographs is challenging. The night before, Thomas Sunamli, who is letting us stay on his land, explained that the bronzewing is common in disturbed habitat and feeds on the red, pine-cone-like flowers of a plant called shampoo ginger ( Zingiber zerumbet ). This contradicted our own limited understanding of the bird’s diet and need for old growth.

“It’s hard to imagine what they could be getting out of [those flowers],” Wood had said, frowning as he prodded a clump of shampoo ginger at the edge of camp. Since nectar is rarely an important part of a pigeon’s diet, I was inclined to agree.

Western methods for locating the bird have so far proven ineffective. A week of constant observation, camera trapping, and attempts to attract the bird by playing the call of its closest relative through a makeshift speaker we’ve dubbed the Bronzewing Blaster 5000 have amounted to nothing. Nor is history in our favor. In the late 1950s, zoologists Thomas and Margaret Gilliard spent three months within a few dozen kilometers of our camp, collecting some 500 specimens representing 98 species for the American Museum of Natural History. Among their findings were two species new to science. Absent was a single bronzewing. To our knowledge, no ornithologists have visited here since.

The Gilliard expedition was one of the final episodes of a heyday of scientific exploration in Melanesia that had a profound influence on the fields of ecology and evolution, arguably birthing theories such as island biogeography . This era ended in 1975, when Papua New Guinea gained independence and ended colonial license to travel freely in a region that now has near-complete Indigenous land tenure. In the interim, logging corporations felled the last grand forests of Borneo and Sumatra and began working their way through New Britain. Today, cost, logistics, lack of infrastructure, and sporadic violent crime discourage many foreign biologists from studying how the logging is affecting the island’s biodiversity.
